translation: Consider with thyself how man, and by what part of his, is joined unto God, and how that part of man is affected, when it is said to be diffused. There is nothing more wretched than that soul, which in a kind of circuit compasseth all things, searching (as he saith) even the very depths of the earth; and by all signs and conjectures prying into the very thoughts of other men's souls; and yet of this, is not sensible, that it is sufficient for a man to apply himself wholly, and to confine all his thoughts and cares to the tendance of that spirit which is within him, and truly and really to serve him. His service doth consist in this, that a man keep himself pure from all violent passion and evil affection, from all rashness and vanity, and from all manner of discontent, either in regard of the gods or men. For indeed whatsoever proceeds from the gods, deserves respect for their worth and excellency; and whatsoever proceeds from men, as they are our kinsmen, should by us be entertained, with love, always; sometimes, as proceeding from their ignorance, of that which is truly good and bad, (a blindness no less, than that by which we are not able to discern between white and black:) with a kind of pity and compassion also.
book_theme: mortality and the discipline of the present moment

meaning_fields.situations: 1) You're scrolling through social media obsessing over what others think of you, checking their posts repeatedly to interpret their feelings toward you. 2) At work, you spend the whole meeting analyzing your boss's tone and facial expressions, trying to read their mind instead of focusing on the task. 3) You're stuck in a cycle of worrying about everyone else's opinions, judgments, and what they might be saying about you behind closed doors. 4) You're so caught up in managing your public image and how others perceive you that you neglect your own integrity and values.
meaning_fields.teaching: You waste your mental energy trying to figure out what others think instead of taking care of your own character. The only thing truly in your control is keeping yourself free from rage, greed, and thoughtlessness—focusing on your own inner state is actually the real work. When you stop obsessing over others' minds and tend to your own integrity, you find real peace.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety about being judged, restlessness from constant social comparison, frustration at not being able to control how others see you, exhaustion from the endless mental detective work of trying to read people.
meaning_fields.concepts: Austerity of mind (focusing only on what is within your control); the divine spark within (the part of you connected to reason and virtue); the futility of external concerns (worrying about others' thoughts pulls you away from your actual purpose).

translation: If thou shouldst live three thousand, or as many as ten thousands of years, yet remember this, that man can part with no life properly, save with that little part of life, which he now lives: and that which he lives, is no other, than that which at every instant he parts with. That then which is longest of duration, and that which is shortest, come both to one effect. For although in regard of that which is already past there may be some inequality, yet that time which is now present and in being, is equal unto all men. And that being it which we part with whensoever we die, it doth manifestly appear, that it can be but a moment of time, that we then part with. For as for that which is either past or to come, a man cannot be said properly to part with it. For how should a man part with that which he hath not? These two things therefore thou must remember. First, that all things in the world from all eternity, by a perpetual revolution of the same times and things ever continued and renewed, are of one kind and nature; so that whether for a hundred or two hundred years only, or for an infinite space of time, a man see those things which are still the same, it can be no matter of great moment. And secondly, that that life which any the longest liver, or the shortest liver parts with, is for length and duration the very same, for that only which is present, is that, which either of them can lose, as being that only which they have; for that which he hath not, no man can truly be said to lose.
book_theme: mortality and the discipline of the present moment

meaning_fields.situations: Staying up late worrying about how much time you've wasted and how little you have left. Comparing your life span to others—wishing you had more years ahead like someone younger. Feeling paralyzed by regret about the past or anxiety about an uncertain future. Lying awake thinking "I should have done more by now" or "I don't know how much time I have." Realizing you've spent a whole year on something that didn't matter and feeling cheated by time.
meaning_fields.teaching: You can only actually live the moment you're in right now. Everything else—your past, your future, years you haven't lived yet—isn't something you can lose or waste because you don't have it. The length of your life barely matters; what matters is that you're not losing anything but this single present moment, which is the only thing you actually possess.
meaning_fields.emotions: Regret about wasted time, anxiety about the future, the fear of not having enough time left, desperation to make up for lost years, the weight of mortality, feeling cheated by time running out, paralysis when thinking about your lifespan
meaning_fields.concepts: Presence and the present moment (the only real thing you possess); mortality as a teacher (living 100 years or 10,000 comes down to the same thing—one present moment at a time); the illusion that past and future are things you can lose or control; the equality of all human lives in what matters (the now); impermanence and change (perpetual revolution) as universal law.

translation: Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is sweet and pleasing.
book_theme: mortality and the discipline of the present moment

meaning_fields.situations: Getting upset about what someone thinks of you at work or socially, then realizing later that their judgment was just their opinion and doesn't change who you actually are. Obsessing over a critical comment or harsh review, then noticing how much mental energy you wasted on something that exists only in someone else's head. Worrying about how an event looked to others, or how you appeared to people, when what actually matters is what you did and learned. Replaying a social mistake and imagining all the negative judgments people are making about you. Being crushed by criticism and slowly recognizing that the criticism is filtered through that person's biases and limited perspective.
meaning_fields.teaching: Most of what bothers you is not the thing itself—it's the story you or others tell about it. When you strip away opinions and judgments, you're left with the raw facts: what actually happened and what you can actually do about it. The skill is learning to see both the difficult truth and the helpful perspective at the same time, without letting either one paralyze you.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety about judgment and reputation, shame about perceived failures, defensiveness when criticized, the weight of overthinking what others think, relief when you realize an opinion isn't objective fact, irritation at other people's narrow views of you, frustration with yourself for caring so much about external validation
meaning_fields.concepts: Opinion versus reality (doxa versus aletheia in Greek philosophy). The Stoic distinction between what is "in our control" (our judgments and responses) and what is "not in our control" (others' opinions). Monimus the Cynic taught that external things are morally neutral—their meaning comes from the opinions we layer on top of them, not from the things themselves. The practice of stripping away flattering or harsh narratives to see what's actually true and useful.

translation: A man's soul doth wrong and disrespect itself first and especially, when as much as in itself lies it becomes an aposteme, and as it were an excrescency of the world, for to be grieved and displeased with anything that happens in the world, is direct apostacy from the nature of the universe; part of which, all particular natures of the world, are. Secondly, when she either is averse from any man, or led by contrary desires or affections, tending to his hurt and prejudice; such as are the souls of them that are angry. Thirdly, when she is overcome by any pleasure or pain. Fourthly, when she doth dissemble, and covertly and falsely either doth or saith anything. Fifthly, when she doth either affect or endeavour anything to no certain end, but rashly and without due ratiocination and consideration, how consequent or inconsequent it is to the common end. For even the least things ought not to be done, without relation unto the end; and the end of the reasonable creatures is, to follow and obey him, who is the reason as it were, and the law of this great city, and ancient commonwealth.
book_theme: mortality and the discipline of the present moment

meaning_fields.teaching: You damage your own integrity when you resist what happens, blame others, lose yourself to pleasure or pain, lie about what you're doing, or act without thinking through how your choices fit into your actual values. Your soul's strength comes from accepting reality as it is, treating others fairly, staying in control of your emotions, being honest, and acting deliberately in line with what matters most to you.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anger at circumstances, resentment toward others, being swept away by desire or fear, shame at your own dishonesty, frustration at wasting time on things that don't matter, regret at acting without thinking
meaning_fields.situations: You get angry at traffic or bad luck and realize you're just making yourself miserable; You're tempted to sabotage a coworker's project because you resent them; You find yourself binge-watching or overspending without knowing why, and it leaves you feeling empty; You catch yourself lying to avoid looking bad, then feel hollow about it; You've been grinding away at work that has no connection to what you actually value, and you wake up wondering what you're doing with your time; You act impulsively in a conflict and later realize you made things worse without thinking it through
meaning_fields.concepts: Self-respect and integrity (the soul "wronging itself"); alignment with nature and universal reason (not being "an excrescency" or outgrowth that doesn't belong); emotional discipline or mastery over pleasure and pain; the relationship between action and purpose (all acts should serve the "common end," the shared good of the rational community)

translation: The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption. His soul is restless, fortune uncertain, and fame doubtful; to be brief, as a stream so are all things belonging to the body; as a dream, or as a smoke, so are all that belong unto the soul. Our life is a warfare, and a mere pilgrimage. Fame after life is no better than oblivion. What is it then that will adhere and follow? Only one thing, philosophy. And philosophy doth consist in this, for a man to preserve that spirit which is within him, from all manner of contumelies and injuries, and above all pains or pleasures; never to do anything either rashly, or feignedly, or hypocritically: wholly to depend from himself and his own proper actions: all things that happen unto him to embrace contentedly, as coming from Him from whom he himself also came; and above all things, with all meekness and a calm cheerfulness, to expect death, as being nothing else but the resolution of those elements, of which every creature is composed. And if the elements themselves suffer nothing by this their perpetual conversion of one into another, that dissolution, and alteration, which is so common unto all, why should it be feared by any? Is not this according to nature? But nothing that is according to nature can be evil. _Whilst I was at Carnuntum._
book_theme: mortality and the discipline of the present moment

meaning_fields.situations: You're lying awake at 3 AM worrying about your reputation at work and whether people will remember your name. You're scrolling through social media and noticing how quickly posts vanish and how little anyone cares about old achievements. You're facing a health scare and suddenly realize how fragile your body is. You're spending hours on a project that feels pointless because you know the company could be gone in five years. You're in your 50s and realizing that the career success you worked toward hasn't made you feel secure or happy.
meaning_fields.teaching: Everything you are—your body, your reputation, your accomplishments—is temporary and constantly breaking down. The only thing worth building is your character and how you respond to what happens to you. Stop chasing things that vanish, and instead focus on staying honest, not overreacting, and accepting what life brings without fear.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety about being forgotten, fear of bodily decay and death, restlessness about legacy and what your life means, the hollow feeling after achieving something you thought mattered, dread about loss of control, the burden of keeping up appearances.
meaning_fields.concepts: Memento mori (remembering you will die) used not as morbid obsession but as clarity—stripping away false priorities. Amor fati (love of fate)—accepting dissolution and change as natural rather than catastrophic. Ataraxia (freedom from fear through understanding nature). Premeditatio malorum (negative visualization) applied to mortality as a tool for acceptance, not anxiety.

translation: A man must not only consider how daily his life wasteth and decreaseth, but this also, that if he live long, he cannot be certain, whether his understanding shall continue so able and sufficient, for either discreet consideration, in matter of businesses; or for contemplation: it being the thing, whereon true knowledge of things both divine and human, doth depend. For if once he shall begin to dote, his respiration, nutrition, his imaginative, and appetitive, and other natural faculties, may still continue the same: he shall find no want of them. But how to make that right use of himself that he should, how to observe exactly in all things that which is right and just, how to redress and rectify all wrong, or sudden apprehensions and imaginations, and even of this particular, whether he should live any longer or no, to consider duly; for all such things, wherein the best strength and vigour of the mind is most requisite; his power and ability will be past and gone. Thou must hasten therefore; not only because thou art every day nearer unto death than other, but also because that intellective faculty in thee, whereby thou art enabled to know the true nature of things, and to order all thy actions by that knowledge, doth daily waste and decay: or, may fail thee before thou die.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.teaching: Your mind—the part that lets you see what's actually true and make real choices—gets weaker as you age, and it might fail before you die. You can't count on having it forever. This means you need to use it now, while it's still sharp, to understand what matters and live right. Waiting is the real mistake.
meaning_fields.emotions: Urgency mixed with dread. The creeping fear that you're losing your edge. Anxiety about becoming less capable, less yourself. The specific sting of realizing you can't just put off hard thinking until later.
meaning_fields.situations: A person in their 50s or 60s noticing they can't focus the way they used to and wondering if they've already wasted their sharp years. Someone avoiding a difficult life decision—a career change, ending a bad relationship, moving—and telling themselves they have time later. A middle-aged person visiting a parent with dementia or Alzheimer's and suddenly grasping that mental clarity isn't guaranteed. Someone at 40 realizing they've spent two decades on work they don't believe in, and now questioning whether their mind is still clear enough to change course. A person facing a moral choice they've postponed, noticing their ability to think clearly about it feels duller than it once was.
meaning_fields.concepts: The ruling faculty (Greek: hegemonikon)—the rational part of the mind that judges, decides, and understands truth. This is what Marcus means by the intellective faculty. Logos—the universal reason or truth that order requires you to perceive and live by. Duty and right action (Greek: orthos, meaning straight or correct) depend on this faculty working well. Decay of the mind as a real risk, not just a metaphor—the passage distinguishes between body still functioning but mind failing.

translation: This also thou must observe, that whatsoever it is that naturally doth happen to things natural, hath somewhat in itself that is pleasing and delightful: as a great loaf when it is baked, some parts of it cleave as it were, and part asunder, and make the crust of it rugged and unequal, and yet those parts of it, though in some sort it be against the art and intention of baking itself, that they are thus cleft and parted, which should have been and were first made all even and uniform, they become it well nevertheless, and have a certain peculiar property, to stir the appetite. So figs are accounted fairest and ripest then, when they begin to shrink, and wither as it were. So ripe olives, when they are next to putrefaction, then are they in their proper beauty. The hanging down of grapes--the brow of a lion, the froth of a foaming wild boar, and many other like things, though by themselves considered, they are far from any beauty, yet because they happen naturally, they both are comely, and delightful; so that if a man shall with a profound mind and apprehension, consider all things in the world, even among all those things which are but mere accessories and natural appendices as it were, there will scarce appear anything unto him, wherein he will not find matter of pleasure and delight. So will he behold with as much pleasure the true _rictus_ of wild beasts, as those which by skilful painters and other artificers are imitated. So will he be able to perceive the proper ripeness and beauty of old age, whether in man or woman: and whatsoever else it is that is beautiful and alluring in whatsoever is, with chaste and continent eyes he will soon find out and discern. Those and many other things will he discern, not credible unto every one, but unto them only who are truly and familiarly acquainted, both with nature itself, and all natural things.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: A parent frustrated watching their child's messy room or unruly hair, suddenly realizing this disorder belongs to childhood and has its own rightness. Someone aging, noticing their wrinkles and sagging skin, and choosing to see this as natural ripeness rather than decay. An employee noticing their project came out rough and imperfect, then recognizing the cracks and flaws as part of what makes it real and useful. A person watching someone they love age, and finding themselves drawn to the particular beauty of that aging face rather than mourning lost youth. Someone struggling with their body's changes—scars, asymmetry, wear—and learning to see these as having their own strange appeal.
meaning_fields.teaching: When you stop judging things by an imaginary standard of perfection and look at what actually happens in nature, you find beauty and delight everywhere—in the cracks of bread, the wrinkles of age, the awkward angles of wild animals. The flaws and decay you instinctively reject are often more real and more worth savoring than anything artificial. This shift in perception doesn't require changing what you see; it requires training your eyes to find what's genuinely pleasing in the natural world as it actually is.
meaning_fields.emotions: Disgust at imperfection turning into unexpected appreciation. Disappointment when something doesn't turn out clean or polished, then surprise at finding appeal in the roughness. Dread about aging and physical decline, replaced by a sense of watching something ripen into its proper state. Resistance to accepting the body's natural changes, gradually softening into recognition of a different kind of beauty.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis) and natural necessity—things that happen according to their own nature are inherently fitting and right. The distinction between artificial expectations (what we think should happen) and natural reality (what does happen). Perception and discernment—the trained eye learns to see beauty where untrained perception sees only flaw or decay. Temperance of the senses (continence)—the ability to appreciate natural things purely, without being distorted by vanity or projection.

Disgust at imperfection turning into unexpected appreciation. Disappointment when something doesn't turn out clean or polished, then surprise at finding appeal in the roughness. Dread about aging and physical decline, replaced by a sense of watching something ripen into its proper state. Resistance to accepting the body's natural changes, gradually softening into recognition of a different kind of beauty.
Nature (physis) and natural necessity—things that happen according to their own nature are inherently fitting and right. The distinction between artificial expectations (what we think should happen) and natural reality (what does happen). Perception and discernment—the trained eye learns to see beauty where untrained perception sees only flaw or decay. Temperance of the senses (continence)—the ability to appreciate natural things purely, without being distorted by vanity or projection.

translation: Hippocrates having cured many sicknesses, fell sick himself and died. The Chaldeans and Astrologians having foretold the deaths of divers, were afterwards themselves surprised by the fates. Alexander and Pompeius, and Caius Cæsar, having destroyed so many towns, and cut off in the field so many thousands both of horse and foot, yet they themselves at last were fain to part with their own lives. Heraclitus having written so many natural tracts concerning the last and general conflagration of the world, died afterwards all filled with water within, and all bedaubed with dirt and dung without. Lice killed Democritus; and Socrates, another sort of vermin, wicked ungodly men. How then stands the case? Thou hast taken ship, thou hast sailed, thou art come to land, go out, if to another life, there also shalt thou find gods, who are everywhere. If all life and sense shall cease, then shalt thou cease also to be subject to either pains or pleasures; and to serve and tend this vile cottage; so much the viler, by how much that which ministers unto it doth excel; the one being a rational substance, and a spirit, the other nothing but earth and blood.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: A surgeon spends decades perfecting their craft and saving lives, then faces a terminal diagnosis. A successful executive has built an empire through ruthlessness and ambition, but realizes it will all crumble when they're gone. A scientist devotes their life to understanding nature and solving cosmic mysteries, but dies from a mundane illness. Someone has worked tirelessly to climb the ladder, accumulate money and status, only to realize none of it follows them into death. An aging person looks back on all their schemes, planning, and worry about outcomes, knowing they'll soon lose the ability to worry at all.
meaning_fields.teaching: Everything you've built, mastered, or conquered will be taken from you—not because you failed, but because you're human and will die like everyone else. The irony is that the greater your achievement, the more absurd it becomes when stripped away by time. But once you grasp this, you're freed from the exhausting illusion that your plans and victories matter in any ultimate sense. What remains is only how you've trained your mind to handle what comes.
meaning_fields.emotions: The unsettling realization that no accomplishment is permanent. Shame at how much energy you've spent on things that won't outlast you. A strange relief at accepting that striving can stop. Anxiety about whether your life has meant anything if it ends anyway. Humility when comparing your efforts to the indifference of time.
meaning_fields.concepts: The equality of all mortals (isonomia) — that death and fate level all humans regardless of power, knowledge, or achievement. The futility of attachment to outcomes you don't control. The distinction between your rational faculty (your capacity for right judgment) and your body (the "vile cottage" that decays). Amor fati — accepting that your end is fixed and learning to live with that knowledge rather than deny it.

translation: Spend not the remnant of thy days in thoughts and fancies concerning other men, when it is not in relation to some common good, when by it thou art hindered from some other better work. That is, spend not thy time in thinking, what such a man doth, and to what end: what he saith, and what he thinks, and what he is about, and such other things or curiosities, which make a man to rove and wander from the care and observation of that part of himself, which is rational, and overruling. See therefore in the whole series and connection of thy thoughts, that thou be careful to prevent whatsoever is idle and impertinent: but especially, whatsoever is curious and malicious: and thou must use thyself to think only of such things, of which if a man upon a sudden should ask thee, what it is that thou art now thinking, thou mayest answer This, and That, freely and boldly, that so by thy thoughts it may presently appear that in all thee is sincere, and peaceable; as becometh one that is made for society, and regards not pleasures, nor gives way to any voluptuous imaginations at all: free from all contentiousness, envy, and suspicion, and from whatsoever else thou wouldest blush to confess thy thoughts were set upon. He that is such, is he surely that doth not put off to lay hold on that which is best indeed, a very priest and minister of the gods, well acquainted and in good correspondence with him especially that is seated and placed within himself, as in a temple and sacrary: to whom also he keeps and preserves himself unspotted by pleasure, undaunted by pain; free from any manner of wrong, or contumely, by himself offered unto himself: not capable of any evil from others: a wrestler of the best sort, and for the highest prize, that he may not be cast down by any passion or affection of his own; deeply dyed and drenched in righteousness, embracing and accepting with his whole heart whatsoever either happeneth or is allotted unto him. One who not often, nor without some great necessity tending to some public good, mindeth what any other, either speaks, or doth, or purposeth: for those things only that are in his own power, or that are truly his own, are the objects of his employments, and his thoughts are ever taken up with those things, which of the whole universe are by the fates or Providence destinated and appropriated unto himself. Those things that are his own, and in his own power, he himself takes order, for that they be good: and as for those that happen unto him, he believes them to be so. For that lot and portion which is assigned to every one, as it is unavoidable and necessary, so is it always profitable. He remembers besides that whatsoever partakes of reason, is akin unto him, and that to care for all men generally, is agreeing to the nature of a man: but as for honour and praise, that they ought not generally to be admitted and accepted of from all, but from such only, who live according to nature. As for them that do not, what manner of men they be at home, or abroad; day or night, how conditioned themselves with what manner of conditions, or with men of what conditions they moil and pass away the time together, he knoweth, and remembers right well, he therefore regards not such praise and approbation, as proceeding from them, who cannot like and approve themselves.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.teaching: Stop spending mental energy obsessing over what other people are doing, saying, or thinking—unless it directly serves the common good. Guard your mind like a sacred space, keeping it focused only on what you control and what's truly yours. The integrity of your inner ruling faculty depends on thoughts you'd be willing to announce to anyone without shame.
meaning_fields.emotions: The anxiety and preoccupation that comes from endlessly wondering about others' behavior and motives; the shame or defensiveness when you realize you're dwelling on petty grievances, gossip, or envious comparisons; the relief and peace that comes from a clear conscience about your own thoughts.
meaning_fields.situations: You catch yourself replaying a conversation with a coworker, analyzing what she really meant and whether she was criticizing you. You're scrolling through social media, comparing your life to a friend's highlight reel and feeling bitter. You're in a meeting, distracted by speculation about what your boss thinks of you instead of focusing on the work. You hear a rumor about a colleague and spend hours wondering if it's true and what it means. You're alone and realize most of your recent thoughts have been judgmental commentary on people around you, none of which affects what you need to do today.
meaning_fields.concepts: The ruling faculty (prohairesis)—the core of rational self-direction that belongs entirely to you; oikeiosis—the natural kinship between rational beings that grounds genuine concern for others, distinct from idle curiosity; what is "up to us" versus what is not; the Stoic virtue of integrity (homologia) as alignment between inner thought and outer word; Providence and natural law as the ordering principle behind what happens to you.

translation: Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor without due examination, nor with reluctancy. Affect not to set out thy thoughts with curious neat language. Be neither a great talker, nor a great undertaker. Moreover, let thy God that is in thee to rule over thee, find by thee, that he hath to do with a man; an aged man; a sociable man; a Roman; a prince; one that hath ordered his life, as one that expecteth, as it were, nothing but the sound of the trumpet, sounding a retreat to depart out of this life with all expedition. One who for his word or actions neither needs an oath, nor any man to be a witness.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: A coworker pressures you into a project you don't believe in, and you're torn between keeping the peace and staying true to your own judgment. You're in a meeting where everyone expects you to perform and impress, but you feel hollow doing it. A friend asks you to keep a secret that conflicts with your values, and you have to choose between loyalty and integrity. You catch yourself crafting an elaborate excuse for something you did wrong instead of just owning it. You're staying late at work for the third time this week on tasks that don't matter to you, and you wonder if this is really how you want to spend your life.
meaning_fields.teaching: Stop doing things you don't genuinely believe in, or that harm others, or that you haven't thought through carefully. Don't waste energy performing or dressing up your words to impress. The real test is whether you can live so cleanly and with such clear intent that your word alone is enough—no apologies, no witnesses, no excuses needed.
meaning_fields.emotions: Exhaustion from constantly managing what others think of you, the hollow feeling of pretending, frustration when your integrity gets compromised for the sake of fitting in, relief when you can finally just be direct instead of performing, the quiet confidence that comes from knowing your own word means something.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (the ruling faculty or free will)—the part of you that makes actual choices and should never be surrendered to external pressure. Oikeiosis (right relationship)—living as your actual self rather than a constructed persona. Living as though you might leave at any moment (memento mori)—which clarifies what actually deserves your time and energy.

translation: To be cheerful, and to stand in no need, either of other men's help or attendance, or of that rest and tranquillity, which thou must be beholding to others for. Rather like one that is straight of himself, or hath ever been straight, than one that hath been rectified.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.teaching: You're strongest when you don't need to lean on anyone else to feel okay. It's better to build yourself as someone naturally steady than to keep needing other people to fix you or calm you down whenever things get hard.
meaning_fields.situations: Your friend keeps checking in to make sure you're doing okay after a setback, and you realize you've gotten used to needing those check-ins to feel stable. You're at a social event and notice you're only relaxed when certain people are nearby, anxious when they're not. You catch yourself waiting for your partner's reassurance before making a decision at work. You realize you bring up the same problem to different people repeatedly, seeking sympathy each time rather than handling it. You notice you dread the quiet moments alone because that's when the anxiety hits, so you keep scheduling things to avoid being by yourself.
meaning_fields.emotions: Dependence, the exhaustion of always needing reassurance, anxiety when alone, the shame of repeatedly leaning on others, restlessness without external validation, the temporary relief that fades quickly when someone comforts you.
meaning_fields.concepts: Autarkeia (self-sufficiency or inner strength that doesn't depend on external props). The distinction between someone who has trained themselves to be steady versus someone who falls apart and needs constant repair—between a straight timber and one perpetually warped and straightened by others' hands. The integrity of your ruling faculty (prohairesis), the core judgment power that should operate independently.

translation: If thou shalt find anything in this mortal life better than righteousness, than truth, temperance, fortitude, and in general better than a mind contented both with those things which according to right and reason she doth, and in those, which without her will and knowledge happen unto thee by the providence; if I say, thou canst find out anything better than this, apply thyself unto it with thy whole heart, and that which is best wheresoever thou dost find it, enjoy freely. But if nothing thou shalt find worthy to be preferred to that spirit which is within thee; if nothing better than to subject unto thee thine own lusts and desires, and not to give way to any fancies or imaginations before thou hast duly considered of them, nothing better than to withdraw thyself (to use Socrates his words) from all sensuality, and submit thyself unto the gods, and to have care of all men in general: if thou shalt find that all other things in comparison of this, are but vile, and of little moment; then give not way to any other thing, which being once though but affected and inclined unto, it will no more be in thy power without all distraction as thou oughtest to prefer and to pursue after that good, which is thine own and thy proper good. For it is not lawful, that anything that is of another and inferior kind and nature, be it what it will, as either popular applause, or honour, or riches, or pleasures; should be suffered to confront and contest as it were, with that which is rational, and operatively good. For all these things, if once though but for a while, they begin to please, they presently prevail, and pervert a man's mind, or turn a man from the right way. Do thou therefore I say absolutely and freely make choice of that which is best, and stick unto it. Now, that they say is best, which is most profitable. If they mean profitable to man as he is a rational man, stand thou to it, and maintain it; but if they mean profitable, as he is a creature, only reject it; and from this thy tenet and conclusion keep off carefully all plausible shows and colours of external appearance, that thou mayest be able to discern things rightly.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: A job offer comes with great money and status, but you'd have to compromise your values or abandon work you find meaningful. Your friend pressures you to join in something you know is dishonest because everyone else is doing it. You're tempted to chase social media validation or impress people at work by cutting corners. You have to choose between taking credit for an idea (which would boost your reputation) or giving it to someone who actually deserves it. You're offered a promotion that would require you to treat people badly or make decisions you'd feel guilty about.
meaning_fields.teaching: When choosing how to live, the only things worth protecting are your integrity, truthfulness, self-control, and courage—plus the ability to accept what's outside your control. Everything else—money, status, applause, pleasure—will cloud your judgment the moment you start pursuing it. Once you let external rewards become tempting, they take over your mind and pull you away from what actually matters. So decide right now: is being a person of solid character and reason more important than anything else? If yes, defend that choice fiercely and don't let flashy external rewards talk you out of it.
meaning_fields.emotions: The hollow feeling after getting something you thought you wanted but compromised for it. Pressure and anxiety when facing a choice between what looks good and what feels right. The pull of temptation when you see others succeeding through shortcuts. Confusion about whether you're being practical or just rationalizing a compromise. Relief and clarity when you finally decide that some things are not for sale.
meaning_fields.concepts: The ruling faculty (prohairesis)—your core capacity to make judgments and choices based on reason rather than impulse. Virtue as the highest good: righteousness, truth, self-control, and courage form the stable bedrock of a good life. Adiaphora—things indifferent or external: money, status, pleasure, and reputation have no real bearing on whether you live well. The corruption that happens when you permit inferior goods to compete with virtue in your mind. Prosoche—focused attention to distinguish genuine goods from illusions masked by social approval and external rewards.

translation: Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man, to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that requireth the secret of walls or veils. But he that preferreth before all things his rational part and spirit, and the sacred mysteries of virtue which issueth from it, he shall never lament and exclaim, never sigh; he shall never want either solitude or company: and which is chiefest of all, he shall live without either desire or fear. And as for life, whether for a long or short time he shall enjoy his soul thus compassed about with a body, he is altogether indifferent. For if even now he were to depart, he is as ready for it, as for any other action, which may be performed with modesty and decency. For all his life long, this is his only care, that his mind may always be occupied in such intentions and objects, as are proper to a rational sociable creature.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.teaching: Your integrity matters more than any gain. When you face a choice between what benefits you and what keeps you honest, honest wins—even when no one would know the difference. A person who genuinely lives this way stops being torn apart by regret, shame, or the exhausting need to hide.
meaning_fields.emotions: The guilt and dread of knowing you've compromised yourself; the relief of not having to keep secrets or pretend; the anxiety of wanting something badly enough that you'd hide it; the restlessness of living dishonestly; the peace of having nothing to conceal.
meaning_fields.situations: You're offered a promotion if you stay quiet about a colleague's mistake, but speaking up would hurt your chances; a financial opportunity requires you to shade the truth on an application; you want something (money, status, a person) badly enough that you'd have to hide it from people who matter to you; you're tempted to badmouth someone to protect your reputation; you realize you've been performing a false version of yourself at work for years.
meaning_fields.concepts: The ruling faculty (prohairesis): the part of you that makes choices and decides who you are. Virtue (arete): not morality imposed from outside, but the integrity that comes from using reason well. The indifference to external outcomes when internal character is intact—you can accept whatever comes (including death) because you haven't betrayed yourself to get it.

translation: In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, thou canst not find anything, either foul or impure, or as it were festered: nothing that is either servile, or affected: no partial tie; no malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed. The life of such an one, death can never surprise as imperfect; as of an actor, that should die before he had ended, or the play itself were at an end, a man might speak.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: A person stays up late obsessing over a past argument and replaying what they should have said; someone harbors resentment against a colleague for years, letting it poison how they view that person; a parent realizes they've been keeping score of small slights against their spouse; someone catches themselves being fake or people-pleasing in a situation where they normally wouldn't; a person nearing the end of their life wishes they'd spent less time on grudges and more on what actually mattered to them.
meaning_fields.teaching: A mind that has genuinely trained itself stays clean—free of hidden resentments, fakeness, petty grievances, and unexamined bitterness. When you're like that, you can face the end of your life without regret, the way an actor who gave their full performance feels complete even if the curtain falls suddenly. The opposite is a life cluttered with unfinished business you're ashamed of.
meaning_fields.emotions: Regret about wasted emotional energy; the heaviness of carrying old grudges; shame about being inauthentic; the relief of letting go of resentment; the anxiety of having unfinished personal business; the peace of knowing you've been honest with yourself.
meaning_fields.concepts: The ruling faculty (prohairesis) — the core decision-making part of you that can choose what you hold onto mentally; purification or catharsis — the active work of clearing out mental and moral corruption; integrity (holoteleia) — wholeness and completeness in how you've lived; the Stoic belief that virtue and self-honesty are the only real goods, and that a corrupted inner life is the only true evil.

translation: Use thine opinative faculty with all honour and respect, for in her indeed is all: that thy opinion do not beget in thy understanding anything contrary to either nature, or the proper constitution of a rational creature. The end and object of a rational constitution is, to do nothing rashly, to be kindly affected towards men, and in all things willingly to submit unto the gods. Casting therefore all other things aside, keep thyself to these few, and remember withal that no man properly can be said to live more than that which is now present, which is but a moment of time. Whatsoever is besides either is already past, or uncertain. The time therefore that any man doth live, is but a little, and the place where he liveth, is but a very little corner of the earth, and the greatest fame that can remain of a man after his death, even that is but little, and that too, such as it is whilst it is, is by the succession of silly mortal men preserved, who likewise shall shortly die, and even whiles they live know not what in very deed they themselves are: and much less can know one, who long before is dead and gone.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: A person realizes they've wasted months pursuing a promotion that won't matter in ten years. Someone is anxious about their legacy or how they'll be remembered after they're gone. A parent catches themselves making a harsh judgment about their kid instead of responding with kindness. An employee feels paralyzed before making a decision at work and can't figure out what actually matters. Someone is stressing over their reputation or what people think of them on social media.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your opinions and judgments are the only thing you actually control—guard them fiercely so they align with reason and nature, not with fear or impulse. You're only truly alive in this exact moment, everything else is gone or not yet real; your lifespan is tiny, your fame will be forgotten in a heartbeat, and worrying about either is a waste of the little time you have. Focus on what's in your power: thinking clearly, treating people decently, and accepting what you can't control.

translation: To these ever-present helps and mementoes, let one more be added, ever to make a particular description and delineation as it were of every object that presents itself to thy mind, that thou mayest wholly and throughly contemplate it, in its own proper nature, bare and naked; wholly, and severally; divided into its several parts and quarters: and then by thyself in thy mind, to call both it, and those things of which it doth consist, and in which it shall be resolved, by their own proper true names, and appellations. For there is nothing so effectual to beget true magnanimity, as to be able truly and methodically to examine and consider all things that happen in this life, and so to penetrate into their natures, that at the same time, this also may concur in our apprehensions: what is the true use of it? and what is the true nature of this universe, to which it is useful? how much in regard of the universe may it be esteemed? how much in regard of man, a citizen of the supreme city, of which all other cities in the world are as it were but houses and families?
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: You're upset about something that happened at work and can't stop catastrophizing about it. You're facing a difficult decision and every option feels equally terrible and all-consuming. Someone has done something that feels deeply insulting, and you keep replaying it in your mind. You're stuck in anxiety about a future event and can't see past the worst-case scenario. You've suffered a setback and are treating it as if your whole life is ruined.
meaning_fields.teaching: When something upsets you, zoom out and look at it clearly—break it down into what's actually there, strip away the story you're telling yourself about it, and ask what this thing actually matters for. Does it matter to the whole universe? Does it matter to who you really are? Most of the time, when you look directly at what's really happening instead of the panic version in your head, it shrinks to its actual size.
meaning_fields.emotions: Panic, catastrophizing, wounded pride, the feeling that one incident defines everything, anxiety that won't let go, shame spiraling into self-condemnation

translation: What is this, that now my fancy is set upon? of what things doth it consist? how long can it last? which of all the virtues is the proper virtue for this present use? as whether meekness, fortitude, truth, faith, sincerity, contentation, or any of the rest? Of everything therefore thou must use thyself to say, This immediately comes from God, this by that fatal connection, and concatenation of things, or (which almost comes to one) by some coincidental casualty. And as for this, it proceeds from my neighbour, my kinsman, my fellow: through his ignorance indeed, because he knows not what is truly natural unto him: but I know it, and therefore carry myself towards him according to the natural law of fellowship; that is kindly, and justly. As for those things that of themselves are altogether indifferent, as in my best judgment I conceive everything to deserve more or less, so I carry myself towards it.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: Your boss makes an unreasonable demand and you feel irritated, but then you remember she's probably overwhelmed and doesn't know better. You're stuck in traffic and someone cuts you off aggressively; instead of staying angry, you think about what might be driving their behavior. A family member says something hurtful; you pause and consider whether they understand how it lands. You're tempted to buy something you don't need and you catch yourself, asking whether this deserves your attention. Someone at work gets promoted over you and you have to decide how much to let it consume your thoughts.
meaning_fields.teaching: Before you give your attention or emotional energy to anything—whether it's an annoyance, a desire, or anger at someone—stop and ask yourself which virtue this situation actually calls for. Then recognize that other people's harmful actions come from their own ignorance about what's genuinely good for them, not from malice toward you. Knowing better gives you the power to respond with kindness and fairness instead of resentment. For things that don't really matter—status, possessions, small slights—deliberately reduce how much weight you give them.
meaning_fields.emotions: irritation at other people's behavior, resentment over feeling disrespected, frustration when ignored or dismissed, the pull of desire for things that don't matter, anger that festers when you replay someone's mistake, shame at your own harsh reactions
meaning_fields.concepts: The ruling faculty (prohairesis) — the core of who you are; the part that chooses your response, not your circumstances. Natural law — the truth that humans are made to live together fairly and with good will. Indifferents — things outside your control that don't actually determine your character or happiness: status, money, opinion, minor discomforts. Virtue — practical wisdom about what response actually fits the situation. Fate and causation — everything that happens has reasons; nothing is random malice.

translation: If thou shalt intend that which is present, following the rule of right and reason carefully, solidly, meekly, and shalt not intermix any other businesses, but shall study this only to preserve thy spirit unpolluted, and pure, and shall cleave unto him without either hope or fear of anything, in all things that thou shalt either do or speak, contenting thyself with heroical truth, thou shalt live happily; and from this, there is no man that can hinder thee.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: You're juggling work emails while trying to focus on one important task. You catch yourself splitting your attention because you're worried about missing something or hoping for good news. You're in the middle of a conversation but half-listening because you're mentally rehearsing what you'll say next. You're making a decision but keep second-guessing yourself based on what others might think. You're trying to do something meaningful but keep getting pulled by anxiety about outcomes or desire for approval.
meaning_fields.teaching: Real peace and effectiveness come from giving your complete, undivided attention to what's in front of you right now—following your best judgment with steadiness and gentleness. When you stop mixing in other concerns, stop hoping for rewards or fearing losses, and commit to doing what's genuinely right, no one and nothing can actually undermine you. Your integrity itself becomes your protection.
meaning_fields.emotions: The scattered anxiety of divided attention. The frustration of being pulled in multiple directions. The creeping worry that you're missing something important. The exhaustion of constant self-doubt. The quiet satisfaction of focused, purposeful action. The relief of knowing you've done what you genuinely believe is right.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (the ruling faculty—your capacity to choose and direct your mind). Arete (excellence; heroical truth means the honest standard of what's actually right, not what flatters or pleases). Prosoche (attention, presence, vigilance of mind). Apatheia (freedom from destructive hope and fear, not numbness but clarity). Monastic focus: treating one task at a time as sacred.

translation: As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between these two things divine, and things human. For without relation unto God, thou shalt never speed in any worldly actions; nor on the other side in any divine, without some respect had to things human.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: You're making a business decision and realize you're only thinking about profit, forgetting how it affects the people involved. You're trying to live ethically but feel disconnected from why it matters. You're handling a difficult conversation at work and suddenly realize you're treating the person as just an obstacle instead of another person. You're facing a choice between what's practical and what's right, and you're frozen because you haven't thought through how they actually connect. You're busy solving small problems all day and can't remember what any of it is for.
meaning_fields.teaching: Everything you do—no matter how small or routine—requires you to hold two things in mind at once: the human cost and the larger purpose. You can't make good decisions by only looking at practical results, and you can't live by principles alone if they ignore real people. Like a surgeon who keeps both skills and tools ready before an emergency, you need to have your thinking about what matters in constant readiness.
meaning_fields.emotions: Feeling disconnected between your practical actions and your values. Anxiety that you're making wrong choices because you're only seeing half the picture. Frustration when trying to do the right thing but sensing you're missing something important. Guilt or unease when you realize your efficiency or principles ignored actual human consequences.
meaning_fields.concepts: The integration of the practical and the transcendent—the idea that human affairs and divine purpose (or ultimate meaning) cannot be separated. The ruling faculty (prohairesis) as the part of you that maintains this double vision and readiness. Virtue through wholeness rather than through compartmentalization.

translation: Be not deceived; for thou shalt never live to read thy moral commentaries, nor the acts of the famous Romans and Grecians; nor those excerpta from several books; all which thou hadst provided and laid up for thyself against thine old age. Hasten therefore to an end, and giving over all vain hopes, help thyself in time if thou carest for thyself, as thou oughtest to do.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: You're putting off learning something important because you tell yourself you'll do it "when things calm down" or "after this project ends." You're collecting books you never read, signing up for courses you never take, or saving interesting articles in folders you never revisit. You catch yourself thinking about what you'll accomplish "next year" or "once I retire." You're procrastinating on a conversation you know you need to have, a skill you want to develop, or something that matters to you personally because you're too busy with urgent things. You realize you've been saying you'll spend more time with someone important for months or years, but you haven't.
meaning_fields.teaching: You won't actually do the things you're planning to do later. Stop waiting for the perfect time to act on what matters to you—that time will never come. If you care about something, start now with what you actually have, not with fantasies about your future self. The life you want is only built through actions you take today.
meaning_fields.emotions: Quiet desperation about wasted potential, the sting of recognizing your own self-deception, frustration at time slipping away, anxiety about whether you'll ever actually become the person you imagine yourself being, shame at the gap between who you say you want to be and what you actually do.
meaning_fields.concepts: Premeditatio malorum (negative visualization, contemplating that our plans may never happen); the dichotomy of control (you control your actions now, not whether you'll have time later); living in reality rather than comforting illusions; the ruling faculty or prohairesis (your capacity to direct your own will and choices in the present moment).

translation: To steal, to sow, to buy, to be at rest, to see what is to be done (which is not seen by the eyes, but by another kind of sight:) what these words mean, and how many ways to be understood, they do not understand. The body, the soul, the understanding. As the senses naturally belong to the body, and the desires and affections to the soul, so do the dogmata to the understanding.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: You're scrolling through your phone instead of working on something important, but you can't quite name what you're actually avoiding. Someone asks what you're doing and you can only describe the physical action—"checking emails"—but not the real problem underneath. You're in a meeting where everyone's talking about next steps, but nobody seems to understand what actually needs to happen. You're stuck between what your gut is telling you to do and what your rational mind says makes sense. You finish a task but feel empty because you never stopped to think about whether it actually mattered.
meaning_fields.teaching: Most people live on the surface—they see the physical action but miss what's actually going on underneath. Your body has basic needs, your emotions drive desires, but your thinking mind is supposed to grasp the deeper truth about what's really happening and what actually matters. The problem is we confuse the level of the eyes (what we physically see) with the level of understanding (what we need to actually perceive). Learning to see clearly means separating these three parts and letting your rational mind do its actual job.
meaning_fields.emotions: Confusion about what you're really doing or why; the frustration of being stuck on surface level; the anxiety that comes from not understanding something that matters; the numbness of going through motions without purpose; restlessness when action doesn't align with understanding.
meaning_fields.concepts: Dianoia (clear thinking, seeing with the mind rather than the eyes); the three-part nature of human beings (body, soul/emotions, reasoning faculty); the difference between sensory perception and true understanding; logos (the ordering principle that the mind grasps); prohairesis (the ruling faculty's ability to judge and choose).

translation: To be capable of fancies and imaginations, is common to man and beast. To be violently drawn and moved by the lusts and desires of the soul, is proper to wild beasts and monsters, such as Phalaris and Nero were. To follow reason for ordinary duties and actions is common to them also, who believe not that there be any gods, and for their advantage would make no conscience to betray their own country; and who when once the doors be shut upon them, dare do anything. If therefore all things else be common to these likewise, it follows, that for a man to like and embrace all things that happen and are destinated unto him, and not to trouble and molest that spirit which is seated in the temple of his own breast, with a multitude of vain fancies and imaginations, but to keep him propitious and to obey him as a god, never either speaking anything contrary to truth, or doing anything contrary to justice, is the only true property of a good man. And such a one, though no man should believe that he liveth as he doth, either sincerely and conscionably, or cheerful and contentedly; yet is he neither with any man at all angry for it, nor diverted by it from the way that leadeth to the end of his life, through which a man must pass pure, ever ready to depart, and willing of himself without any compulsion to fit and accommodate himself to his proper lot and portion.
book_theme: the value of time and the integrity of the ruling faculty

meaning_fields.situations: You're being treated unfairly at work—passed over, doubted, or blamed—and no one sees your side of the story. You're doing the right thing in a relationship, but the other person doesn't trust or appreciate your integrity. You keep your word despite knowing it costs you something and no one will ever know you did. You're facing a setback or loss, and people around you assume you're either bitter or putting on a brave face. You're trying to live by your values in a place where others cut corners and get ahead.
meaning_fields.teaching: What makes you actually good is how you treat your own mind when no one is watching. Staying truthful and fair-dealing matters only because you decide it does—not because you get credit for it, not because people believe in you, not because it pays off. The only real integrity is the kind that survives being unseen and unrewarded. Your peace comes from knowing you didn't betray what you believe in, even if the world gives you nothing back for it.
meaning_fields.emotions: Loneliness when doing the right thing seems pointless. Frustration at being misunderstood or mistrusted despite trying hard. Quiet satisfaction that comes from knowing your own conscience is clean. Resentment that surfaces when your integrity goes unnoticed. Determination mixed with sadness—choosing to act right anyway.
meaning_fields.concepts: The ruling faculty (prohairesis)—the part of your mind that governs your choices and character. Virtue as an internal state that exists independent of external outcome or recognition. The distinction between what you can control (your choices, truthfulness, fairness) and what you cannot (others' beliefs, rewards, whether you're seen as good). Acceptance of your lot without needing the world to validate it.

translation: That inward mistress part of man if it be in its own true natural temper, is towards all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and affected, that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may be, and is within its own power to compass, when that cannot be which at first it intended. For it never doth absolutely addict and apply itself to any one object, but whatsoever it is that it doth now intend and prosecute, it doth prosecute it with exception and reservation; so that whatsoever it is that falls out contrary to its first intentions, even that afterwards it makes its proper object. Even as the fire when it prevails upon those things that are in his way; by which things indeed a little fire would have been quenched, but a great fire doth soon turn to its own nature, and so consume whatsoever comes in his way: yea by those very things it is made greater and greater.
book_theme: retreat into oneself; opinion as the source of disturbance

meaning_fields.teaching: Your core power is the ability to redirect your focus toward what you can actually control right now, instead of fighting reality. When something doesn't go the way you planned, the strongest move is to treat that new situation as your actual objective—to work with what's in front of you rather than resent what didn't happen. This flexibility itself is what makes you resilient.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration when plans fall apart; the sting of disappointment; feeling trapped or powerless when circumstances change; the relief of letting go and moving forward; the quiet strength of adapting instead of resisting.
meaning_fields.situations: You lose a job you wanted and have to figure out a different career path; a relationship ends and you have to build a new life; a major project gets cancelled and you're reassigned to something unexpected; travel plans get disrupted and you have to enjoy what's actually available instead; someone rejects your idea and you have to find a way to contribute differently.
meaning_fields.concepts: Premeditatio malorum (negative visualization) and amor fati (love of fate)—not as passive resignation, but as active mental flexibility. The Stoic dichotomy of control: distinguish between what you can control (your intention, your response) and what you cannot (outcomes, circumstances). Apatheia (freedom from destructive emotion) achieved through accepting reality rather than opposing it.

translation: They seek for themselves private retiring places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself art wont to long much after such places. But all this thou must know proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity I understand a decent orderly disposition and carriage, free from all confusion and tumultuousness. Afford then thyself this retiring continually, and thereby refresh and renew thyself. Let these precepts be brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou dost call them to mind, may suffice thee to purge thy soul throughly, and to send thee away well pleased with those things whatsoever they be, which now again after this short withdrawing of thy soul into herself thou dost return unto. For what is it that thou art offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of men, when thou dost call to mind this conclusion, that all reasonable creatures are made one for another? and that it is part of justice to bear with them? and that it is against their wills that they offend? and how many already, who once likewise prosecuted their enmities, suspected, hated, and fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched out, and reduced unto ashes? It is time for thee to make an end. As for those things which among the common chances of the world happen unto thee as thy particular lot and portion, canst thou be displeased with any of them, when thou dost call that our ordinary dilemma to mind, either a providence, or Democritus his atoms; and with it, whatsoever we brought to prove that the whole world is as it were one city? And as for thy body, what canst thou fear, if thou dost consider that thy mind and understanding, when once it hath recollected itself, and knows its own power, hath in this life and breath (whether it run smoothly and gently, or whether harshly and rudely), no interest at all, but is altogether indifferent: and whatsoever else thou hast heard and assented unto concerning either pain or pleasure? But the care of thine honour and reputation will perchance distract thee? How can that be, if thou dost look back, and consider both how quickly all things that are, are forgotten, and what an immense chaos of eternity was before, and will follow after all things: and the vanity of praise, and the inconstancy and variableness of human judgments and opinions, and the narrowness of the place, wherein it is limited and circumscribed? For the whole earth is but as one point; and of it, this inhabited part of it, is but a very little part; and of this part, how many in number, and what manner of men are they, that will commend thee? What remains then, but that thou often put in practice this kind of retiring of thyself, to this little part of thyself; and above all things, keep thyself from distraction, and intend not anything vehemently, but be free and consider all things, as a man whose proper object is Virtue, as a man whose true nature is to be kind and sociable, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. Among other things, which to consider, and look into thou must use to withdraw thyself, let those two be among the most obvious and at hand. One, that the things or objects themselves reach not unto the soul, but stand without still and quiet, and that it is from the opinion only which is within, that all the tumult and all the trouble doth proceed. The next, that all these things, which now thou seest, shall within a very little while be changed, and be no more: and ever call to mind, how many changes and alterations in the world thou thyself hast already been an eyewitness of in thy time. This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.

meaning_fields.situations: You're scrolling through social media and see someone criticizing you, and you can't put your phone down for hours. Your boss didn't acknowledge your work in a meeting and you're replaying it constantly. You're stuck in traffic and angry at the world's unfairness. Someone spreads a rumor about you and you keep imagining what people think. You're worried about looking foolish at an upcoming event and can't focus on anything else.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your disturbance doesn't come from what actually happened—it comes from the opinion you're holding about it. The event itself is silent and passive; only your judgment creates the turmoil. Withdraw mentally, examine your thoughts, and you'll find the power to return to calm. This is a skill you can use right now, not something you need to escape to mountains to find.
meaning_fields.emotions: Obsessive replaying of events, shame about reputation, rage at seeming injustice, anxiety about what others think, restlessness that won't let you be still, defensiveness when challenged.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (choice, or the will—the only thing actually within your control). Phantasia (impression or opinion—the initial appearance before judgment). The distinction between what happens externally and what you decide about it internally. Ataraxia (tranquility as a state of orderly, undisturbed mind). The practice of prosoche (mindful attention to where disturbance originates).

translation: If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is to be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law, then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other commonweal is it, that all men can be said to be members of? From this common city it is, that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto us, for from whence else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from some common earth; and that which is moist from some other element is imparted; as my breath and life hath its proper fountain; and that likewise which is dry and fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth not proceed from something; as also there is nothing that can be reduced unto mere nothing:) so also is there some common beginning from whence my understanding hath proceeded.
book_theme: retreat into oneself; opinion as the source of disturbance

meaning_fields.situations: You feel isolated after a conflict and wonder if the other person is just fundamentally different from you. You're in a meeting where someone's perspective seems completely alien to your own. You're angry at humanity generally and see people as divided into "us" and "them." You face a decision where you realize both you and someone you dislike probably value the same underlying things. You're grieving and feel alone, but catch yourself noticing how your body and mind work the same as everyone else's.
meaning_fields.teaching: You share the same capacity for reason and judgment as every other human being alive. This shared ability to think isn't something you earned or they didn't—it's built into all of us equally. Because of this fundamental sameness, you and every person are already members of one common human community, not separate camps. When you understand this, you stop seeing others as fundamentally foreign.
meaning_fields.emotions: Loneliness, alienation from others, anger at people who think differently, the shock of recognizing kinship with someone you dislike, grief that feels like it separates you from the world, relief at discovering unexpected common ground.
meaning_fields.concepts: Universal reason (the capacity all humans share to think and judge); cosmopolitanism (the idea that all humans belong to one city or community, not separate nations or groups); the physical elements we share with the material world (the point being that just as your body comes from shared matter, your mind comes from shared sources).

translation: As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing surely which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal events and consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto, not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper constitution of man himself.
book_theme: retreat into oneself; opinion as the source of disturbance

meaning_fields.teaching: Death is a natural process, as ordinary and unremarkable as birth—just materials breaking apart the way they came together. There's nothing shameful or wrong about it; it's simply what happens to thinking beings who are made of physical stuff. Accepting this as normal, not tragic, helps you stop treating it as an outrage against you personally.
meaning_fields.emotions: Dread about dying, shame about mortality, the sick feeling when you suddenly remember you're not permanent, fear that death makes life meaningless, anxiety about your body breaking down
meaning_fields.situations: Lying awake at 3 a.m. thinking about your own death or a parent's aging; scrolling through your phone and seeing news about someone your age who died; noticing your body isn't what it used to be and feeling a wave of panic; sitting at a funeral and realizing that will be you someday; making a big life plan and then freezing because 'what's the point if I die anyway'
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis) as the rational organizing principle of all events, including decay and dissolution; the material composition of humans (made of elements that return to elements), which undercuts the illusion that we're separate from or above natural law; amor fati (love of fate)—the practice of accepting necessary natural events rather than resisting them as alien or insulting

translation: Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity proceed. He that would not have such things to happen, is as he that would have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum, remember this, that within a very little while, both thou and he shall both be dead, and after a little while more, not so much as your names and memories shall be remaining.
book_theme: retreat into oneself; opinion as the source of disturbance

meaning_fields.situations: A coworker keeps making mistakes that affect your project and you're exhausted from trying to fix things. Your boss keeps scheduling meetings at inconvenient times no matter how many times you ask. A family member won't stop interrupting you during conversations. A contractor consistently misses deadlines on work you've hired them for. Someone you trusted betrays your confidence and you can't let it go.
meaning_fields.teaching: Some things happen because of how the world works—you can't stop a fig tree from needing water any more than you can stop people from acting according to their nature. Fighting against what must happen wastes your energy on the impossible. Within a short time, you and everyone frustrating you will be dead, and your names will be forgotten. So the things you're fighting to control or change right now matter less than you think.
meaning_fields.emotions: Exasperation at things you can't control. Exhaustion from resisting what feels inevitable. Anger at people for being the way they are. The sting of wanting to change something that won't change. Fear that small annoyances matter deeply.
meaning_fields.concepts: Necessity (the idea that some outcomes follow naturally from causes, like effects following from their causes). Acceptance of nature and human nature—that people and things behave according to their own nature, not your wishes. Memento mori (remembering that you will die), used here to diminish the apparent importance of temporary frustrations.
