translation: Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I, to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come. For as for this, it might have happened unto any man, but any man having such a thing befallen him, could not have continued without grief. Why then should that rather be an unhappiness, than this a happiness? But however, canst thou, O man! term that unhappiness, which is no mischance to the nature of man I Canst thou think that a mischance to the nature of man, which is not contrary to the end and will of his nature? What then hast thou learned is the will of man's nature? Doth that then which hath happened unto thee, hinder thee from being just? or magnanimous? or temperate? or wise? or circumspect? or true? or modest? or free? or from anything else of all those things in the present enjoying and possession whereof the nature of man, (as then enjoying all that is proper unto her,) is fully satisfied? Now to conclude; upon all occasion of sorrow remember henceforth to make use of this dogma, that whatsoever it is that hath happened unto thee, is in very deed no such thing of itself, as a misfortune; but that to bear it generously, is certainly great happiness.
book_theme: retreat into oneself; opinion as the source of disturbance

meaning_fields.situations: You lose your job and feel like a failure, then realize you can still act with integrity and self-respect regardless. Your relationship ends and you're devastated, but you recognize the breakup doesn't prevent you from being kind or honest. You make a public mistake at work and feel humiliated, but then ask yourself: does this actually stop me from doing good work going forward? Your plans fall through and you spiral, then catch yourself and ask what virtue this setback is really blocking. Someone betrays your trust and you want to spiral into bitterness, but you notice the betrayal doesn't touch your ability to be truthful or fair.
meaning_fields.teaching: Bad things happen to everyone, but what makes you miserable is treating them as catastrophes rather than just difficulties. The real question after any setback is whether it actually stops you from doing what matters—being honest, fair, courageous, thoughtful. If it doesn't block those things, then the setback isn't actually a catastrophe; handling it well is where your real strength lies.
meaning_fields.emotions: The crushing weight of feeling like something ruined you; the quiet realization that you're still intact; the shift from despair to a kind of stubborn dignity; the relief of seeing a problem shrink when you stop treating it as the end of everything.
meaning_fields.concepts: The distinction between what happens to you and your judgment about what it means (prohairesis—your choice to interpret events). The Stoic view that virtue is the only true good, and external events are "indifferents"—they can be preferred or dispreferred, but they don't determine your moral worth. Eudaimonia, or true flourishing, which comes from exercising your highest capacities (wisdom, justice, courage, self-discipline) regardless of circumstances.

translation: It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a long time enjoy their lives. What have they got more, than they whose deaths have been untimely? Are not they themselves dead at the last? as Cadiciant's, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, or any other who in their lifetime having buried many, were at the last buried themselves. The whole space of any man's life, is but little; and as little as it is, with what troubles, with what manner of dispositions, and in the society of how wretched a body must it be passed! Let it be therefore unto thee altogether as a matter of indifferency. For if thou shalt look backward; behold, what an infinite chaos of time doth present itself unto thee; and as infinite a chaos, if thou shalt look forward. In that which is so infinite, what difference can there be between that which liveth but three days, and that which liveth three ages?
book_theme: retreat into oneself; opinion as the source of disturbance

meaning_fields.teaching: Death comes for everyone eventually, no matter how long or successfully you live. When you zoom out to see the infinite span of time before your birth and after your death, the difference between a short life and a long one disappears. So clinging to extra years or worrying about dying young both miss the point—the length of life matters far less than what you do with the time you have.
meaning_fields.emotions: Dread about not living long enough; anxiety that your time is running out; the clutching fear that death is coming too soon; the despair of feeling that others got more years than you deserve to lose.
meaning_fields.situations: You're diagnosed with a serious illness and can't stop calculating how many years you might lose. A friend dies young and you spiral worrying it could happen to you. You turn 40 or 50 and suddenly panic that your best years are behind you. You compare your life span to your parents' or grandparents' and feel cheated. You're lying awake at 3 a.m. thinking about how fast time passes and how little you've accomplished.
meaning_fields.concepts: Memento mori (remembering you will die)—the ancient practice of meditating on death not to depress yourself but to cut through the illusion that you have infinite time. Indifference (apatheia in Stoic terms: freedom from destructive emotions, not numbness, but clear sight). The perspective shift—seeing your individual lifespan against cosmic time, so your personal duration stops looking like the center of the universe.

translation: Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect. For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife, dissembling, and ostentation.
book_theme: retreat into oneself; opinion as the source of disturbance

meaning_fields.teaching: Stop overcomplicating your responses and choices. When you stick to what's genuinely sound and right—without the performance, without the games—you eliminate most of the stress and conflict in your life. The straight path is the peaceful one.
meaning_fields.emotions: exhaustion from pretending, frustration with unnecessary complexity, relief when you can just be direct, dread of being found out, the weight of maintaining a false image
meaning_fields.situations: You're in a meeting and realize you've been softening your real opinion to seem agreeable, and it's draining; A friend asks what you think and you catch yourself crafting an answer to impress them instead of telling the truth; You're working hard to manage how others perceive you and it's eating up mental energy; You make a simple choice but then second-guess it because you're worried what people will think; You notice you're using extra words or gestures to convince someone of something you already know is right
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis)—the way things actually work, stripped of human invention; virtue—choosing what is genuinely excellent rather than what looks good; simplicity as strength; the difference between authentic action and performance.

translation: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up. Am I then yet unwilling to go about that, for which I myself was born and brought forth into this world? Or was I made for this, to lay me down, and make much of myself in a warm bed? 'O but this is pleasing.' And was it then for this that thou wert born, that thou mightest enjoy pleasure? Was it not in very truth for this, that thou mightest always be busy and in action? Seest thou not how all things in the world besides, how every tree md plant, how sparrows and ants, spiders and bees: how all in their kind are intent as it were orderly to perform whatsoever (towards the preservation of this orderly universe) naturally doth become and belong unto thin? And wilt not thou do that, which belongs unto a man to do? Wilt not thou run to do that, which thy nature doth require? 'But thou must have some rest.' Yes, thou must. Nature hath of that also, as well as of eating and drinking, allowed thee a certain stint. But thou guest beyond thy stint, and beyond that which would suffice, and in matter of action, there thou comest short of that which thou mayest. It must needs be therefore, that thou dost not love thyself, for if thou didst, thou wouldst also love thy nature, and that which thy nature doth propose unto herself as her end. Others, as many as take pleasure in their trade and profession, can even pine themselves at their works, and neglect their bodies and their food for it; and doest thou less honour thy nature, than an ordinary mechanic his trade; or a good dancer his art? than a covetous man his silver, and vainglorious man applause? These to whatsoever they take an affection, can be content to want their meat and sleep, to further that every one which he affects: and shall actions tending to the common good of human society, seem more vile unto thee, or worthy of less respect and intention?
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: Waking up Monday morning and dreading work, scrolling on your phone instead of getting out of bed. Choosing comfort and rest when you know you should be tackling something important. Spending the evening on entertainment instead of working on a project that matters to your community. Feeling torn between the ease of staying in bed and the pull of your daily responsibilities. Watching someone else dedicate themselves intensely to their passion—their art or craft or business—while you hold back from doing the same with your own work.
meaning_fields.teaching: You were made for action and contribution, not comfort. When you choose laziness and pleasure over work, you're actually betraying yourself—because your real nature isn't to be coddled. Look at how everything in nature does its job without complaining: trees grow, ants work, bees build. If a craftsman or artist can sacrifice sleep and food for their trade, why would you do less for work that serves the common good? Not loving your nature means avoiding the action your nature was designed for.
meaning_fields.emotions: The seductive pull of staying comfortable and warm instead of facing the day. Resentment at having to get up and work. Guilt about not doing enough. Envy or admiration when you see someone else fully committed to their work. The shame of knowing you're capable of more but choosing ease instead. Frustration with your own resistance and laziness.
meaning_fields.concepts: Duty (the obligations your nature requires of you). Acting according to nature (doing what you are designed and built to do, not what your momentary desires push you toward). The natural order (how all things in the world fulfill their role without complaint). Self-love properly understood (loving yourself means honoring what you actually are, not indulging every want).

translation: How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and tranquillity!
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: You can clear out the noise in your head much faster than you think. The anxious thoughts, the scenarios you keep replaying, the worries about what might happen—they're not as stuck there as they feel. You have the power to set them down and find quiet.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety, overwhelm, mental restlessness, the pressure of racing thoughts, feeling trapped in your own head
meaning_fields.situations: You're lying awake at 3 a.m. replaying an awkward conversation from work. Your mind won't stop spinning through worst-case scenarios about a presentation tomorrow. You've been stewing on an insult a friend made and can't shake it. You're at a family dinner but mentally rehearsing an argument that happened last week. You sit down to focus on something important but your head is full of random fears and "what-ifs".
meaning_fields.concepts: Turbulent adventitious imaginations refers to unwanted thoughts that are not essential to your nature but pile up like debris. The passage draws on Stoic physics: just as a still pond naturally reflects clearly without effort, your mind naturally settles when you stop feeding it false impressions. "According to nature" means acting from your rational core, not from the panic generated by imagined futures.

translation: Think thyself fit and worthy to speak, or to do anything that is according to nature, and let not the reproach, or report of some that may ensue upon it, ever deter thee. If it be right and honest to be spoken or done, undervalue not thyself so much, as to be discouraged from it. As for them, they have their own rational over-ruling part, and their own proper inclination: which thou must not stand and look about to take notice of, but go on straight, whither both thine own particular, and the common nature do lead thee; and the way of both these, is but one.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: You have the right to act on what you genuinely believe is honest and correct, even when others will judge you for it. Don't shrink away from doing the right thing just because it might trigger criticism or damage your reputation. Everyone else has their own mind and values—you can't control what they think, so focus only on what your own reason and human nature call you to do.
meaning_fields.emotions: Fear of judgment, shame about standing out, anxiety that speaking up will isolate you, self-doubt that makes you second-guess what you actually believe is right, frustration at being held back by what others might say
meaning_fields.situations: You want to give honest feedback in a meeting but worry your boss will see you as disloyal; you believe a friend is making a serious mistake but stay silent because confronting them feels risky; you know you should set a boundary with family but fear their anger or disappointment; you have an unpopular opinion at work and convince yourself it's safer to keep quiet; you recognize something unethical happening but tell yourself it's not your place to say anything
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (your rational choice or will)—the part of you that can reason about what is right; nature as the standard (both your individual nature and human nature in general)—what you're built to do and be; logos (the rational order)—the shared reason that should guide both you and everyone else; virtue as the only reliable guide to action, independent of external opinion

translation: I continue my course by actions according to nature, until I fall and cease, breathing out my last breath into that air, by which continually breathed in I did live; and falling upon that earth, out of whose gifts and fruits my father gathered his seed, my mother her blood, and my nurse her milk, out of which for so many years I have been provided, both of meat and drink. And lastly, which beareth me that tread upon it, and beareth with me that so many ways do abuse it, or so freely make use of it, so many ways to so many ends.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: You're grinding through another day at work and feel like you're just going through the motions—showing up, doing your job, trying to get through it. You catch yourself worrying about what comes after retirement or what legacy you'll leave. You're standing outside and suddenly notice how much you depend on things you take for granted—food, water, shelter—that come from the earth. You're overwhelmed by how many people are taking, using, and demanding from the world's resources, including yourself.
meaning_fields.teaching: You're part of a continuous chain of life that started long before you and will continue after you die. Everything you need—your body, your food, your existence—comes from the earth and returns to it. Showing up and doing your work faithfully, using what nature gives you responsibly, and accepting that you're just one person among billions all drawing from the same source—that's what it means to live according to your place in nature. There's peace in accepting this temporary role rather than pretending you're separate or entitled to more.
meaning_fields.emotions: Humility mixed with strange comfort; feeling small but also connected to something larger; acceptance of mortality; gratitude for ordinary things you normally overlook; relief at letting go of the need to be special or permanent; sometimes dread when you think about death, sometimes calm when you remember your debts to the earth.
meaning_fields.concepts: Living according to nature (the Stoic idea that virtue means aligning yourself with the rational order of the universe, not fighting it). Interconnection and debt—your body is literally made of the earth's gifts; you owe your existence to sources beyond yourself. Temporary participation (you're not an owner of anything, just a temporary user). Acceptance of your place in the natural cycle rather than seeing yourself as separate or superior to it.

translation: No man can admire thee for thy sharp acute language, such is thy natural disability that way. Be it so: yet there be many other good things, for the want of which thou canst not plead the want or natural ability. Let them be seen in thee, which depend wholly from thee; sincerity, gravity, laboriousness, contempt of pleasures; be not querulous, be Content with little, be kind, be free; avoid all superfluity, all vain prattling; be magnanimous. Doest not thou perceive, how many things there be, which notwithstanding any pretence of natural indisposition and unfitness, thou mightest have performed and exhibited, and yet still thou doest voluntarily continue drooping downwards? Or wilt thou say that it is through defect of thy natural constitution, that thou art constrained to murmur, to be base and wretched to flatter; now to accuse, and now to please, and pacify thy body: to be vainglorious, to be so giddy-headed., and unsettled in thy thoughts? nay (witnesses be the Gods) of all these thou mightest have been rid long ago: only, this thou must have been contented with, to have borne the blame of one that is somewhat slow and dull, wherein thou must so exercise thyself, as one who neither doth much take to heart this his natural defect, nor yet pleaseth himself in it.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: You blame your poor performance on bad timing, lack of talent, or circumstances beyond your control, even though you know you could try harder. Someone at work keeps saying they're not good with numbers or organization, but you notice they simply don't put in the effort. You find yourself making excuses for why you can't be patient, kind, or disciplined—saying "that's just how I am"—while watching someone else change habits through deliberate practice. You tell yourself you're naturally bad at public speaking so you don't bother preparing. A friend constantly complains about being stressed and unfocused, blaming their brain, but never actually attempts the simple routines that might help.
meaning_fields.teaching: You cannot blame your character flaws on nature or ability. Whatever real limitations you have, you can always choose sincerity, hard work, kindness, self-control, and gratitude—these depend entirely on you. The things you do wrong—complaining, flattery, self-pity, restlessness—are choices, not necessities. Stop hiding behind excuses and start owning what you can change right now.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at your own excuses, shame when you catch yourself blaming circumstances, stubborn resistance to admitting you could do better, a mix of defensive self-pity and quiet knowing that you're capable of more.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (moral choice)—the idea that your character comes from what you choose to do, not from what you were born with. Nature (physis) and determinism—the false belief that your behavior is fixed by your temperament. Arete (excellence)—virtue is not a talent you either have or lack; it is developed through action.

translation: Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation. Others there be, who though they stand not upon retaliation, to require any, yet they think with themselves nevertheless, that such a one is their debtor, and they know as their word is what they have done. Others again there be, who when they have done any such thing, do not so much as know what they have done; but are like unto the vine, which beareth her grapes, and when once she hath borne her own proper fruit, is contented and seeks for no further recompense. As a horse after a race, and a hunting dog when he hath hunted, and a bee when she hath made her honey, look not for applause and commendation; so neither doth that man that rightly doth understand his own nature when he hath done a good turn: but from one doth proceed to do another, even as the vine after she hath once borne fruit in her own proper season, is ready for another time. Thou therefore must be one of them, who what they do, barely do it without any further thought, and are in a manner insensible of what they do. 'Nay but,' will some reply perchance, 'this very thing a rational man is bound unto, to understand what it is, that he doeth.' For it is the property, say they, of one that is naturally sociable, to be sensible, that he doth operate sociably: nay, and to desire, that the party him self that is sociably dealt with, should be sensible of it too. I answer, That which thou sayest is true indeed, but the true meaning of that which is said, thou dost not understand. And therefore art thou one of those first, whom I mentioned. For they also are led by a probable appearance of reason. But if thou dost desire to understand truly what it is that is said, fear not that thou shalt therefore give over any sociable action.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: A friend helps you move, and when you try to thank them, they brush it off and move on to something else. You find yourself waiting for an acknowledgment that never comes. // You do a colleague a favor—cover their meeting, pick up a project—and you can't help mentally tracking it, waiting for them to return the favor. // After volunteering at an event, you notice the organizers thanked everyone publicly except you, and you spend the day replaying your contributions. // You give someone money when they're short on rent, and weeks later they haven't mentioned it, much less paid you back or shown gratitude. // You spend hours helping a friend with a problem, and they casually move on without even saying thanks, like it didn't cost you anything.
meaning_fields.teaching: When you do something good, let it be complete in itself—don't carry a mental ledger waiting for thanks or repayment. The natural world works this way: a vine produces grapes and asks nothing in return, a bee makes honey without expecting applause. If you do good work and then keep score, you're not actually helping—you're making a transaction and waiting to be repaid. Understanding your nature means recognizing that helping others *is* your function, like digestion is for your body, not something you do to earn something back.
meaning_fields.emotions: Resentment that builds when help goes unacknowledged. The exhausting weight of keeping mental score. Disappointment when someone doesn't recognize your sacrifice. Bitterness that grows when you wait for gratitude that never comes. The hollow feeling of doing something good and feeling invisible afterward.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis)—your essential function as a rational and social being is to act for the common good, the way a bee's nature is to make honey. Virtue and natural function are one—acting well *is* what you're made for, not a favor you do expecting repayment. The difference between instrumental action (doing something *to get* something) and action as living out your nature (doing something because that's what a human does).

translation: The form of the Athenians' prayer did run thus: 'O rain, rain, good Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.' Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not every one for himself in particular alone.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: When you pray or ask for something, don't only think about yourself. Ask for what benefits everyone, not just what helps you personally. Real prayer is either total surrender to what happens, or it's asking for the good of the whole community—never just personal gain.
meaning_fields.emotions: Guilt about wanting things only for yourself, the relief of thinking beyond yourself, frustration with people who only care about their own needs, the pull between self-interest and the common good
meaning_fields.situations: You're about to ask your boss for a promotion but pause—wondering if you should actually be hoping the whole team gets stronger; A relative prays only for their own health while you're in the hospital; You catch yourself wishing for rain only because you have outdoor plans, then realize the farmers need it more; Your friend constantly asks the universe for their specific desires without thinking about others; You're negotiating something and realize you could either push for your maximum benefit or propose something fair for both sides
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (human nature is social and interconnected—we are part of a larger whole, not isolated individuals); duty and alignment with the universal order (acting according to nature means considering the community, not just yourself); the distinction between legitimate need and selfish appetite (praying for what truly serves everyone versus what only serves one person's desires)

translation: As we say commonly, The physician hath prescribed unto this man, riding; unto another, cold baths; unto a third, to go barefoot: so it is alike to say, The nature of the universe hath prescribed unto this man sickness, or blindness, or some loss, or damage or some such thing. For as there, when we say of a physician, that he hath prescribed anything, our meaning is, that he hath appointed this for that, as subordinate and conducing to health: so here, whatsoever doth happen unto any, is ordained unto him as a thing subordinate unto the fates, and therefore do we say of such things, that they do συμβαίνειν, that is, happen, or fall together; as of square stones, when either in walls, or pyramids in a certain position they fit one another, and agree as it were in an harmony, the masons say, that they do συμβαίνειν; as if thou shouldest say, fall together: so that in the general, though the things be divers that make it, yet the consent or harmony itself is but one. And as the whole world is made up of all the particular bodies of the world, one perfect and complete body, of the same nature that particular bodies; so is the destiny of particular causes and events one general one, of the same nature that particular causes are. What I now say, even they that are mere idiots are not ignorant of: for they say commonly τοῦτο ἔφερεν ἀυτῷ, that is, This his destiny hath brought upon him. This therefore is by the fates properly and particularly brought upon this, as that unto this in particular is by the physician prescribed. These therefore let us accept of in like manner, as we do those that are prescribed unto us our physicians. For them also in themselves shall We find to contain many harsh things, but we nevertheless, in hope of health, and recovery, accept of them. Let the fulfilling and accomplishment of those things which the common nature hath determined, be unto thee as thy health. Accept then, and be pleased with whatsoever doth happen, though otherwise harsh and un-pleasing, as tending to that end, to the health and welfare of the universe, and to Jove's happiness and prosperity. For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced, had it not conduced to the good of the universe. For neither doth any ordinary particular nature bring anything to pass, that is not to whatsoever is within the sphere of its own proper administration and government agreeable and subordinate. For these two considerations then thou must be well pleased with anything that doth happen unto thee. First, because that for thee properly it was brought to pass, and unto thee it was prescribed; and that from the very beginning by the series and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto thee. And secondly, because the good success and perfect welfare, and indeed the very continuance of Him, that is the Administrator of the whole, doth in a manner depend on it. For the whole (because whole, therefore entire and perfect) is maimed, and mutilated, if thou shalt cut off anything at all, whereby the coherence, and contiguity as of parts, so of causes, is maintained and preserved. Of which certain it is, that thou doest (as much as lieth in thee) cut off, and in some sort violently take somewhat away, as often as thou art displeased with anything that happeneth.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: A parent dealing with their child's serious illness and struggling to accept it as anything other than random cruelty. Someone who lost their job and can't stop viewing it as pure bad luck that derailed their life. A person facing chronic pain who feels punished by their body rather than seeing it as part of any larger order. Someone experiencing a relationship breakdown and viewing it only as a personal failure rather than something that serves a larger purpose. A worker frustrated by a setback on a major project, seeing it only as an obstacle instead of something that might be necessary.
meaning_fields.teaching: Hard things that happen to you aren't random punishment—they're prescribed for you specifically, like medicine a doctor orders. Just as you accept bitter medicine because you trust it leads to health, accept difficult events because they're part of the universal order working toward the good of the whole. Rejecting what happens is like refusing your medicine; it cuts you off from the coherence that holds everything together. You're stronger and more at peace when you stop fighting reality and instead ask what purpose this serves.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at unfairness or bad luck. Resistance and resentment toward pain, loss, or setback. Feeling singled out or punished. The weight of accepting something you never wanted. Relief when you stop fighting what you can't change. A strange calm that comes from trusting you're part of something bigger.
meaning_fields.concepts: Fate and cosmic order—the idea that events aren't chaotic but connected in a rational chain (symphainein, "falling together" like stones in a wall). Divine rationality or providence—the assumption that the universe is governed by an intelligent principle (referenced as Jove, or the "Administrator") that includes your suffering in a larger design. Nature according to reason—the view that accepting your role in the whole is living in accordance with reason, not against it. The interconnectedness of all causes—nothing can be removed without damaging the whole system.

translation: Be not discontented, be not disheartened, be not out of hope, if often it succeed not so well with thee punctually and precisely to do all things according to the right dogmata, but being once cast off, return unto them again: and as for those many and more frequent occurrences, either of worldly distractions, or human infirmities, which as a man thou canst not but in some measure be subject unto, be not thou discontented with them; but however, love and affect that only which thou dust return unto: a philosopher's life, and proper occupation after the most exact manner. And when thou dust return to thy philosophy, return not unto it as the manner of some is, after play and liberty as it were, to their schoolmasters and pedagogues; but as they that have sore eyes to their sponge and egg: or as another to his cataplasm; or as others to their fomentations: so shalt not thou make it a matter of ostentation at all to obey reason but of ease and comfort. And remember that philosophy requireth nothing of thee, but what thy nature requireth, and wouldest thou thyself desire anything that is not according to nature? for which of these sayest thou; that which is according to nature or against it, is of itself more kind and pleasing? Is it not for that respect especially, that pleasure itself is to so many men's hurt and overthrow, most prevalent, because esteemed commonly most kind, and natural? But consider well whether magnanimity rather, and true liberty, and true simplicity, and equanimity, and holiness; whether these be not most kind and natural? And prudency itself, what more kind and amiable than it, when thou shalt truly consider with thyself, what it is through all the proper objects of thy rational intellectual faculty currently to go on without any fall or stumble? As for the things of the world, their true nature is in a manner so involved with obscurity, that unto many philosophers, and those no mean ones, they seemed altogether incomprehensible, and the Stoics themselves, though they judge them not altogether incomprehensible, yet scarce and not without much difficulty, comprehensible, so that all assent of ours is fallible, for who is he that is infallible in his conclusions? From the nature of things, pass now unto their subjects and matter: how temporary, how vile are they I such as may be in the power and possession of some abominable loose liver, of some common strumpet, of some notorious oppressor and extortioner. Pass from thence to the dispositions of them that thou doest ordinarily converse with, how hardly do we bear, even with the most loving and amiable! that I may not say, how hard it is for us to bear even with our own selves, in such obscurity, and impurity of things: in such and so continual a flux both of the substances and time; both of the motions themselves, and things moved; what it is that we can fasten upon; either to honour, and respect especially; or seriously, and studiously to seek after; I cannot so much as conceive For indeed they are things contrary.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: You're going to fail at living perfectly by philosophy many times. When you do, don't beat yourself up—just come back to it. Philosophy shouldn't feel like punishment or showing off; it should feel like relief, like applying a soothing compress to a wound. The real comfort is in thinking clearly and acting justly, not in the fleeting pleasures that ruin people.
meaning_fields.emotions: Discouragement after failure, frustration with your own weakness, shame about not living up to your own standards, but also the quiet satisfaction that comes from trying again
meaning_fields.situations: You mess up at work or in a relationship and spiral, thinking you're a failure; you commit to being patient, then lose your temper and feel like giving up; you try to live by your values for a few days, slip back into old habits, and wonder if it's even worth trying; you see people around you pursuing status and money and it looks easier than your struggle to act fairly; you're exhausted from trying to think clearly about complicated situations and just want to relax without judgment
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis)—what humans are actually made for, not what we want in the moment; rational faculty—your capacity to think clearly and choose wisely; magnanimity—the courage to do what's right without needing credit; equanimity—staying steady when things go wrong; the Stoic idea that external things are not truly good or bad, just temporary and easily lost

translation: Thou must comfort thyself in the expectation of thy natural dissolution, and in the meantime not grieve at the delay; but rest contented in those two things. First, that nothing shall happen unto thee, which is not according to the nature of the universe. Secondly, that it is in thy power, to do nothing against thine own proper God, and inward spirit. For it is not in any man's power to constrain thee to transgress against him.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: You can find peace by accepting two things: whatever happens to you fits into the natural order of the universe, and no one can force you to act against your own conscience. These certainties are enough to steady you through any difficulty.
meaning_fields.emotions: Worry about the future, grief over delays and setbacks, fear that circumstances will overwhelm you or force you into compromises, anxiety about losing control
meaning_fields.situations: A coworker pressures you to cut corners on a project and you're afraid refusing will cost you the job; you're sick and anxious about when you'll recover, wondering if the delay means you're falling behind; your boss demands you take credit for something unethical or stay silent about a problem; you face a loss and can't stop dreading what comes next; you're tempted to bend your values to fit in or succeed, but feel the internal conflict
meaning_fields.concepts: Logos (the rational order running through nature and the universe); the divine spark within you (also called prohairesis or moral choice); natural dissolution (the acceptance of death and change as part of how things are meant to work); constraint versus freedom (the Stoic distinction between what is truly in your power—your will and character—and what is not)

translation: What is the use that now at this present I make of my soul? Thus from time to time and upon all occasions thou must put this question to thyself; what is now that part of mine which they call the rational mistress part, employed about? Whose soul do I now properly possess? a child's? or a youth's? a woman's? or a tyrant's? some brute, or some wild beast's soul?
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: You're scrolling through social media at 2 AM instead of sleeping, and you catch yourself but don't stop. You're in a meeting and realize you've spent the last ten minutes mentally rehearsing an argument instead of listening. You're about to send an angry text you know you'll regret. You're at work choosing the easier, lazier option because no one will notice. You're reacting to your kid or partner with irritation when you know they didn't deserve it.
meaning_fields.teaching: Right now, in this moment, you're operating from some part of yourself—ask which one. Are you thinking clearly and acting deliberately, or are you running on impulse, reactivity, appetite, or ego? The question isn't about judgment; it's about waking up to what's actually driving you so you can choose differently.
meaning_fields.emotions: Autopilot numbness, shame at not being your best self, the uncomfortable jolt of catching yourself mid-drift, frustration that you acted worse than you wanted to, the gap between who you meant to be and who you just were.
meaning_fields.concepts: The rational faculty (logos)—the distinctly human capacity to observe yourself, make deliberate choices, and align action with reason. The contrast between using your mind to steer your life versus letting instinct, appetite, wounded ego, or cowardice run the show. The idea that the soul can operate at different levels—childish reactivity, youthful passion, tyrannical control, bestial impulse—and that noticing which level you're on is the first step to reclaiming it.

translation: What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this. For if a man shall hear things mentioned as good, which are really good indeed, such as are prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude, after so much heard and conceived, he cannot endure to hear of any more, for the word good is properly spoken of them. But as for those which by the vulgar are esteemed good, if he shall hear them mentioned as good, he doth hearken for more. He is well contented to hear, that what is spoken by the comedian, is but familiarly and popularly spoken, so that even the vulgar apprehend the difference. For why is it else, that this offends not and needs not to be excused, when virtues are styled good: but that which is spoken in commendation of wealth, pleasure, or honour, we entertain it only as merrily and pleasantly spoken? Proceed therefore, and inquire further, whether it may not be that those things also which being mentioned upon the stage were merrily, and with great applause of the multitude, scoffed at with this jest, that they that possessed them had not in all the world of their own, (such was their affluence and plenty) so much as a place where to avoid their excrements. Whether, I say, those ought not also in very deed to be much respected, and esteemed of, as the only things that are truly good.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: Someone gets promoted and your friends congratulate them endlessly, but you notice they seem more stressed and unhappy than before. You're offered a high-paying job that would make you look successful, but it would mean sacrificing time with your family and doing work you don't respect. You see wealthy people on social media who seem empty and anxious despite having everything. You're tempted to chase money or status because that's what everyone around you values, but something in you knows it won't actually make you better or happier. You catch yourself about to brag about something you own and realize you don't actually care about the thing itself—only what others will think.
meaning_fields.teaching: The truly good things—wisdom, self-control, fairness, courage—satisfy you completely when you recognize them. But the things everyone calls good—money, pleasure, reputation—never satisfy because there's always more to chase. Notice how easily we joke about the emptiness of wealth and status, yet we still pursue them anyway. Real value lives only in what makes you genuinely better as a person, not in what impresses others.
meaning_fields.emotions: The hollow feeling of achieving something you thought you wanted and finding it meaningless. Anxiety about whether you're chasing the wrong things. Frustration at watching yourself want approval through possessions. Relief when you see through the trap. Confusion about why society celebrates things that don't actually matter.
meaning_fields.concepts: The distinction between things that are truly good (arete—excellence of character, which develops your capacity for right action) and things the crowd calls good but are actually indifferents (adiaphora—external circumstances like wealth that don't change your moral nature). The idea that virtue is self-sufficient and complete, while external goods create perpetual wanting. The Stoic premise that only what is within your control—your judgment and character—can truly benefit you.

translation: All that I consist of, is either form or matter. No corruption can reduce either of these unto nothing: for neither did I of nothing become a subsistent creature. Every part of mine then will by mutation be disposed into a certain part of the whole world, and that in time into another part; and so _in infinitum;_ by which kind of mutation, I also became what I am, and so did they that begot me, and they before them, and so upwards _in infinitum_. For so we may be allowed to speak, though the age and government of the world, be to some certain periods of time limited, and confined.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: You're lying awake at 3 AM worried about dying and leaving nothing behind. You're at a funeral and it hits you that everyone you've ever known will also be gone someday. You're in your 40s wondering if your career mattered or if it was just busy work. You watch your parent age and realize they won't be around to see your children grow up. You're depressed and feel like your existence doesn't really add up to anything meaningful.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your body will break down and scatter. Your matter will become part of other things—soil, air, other bodies. This isn't failure or loss; it's how the whole system works and always has worked. You came from this same recycling process, as did your parents and everyone before them. Nothing is wasted or reduced to nothing; everything just transforms.
meaning_fields.emotions: fear of death and meaninglessness, dread about being forgotten, despair about impermanence, the ache of watching loved ones age, anxiety about leaving nothing behind, a crushing sense that nothing matters
meaning_fields.concepts: Eternal recurrence (the idea that matter cycles endlessly through the world); the distinction between form and matter in physics; continuity and change as natural law; being part of a larger whole; the material view of existence that rejects both creation from nothing and annihilation into nothing

translation: Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves with themselves, and their own proper operations. And as for their first inclination and motion, that they take from themselves. But their progress is right to the end and object, which is in their way, as it were, and lieth just before them: that is, which is feasible and possible, whether it be that which at the first they proposed to themselves, or no. For which reason also such actions are termed κατορθώσεις, to intimate the directness of the way, by which they are achieved. Nothing must be thought to belong to a man, which doth not belong unto him as he is a man. These, the event of purposes, are not things required in a man. The nature of man doth not profess any such things. The final ends and consummations of actions are nothing at all to a man's nature. The end therefore of a man, or the _summum bonum_ whereby that end is fulfilled, cannot consist in the consummation of actions purposed and intended. Again, concerning these outward worldly things, were it so that any of them did properly belong unto man, then would it not belong unto man, to condemn them and to stand in opposition with them. Neither would he be praiseworthy that can live without them; or he good, (if these were good indeed) who of his own accord doth deprive himself of any of them. But we see contrariwise, that the more a man doth withdraw himself from these wherein external pomp and greatness doth consist, or any other like these; or the better he doth bear with the loss of these, the better he is accounted.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: You work hard on a project and pour yourself into it, but the outcome depends on factors outside your control—your boss's decision, market timing, client response—and you're frustrated because you can't guarantee success no matter how well you execute. You want a promotion and do everything right, but the decision gets postponed or goes to someone else. You prepare thoroughly for a job interview but don't hear back, and you spiral wondering if you wasted effort. You finish a difficult task perfectly but it gets rejected or ignored by others, and you feel cheated that your work didn't "count." You're trying to build a skill, but external circumstances—lack of opportunity, bad luck, someone else's interference—prevent you from reaching the goal you set.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your only real job is to think clearly and act with integrity in whatever situation you face right now. The actual results—whether you succeed, win approval, get promoted, or achieve your goal—are not up to you, and counting on them will destroy your peace. What matters is whether you reasoned well and did the right thing. That's the win. Everything else belongs to luck, and a good person proves their goodness precisely by doing excellent work regardless of whether the world rewards them for it.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at the gap between effort and results; anxiety about outcomes you can't control; resentment when your work doesn't get the recognition you expected; the hollow feeling of succeeding at the process but "failing" at the result; disappointment when circumstances block your intended goals; the temptation to cut corners because results seem arbitrary anyway.
meaning_fields.concepts: Dichotomy of control (what is yours to direct versus what belongs to circumstance); natural function (what reasoning itself is designed to do, versus external achievements); virtue as the only true good (internal excellence independent of worldly outcomes); κατορθώσεις—right action characterized by directness and proper reasoning, not by whether the world validates it.

translation: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it with the assiduity of these cogitations. As for example. Wheresoever thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy. But thou mayest live at the Court, there then also mayest thou live well and happy. Again, that which everything is made for, he is also made unto that, and cannot but naturally incline unto it. That which anything doth naturally incline unto, therein is his end. Wherein the end of everything doth consist, therein also doth his good and benefit consist. Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature. For that we are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated. Or can any man make any question of this, that whatsoever is naturally worse and inferior, is ordinarily subordinated to that which is better? and that those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that have, those best that have rational souls?
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: Someone starting a new job in an unfamiliar place and doubting they can be happy there. A person stuck in an environment they didn't choose—a new city, a corporate office, a school—wondering if they have to change their whole life to make it work. Someone realizing they've been isolating themselves and feeling the gap between their solitary habits and their actual capacity to connect. A person watching their thoughts drift toward cynicism or complaint about their surroundings, noticing the pattern building day after day. Someone at a crossroads wondering whether their good life depends on external circumstances or something they control internally.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your mind becomes shaped by the thoughts you repeatedly dwell on—they dye your soul like a stain that sets deeper over time. So choose your habitual thoughts carefully, because they're building your character. You can live well anywhere, even in difficult circumstances, if you remember that humans are made for connection and community. Your nature as a rational being pulls you toward living with and for others, and that connection—not your location or comfort—is where your real good lies.
meaning_fields.emotions: Doubt about whether you can be okay in your current situation. Homesickness or displacement. Loneliness even when surrounded by people. Frustration that your unhappiness feels tied to external things you can't control. A quiet sense that something is missing when you're isolated. Anxiety about whether you're wired wrong for your circumstances.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature and natural inclination (the idea that everything has a built-in purpose and direction). The soul as something actively shaped by habit and repeated thought patterns. Rationality as the defining human trait. The hierarchy of beings—that rational creatures stand above those without reason. Good as alignment with your actual nature, not external comfort. Society and community as fundamental goods, not luxuries.

translation: To desire things impossible is the part of a mad man. But it is a thing impossible, that wicked man should not commit some such things. Neither doth anything happen to any man, which in the ordinary course of nature as natural unto him doth not happen. Again, the same things happen unto others also. And truly, if either he that is ignorant that such a thing hath happened unto him, or he that is ambitious to be commended for his magnanimity, can be patient, and is not grieved: is it not a grievous thing, that either ignorance, or a vain desire to please and to be commended, should be more powerful and effectual than true prudence? As for the things themselves, they touch not the soul, neither can they have any access unto it: neither can they of themselves any ways either affect it, or move it. For she herself alone can affect and move herself, and according as the dogmata and opinions are, which she doth vouchsafe herself; so are those things which, as accessories, have any co-existence with her.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: Bad things happen to everyone as part of how the world works—not as punishment aimed at you. The only real damage comes when you believe the event is shameful or catastrophic, not from the event itself. What actually hurts you is your judgment about it, not the thing that happened. You can choose whether to let an external event wound your sense of yourself.
meaning_fields.emotions: Shame about misfortune, defensiveness when something goes wrong, the sting of being treated badly or failing, the urge to hide what happened or prove you're better than people think, resentment that bad luck found you instead of someone else
meaning_fields.situations: You make a public mistake at work and can't stop imagining what people think of you. A colleague takes credit for your idea and you feel humiliated and unfairly targeted. You get rejected or criticized and spiral into feeling like something is deeply wrong with you. Someone lies about you and you obsess over correcting the record to protect your reputation. Something genuinely bad happens—illness, loss, failure—and you feel singled out by fate.
meaning_fields.concepts: Amor fati (accepting what happens as part of nature's course, not injustice). Prohairesis (your capacity to choose your own judgment, separate from external events). The distinction between what is "up to you" (your beliefs and responses) and what is not (outcomes, other people's actions, fortune). The Stoic claim that virtue and harm to the soul are the only real goods and evils.

translation: After one consideration, man is nearest unto us; as we are bound to do them good, and to bear with them. But as he may oppose any of our true proper actions, so man is unto me but as a thing indifferent: even as the sun, or the wind, or some wild beast. By some of these it may be, that some operation or other of mine, may be hindered; however, of my mind and resolution itself, there can be no let or impediment, by reason of that ordinary constant both exception (or reservation wherewith it inclineth) and ready conversion of objects; from that which may not be, to that which may be, which in the prosecution of its inclinations, as occasion serves, it doth observe. For by these the mind doth turn and convert any impediment whatsoever, to be her aim and purpose. So that what before was the impediment, is now the principal object of her working; and that which before was in her way, is now her readiest way.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: Other people matter to you and you owe them kindness, but they cannot control your mind or your choices. When someone blocks your plans, obstacles aren't failures—they become the actual work you need to do. Your real power lies in adjusting how you respond, not in forcing circumstances to go your way.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration when people get in your way, helplessness when plans fall apart, the sting of being thwarted, relief when you realize what you can actually control, clarity when you stop fighting reality
meaning_fields.situations: Your boss denies a project you prepared for and you're reassigned to something unexpected; a family member says no to something you want and you have to figure out a different path; someone sabotages your work and you decide how to handle it instead of getting revenge; you miss a deadline because of someone else's delay and have to pivot your strategy; a colleague makes your job harder and you realize their interference is just part of the terrain you're navigating
meaning_fields.concepts: Duty (we must genuinely care for others' wellbeing as human beings), indifference in Stoic philosophy (certain external outcomes simply don't matter to your character), prohairesis (your choice and mental direction remain entirely yours), obstacles as the path (setbacks become material for virtue, not defeats)

translation: Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of. For it is the very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use, and by whom also thy life is governed.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: You're facing a difficult decision at work and feel paralyzed by competing pressures—money, approval, comfort—but you realize that your judgment, your ability to think clearly, is what actually matters. Or: you're caught between doing what's easy and doing what's right, and you recognize that the part of you that can choose between them is the real you. Or: you're getting pulled into office drama or family conflict and suddenly notice that you have the power to step back and decide how to respond. Or: you're sitting at your desk with a dozen urgent demands and you remember that your capacity to prioritize and decide what genuinely matters is your actual strength. Or: you're recovering from a failure and realize that your mind—your ability to assess what happened and move forward—is the one thing no one can take from you.
meaning_fields.teaching: The most powerful thing in existence is the capacity to use everything else. In you, that capacity is your reason—your mind, your judgment, your ability to choose. When you honor that part of yourself above comfort, approval, or circumstance, you tap into the governing force of your own life. Everything else—money, status, other people's opinions—is material. Your mind is the tool that puts all of it to use.
meaning_fields.emotions: Feeling powerless or overwhelmed, then discovering you have more control than you realized. Recognizing your own capacity when everything feels out of control. Respect for your own judgment. Clarity that cuts through noise and confusion. The relief of finding solid ground in yourself when nothing external is stable.
meaning_fields.concepts: Hegemonikon (the ruling principle, the commanding faculty of reason in each person). Nature and natural law (the organizing principle of the universe that also governs human thought and choice). The distinction between what is in your control (your judgment) and what is not (external events, others' opinions). Virtue as the alignment of your reason with universal reason.

translation: That which doth not hurt the city itself; cannot hurt any citizen. This rule thou must remember to apply and make use of upon every conceit and apprehension of wrong. If the whole city be not hurt by this, neither am I certainly. And if the whole be not, why should I make it my private grievance? consider rather what it is wherein he is overseen that is thought to have done the wrong. Again, often meditate how swiftly all things that subsist, and all things that are done in the world, are carried away, and as it were conveyed out of sight: for both the substance themselves, we see as a flood, are in a continual flux; and all actions in a perpetual change; and the causes themselves, subject to a thousand alterations, neither is there anything almost, that may ever be said to be now settled and constant. Next unto this, and which follows upon it, consider both the infiniteness of the time already past, and the immense vastness of that which is to come, wherein all things are to be resolved and annihilated. Art not thou then a very fool, who for these things, art either puffed up with pride, or distracted with cares, or canst find in thy heart to make such moans as for a thing that would trouble thee for a very long time? Consider the whole universe whereof thou art but a very little part, and the whole age of the world together, whereof but a short and very momentary portion is allotted unto thee, and all the fates and destinies together, of which how much is it that comes to thy part and share! Again: another doth trespass against me. Let him look to that. He is master of his own disposition, and of his own operation. I for my part am in the meantime in possession of as much, as the common nature would have me to possess: and that which mine own nature would have me do, I do.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: Someone cuts you off in traffic and you feel your anger rising. A friend doesn't invite you to their wedding and you keep dwelling on it for weeks. Your boss dismisses your idea in a meeting and you replay the moment obsessively. A family member makes a critical comment and you can't let it go, imagining how you'll respond next time.
meaning_fields.teaching: When someone wrongs you, stop and ask: has this actually harmed the whole community, or just your pride? Most slights fade into nothing within days. You're torturing yourself over something tiny that the universe will forget. Do your job, act well—that's all that's yours to control. What others do is their problem, not yours.
meaning_fields.emotions: Resentment that won't let go, the hot feeling of being slighted or disrespected, replaying an insult over and over, feeling like you need to prove yourself or get even, the weight of carrying a grudge.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (living in accordance with your role and duty, not getting tangled in others' choices). Impermanence (things that feel huge today will be dust tomorrow). The dichotomy of control (his offense is his responsibility; your response is yours). Cosmological perspective (you are one grain in an infinite universe across infinite time).

translation: Let not that chief commanding part of thy soul be ever subject to any variation through any corporal either pain or pleasure, neither suffer it to be mixed with these, but let it both circumscribe itself, and confine those affections to their own proper parts and members. But if at any time they do reflect and rebound upon the mind and understanding (as in an united and compacted body it must needs;) then must thou not go about to resist sense and feeling, it being natural. However let not thy understanding to this natural sense and feeling, which whether unto our flesh pleasant or painful, is unto us nothing properly, add an opinion of either good or bad and all is well.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: Your mind has a choice that your body doesn't. Pain and pleasure will hit you—that's physical and automatic. But you get to decide whether you add a story on top of it, treating it as good or bad. Keep that decision-making part of yourself separate from raw sensation, and you stay free.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration when physical discomfort feels like it's taking over your thinking; anxiety that pain means something's wrong with you; the grip of pleasure that makes you feel dependent; relief when you realize the sensation itself isn't the problem.
meaning_fields.situations: You wake up with back pain and immediately spiral into worry about your health and whether you can work today. You eat something delicious and feel guilty afterward, letting that pleasure make you feel weak or indulgent. You get a headache during an important meeting and can't focus because you're fighting the discomfort instead of just noticing it. You injure yourself playing sports and have to separate the sharp pain itself from the story that you're broken or aging. You're sick and physical misery keeps dragging your thoughts toward catastrophe.
meaning_fields.concepts: The hegemonikon (ruling faculty or command center of consciousness)—the part of you that observes and makes judgments, distinct from physical sensation. Prohairesis (your power of choice)—you cannot control what your body feels, but you control the meaning you assign. The stoic dichotomy of control: your faculty of assent (whether you agree with an impression) belongs to you; raw sensation does not.

translation: To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: You're living rightly when you accept what comes your way without complaint and do what your conscience tells you is right. That inner voice isn't a burden—it's actually your connection to something larger and wiser than yourself. When you stop fighting reality and start following that guidance, you're no longer struggling alone.
meaning_fields.emotions: Resignation that transforms into peace; the relief of finally accepting what you can't change; the quiet satisfaction of knowing you did the right thing even when it was hard; the lightness that comes from dropping resentment about unfair circumstances.
meaning_fields.situations: You get passed over for a promotion you felt you deserved, and instead of spiraling, you refocus on doing good work anyway. You're facing a health diagnosis or loss, and you stop asking "why me?" and start asking what you can actually control and do about it. Your plans fall apart and you're forced to take a completely different path, but you move forward without bitterness. You make a difficult choice because it's the right thing to do, even though nobody will praise you for it. You're going through a boring, unglamorous job or phase of life and you choose to do it well rather than resent it.
meaning_fields.concepts: Living according to nature (acting in alignment with your truest self and reason, not fighting reality). The daimon or inner guide (your conscience or moral compass—the part of you that knows right from wrong). Contentment as an active choice, not passive acceptance. The idea that you're never truly alone because you're part of something interconnected and purposeful.

translation: Be not angry neither with him whose breath, neither with him whose arm holes, are offensive. What can he do? such is his breath naturally, and such are his arm holes; and from such, such an effect, and such a smell must of necessity proceed. 'O, but the man (sayest thou) hath understanding in him, and might of himself know, that he by standing near, cannot choose but offend.' And thou also (God bless thee!) hast understanding. Let thy reasonable faculty, work upon his reasonable faculty; show him his fault, admonish him. If he hearken unto thee, thou hast cured him, and there will be no more occasion of anger.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: Someone at work stands too close during meetings and breathes heavily in your face; a family member has poor hygiene but gets upset when you mention it; a roommate leaves food out and the apartment smells, and you're frustrated they won't listen to reason; you're sitting next to someone on a bus whose body odor is intense and you're annoyed; a friend has a habit (loud chewing, coughing without covering) that drives you crazy and you want them to just fix it.
meaning_fields.teaching: Before you snap at someone for being annoying or gross, remember they might not even realize they're bothering you—and even if they do understand, blame won't help. Use your head instead. If you calmly point out the problem, they might actually change. That's the only way forward; anger just makes it worse.
meaning_fields.emotions: Disgust and annoyance at someone's physical habits; frustration that they won't change or seem oblivious; the urge to shame or snap at them; irritation that you have to deal with it at all.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (reasoned choice and agency)—recognizing that a person can think and choose differently if shown clearly. Oikeiosis (acting according to human nature)—our nature as humans includes the capacity for understanding, so appeal to that rather than react with anger. Pathē (reactive emotions like anger)—emotions that arise from judgment and can be redirected by reasoning.

Before you snap at someone for being annoying or gross, remember they might not even realize they're bothering you—and even if they do understand, blame won't help. Use your head instead. If you calmly point out the problem, they might actually change. That's the only way forward; anger just makes it worse.
Disgust and annoyance at someone's physical habits; frustration that they won't change or seem oblivious; the urge to shame or snap at them; irritation that you have to deal with it at all.
Prohairesis (reasoned choice and agency)—recognizing that a person can think and choose differently if shown clearly. Oikeiosis (acting according to human nature)—our nature as humans includes the capacity for understanding, so appeal to that rather than react with anger. Pathē (reactive emotions like anger)—emotions that arise from judgment and can be redirected by reasoning.

translation: 'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here. And if they will not suffer thee, then mayest thou leave thy life rather than thy calling, but so as one that doth not think himself anyways wronged. Only as one would say, Here is a smoke; I will out of it. And what a great matter is this! Now till some such thing force me out, I will continue free; neither shall any man hinder me to do what I will, and my will shall ever be by the proper nature of a reasonable and sociable creature, regulated and directed.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: You can maintain your integrity and your sense of purpose even when surrounded by people who don't share your values. If others absolutely force you to abandon your principles, you can leave—but that's a rare extreme. Most of the time, you have the freedom to act according to your own nature right now, even in a messy world full of people doing things you wouldn't do. That freedom comes from keeping your will aligned with reason, not from waiting for perfect conditions.
meaning_fields.situations: Your workplace is full of office politics and people cutting corners, but you keep doing honest work anyway. Someone is pressuring you to compromise your standards, and you're deciding whether to stay and hold the line or walk away. You're around people with crude values or bad behavior, and you're trying not to let it drag you down or make you cynical. You feel trapped by circumstances but realize you still control how you show up and what you stand for. You're waiting for life to improve before you act with integrity, but you realize the time to start is now.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at being around people who are nothing like you; temptation to compromise just to fit in; the feeling of being trapped or contaminated by others' behavior; quiet determination to keep your standards; relief that you don't actually need perfect conditions to do the right thing; fear that your principles are fragile or will break if tested.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis) in the Stoic sense means your essential function as a human being—to think rationally and live in community. Freedom in Marcus's view is not freedom from obstacles, but freedom to direct your will according to reason, which nobody can take from you. Adiaphoron—literally "indifferent things"—refers to external circumstances like where you live or who surrounds you. These don't define your character; only your choices do. Prosoche means mindful attention to what's in your control and what isn't.

translation: That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for community and society; and therefore hath it both made the things that are worse, for the best, and hath allied and knit together those which are best, as it were in an harmony. Seest thou not how it hath sub-ordinated, and co-ordinated? and how it hath distributed unto everything according to its worth? and those which have the pre-eminency and superiority above all, hath it united together, into a mutual consent and agreement.
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.teaching: Everything in nature is designed to work together as an interconnected system. Your role isn't to stand alone or compete for dominance—it's to function as part of a larger order where each thing has its proper place and purpose. When you act according to your nature, you're serving the whole community, not just yourself.
meaning_fields.emotions: Feeling isolated or self-important; resentment at having to cooperate with people you see as beneath you; anxiety about your status relative to others; frustration that the world doesn't revolve around your goals; relief when you stop fighting the structure of things.
meaning_fields.situations: You're promoted and struggle with the idea that you still answer to others above you; you're tempted to cut corners because rules seem to apply to everyone else; you resent doing unglamorous work that supports the organization; you feel superior to colleagues and wonder why you have to include them in decisions; you notice how a good team works when everyone accepts their role, even the hard ones.
meaning_fields.concepts: Logos (the rational principle governing nature and the universe); natural hierarchy (not domination, but a structure where everything serves the whole); community or koinonia (the interconnected web of society and nature); virtue in context (excellence expressed through your specific role, not through rebellion against order).

translation: How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy domestics? thy servants? Is it so with thee, that hitherto thou hast neither by word or deed wronged any of them? Remember withal through how many things thou hast already passed, and how many thou hast been able to endure; so that now the legend of thy life is full, and thy charge is accomplished. Again, how many truly good things have certainly by thee been discerned? how many pleasures, how many pains hast thou passed over with contempt? how many things eternally glorious hast thou despised? towards how many perverse unreasonable men hast thou carried thyself kindly, and discreetly?
book_theme: duty, rising to work, and acting according to nature

meaning_fields.situations: 1) You're middle-aged and wondering if you've treated people right—parents, spouse, kids, coworkers—and feeling like you might have let someone down. 2) You're exhausted after a difficult period and need to recognize that you've already proven you can handle hard things. 3) You're feeling proud or boastful about your life and need a reality check about what actually matters. 4) You're dealing with someone difficult or unreasonable and wondering if you handled it well. 5) You're tempted by something that seems glamorous or important and need to remember you've already learned better.
meaning_fields.teaching: Stop and honestly examine how you've treated the people actually in your life—not in grand moments, but in your everyday dealings with family, colleagues, and people who depend on you. You've already endured hard things and walked past empty temptations without falling for them; that's your real track record, and it's worth acknowledging. The question isn't whether you've been perfect, but whether you've treated people decently and lived according to what you actually know is right.
meaning_fields.emotions: Guilt about how you've treated someone close to you; exhaustion mixed with quiet pride in surviving difficulty; doubt about whether you've wasted your life; frustration with someone difficult; the pull of wanting credit or admiration for things that don't matter.
meaning_fields.concepts: Duty (the obligation to act rightly toward those dependent on you); living according to nature (acting in alignment with your actual values, not false desires); self-examination (brutally honest review of your character); the arc of a life (recognizing you've already passed through real tests and built a real record).
