translation: That which is a hindrance of the senses, is an evil to the sensitive nature. That which is a hindrance of the appetitive and prosecutive faculty, is an evil to the sensitive nature. As of the sensitive, so of the vegetative constitution, whatsoever is a hindrance unto it, is also in that respect an evil unto the same. And so likewise, whatsoever is a hindrance unto the mind and understanding, must needs be the proper evil of the reasonable nature. Now apply all those things unto thyself. Do either pain or pleasure seize on thee? Let the senses look to that. Hast thou met with Some obstacle or other in thy purpose and intention? If thou didst propose without due reservation and exception now hath thy reasonable part received a blow indeed But if in general thou didst propose unto thyself what soever might be, thou art not thereby either hurt, nor properly hindered. For in those things that properly belong unto the mind, she cannot be hindered by any man. It is not fire, nor iron; nor the power of a tyrant nor the power of a slandering tongue; nor anything else that can penetrate into her.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: You planned to get a promotion, didn't get it, and feel like you've failed. You set out to finish a project a certain way, but circumstances forced you to change course and now you're frustrated. Someone criticizes your judgment or questions your competence and you can't stop thinking about it. You failed at something you were confident about and now doubt yourself. You're stuck in traffic and miss an important meeting, feeling like external events are ruining your day.
meaning_fields.teaching: What actually harms you is not obstacles to your plans or other people's words—only damage to your actual thinking matters. Your body can be harmed, your circumstances can frustrate you, but your mind remains untouchable unless you let it be. Real harm only happens when you treat an external setback as proof that your judgment or character was wrong.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at being blocked, self-doubt when things don't go as planned, defensiveness when criticized, the sting of failure, feeling powerless when circumstances change, shame about not achieving what you intended.
meaning_fields.concepts: Stoic distinction between what is in your control (your judgment, intent, character, reasoning) and what is not (external events, other people's actions, physical obstacles). Proper evil (a corruption of your rational faculty) versus mere inconvenience. The difference between a reservation or exception in your intent (accepting that outcomes depend on factors outside you) and unreserved attachment to a specific result.

translation: If once round and solid, there is no fear that ever it will change.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.teaching: If you build a solid, well-integrated character—where your values and actions are genuinely aligned—external events won't shake or distort you. You become stable from the inside, so outside pressures lose their power to reshape who you are.
meaning_fields.situations: A trusted friend betrays your confidence, but you don't spiral into paranoia about all friendships; your sense of integrity stays intact. You get demoted at work, but it doesn't make you question your core abilities or worth. Someone criticizes your parenting harshly online, but you don't abandon your actual parenting philosophy; you stay grounded in what you know works. You face financial loss, but your identity and values don't collapse with your bank account. A major life plan falls through—moving, a relationship, a job—but your fundamental sense of purpose doesn't shatter.
meaning_fields.emotions: The dread of falling apart when things go wrong; the anxiety that one bad event will unravel everything; the vulnerability of feeling like you're made of fragile pieces that could scatter; the relief of knowing some part of you is unshakeable; the quiet confidence that comes from internal coherence.
meaning_fields.concepts: Wholeness (integrity, the Greek sense of being unified and not fragmented); self-sufficiency (autarkeia in Stoic terms—not needing external validation or circumstances to maintain your character); the distinction between your essential nature and the accidents of fortune that happen to you.

translation: Why should I grieve myself; who never did willingly grieve any other! One thing rejoices one and another thing another. As for me, this is my joy, if my understanding be right and sound, as neither averse from any man, nor refusing any of those things which as a man I am subject unto; if I can look upon all things in the world meekly and kindly; accept all things and carry myself towards everything according to to true worth of the thing itself.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: You realize you're angry at someone but you never intentionally hurt them in the first place; You're frustrated that life keeps throwing unavoidable hardships your way and you're taking it personally; You catch yourself resenting other people's good fortune or different priorities; You're struggling to accept something you can't change and it's eating you up inside; You find yourself judging situations harshly instead of seeing them clearly for what they actually are.
meaning_fields.teaching: Stop turning pain into a moral failure. If you didn't deliberately harm anyone, don't burden yourself with guilt for what's happening to you now. Your real strength lies in keeping your mind clear and your judgments fair—seeing each thing for what it actually is, without bitterness toward others or self-pity toward yourself.
meaning_fields.emotions: resentment, guilt, self-pity, bitterness toward life's unfairness, the frustration of being judged unfairly when you don't deserve it
meaning_fields.concepts: Premeditatio malorum (negative visualization)—here inverted; don't construct narratives of your own guilt. Oikeiosis (appropriate action and relationship)—judge things according to their true nature, not your wounded feelings. The dichotomy of control—distinguish between what you caused and what you cannot control.

translation: This time that is now present, bestow thou upon thyself. They that rather hunt for fame after death, do not consider, that those men that shall be hereafter, will be even such, as these whom now they can so hardly bear with. And besides they also will be mortal men. But to consider the thing in itself, if so many with so many voices, shall make such and such a sound, or shall have such and such an opinion concerning thee, what is it to thee?
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.teaching: Stop waiting for judgment from people who don't matter. The people judging you now will die, and the people judging you later will be just as limited and ordinary as they are. What does it actually change about your life if a thousand people form an opinion about you?
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety about what others think, obsession with your reputation, fear of being forgotten, restlessness about your legacy, the hollow feeling when you realize you're chasing approval that never satisfies
meaning_fields.situations: You're refreshing social media to see if your post got likes and comments; you keep thinking about a critical email someone sent you a week ago; you're working hard on a project partly to impress people you don't even like; you catch yourself imagining how people will remember you after you die; you're doing something you don't want to do because you're afraid of what others will say about you
meaning_fields.concepts: Memento mori (remembering that everyone dies, including those who judge us), and the distinction between what is within your control (your character and effort) versus what is not (others' opinions and judgment). The Stoic practice of testing whether external things—like fame and reputation—actually have any real power to harm you.

For there also I shall have that spirit which is within me propitious; that is well pleased and fully contented both in that constant disposition, and with those particular actions, which to its own proper constitution are suitable and agreeable.

meaning_fields.situations: A friend loses their job and worries about their worth being tied to their title or position. Someone moves to a new city and feels unmoored, wondering if they'll be the same person in different circumstances. A parent faces a major life disruption—divorce, illness, financial setback—and fears losing their sense of self. Someone gets passed over for a promotion they expected and questions their value. A person experiences a major external loss (relationship ends, plans fall through, status changes) and spirals about identity.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your character and your ability to act according to your values don't depend on your circumstances—not your job, location, wealth, or social position. No matter what happens to you externally, you still have access to the one thing that actually matters: your own mind and the choices you make. This means you're genuinely free, because no external force can strip away your capacity to remain true to yourself.
meaning_fields.emotions: Fear of losing yourself when life changes. Despair that your worth is fragile and dependent on things outside your control. Anxiety about upheaval and displacement. Relief and confidence that comes from recognizing you're not defined by circumstances. A kind of quiet resilience when you stop tying your identity to external things.
meaning_fields.concepts: Self-sufficiency (the Stoic idea that virtue and your character are completely independent of fortune or circumstance). Prohairesis—the Greek term for your faculty of choice and will, the only thing truly yours. Indifference to externals (not meaning you don't care about outcomes, but that your inner peace doesn't require a specific outcome). The distinction between what is "up to you" (your judgment, your effort, your character) and what is not (health, wealth, reputation, where you live).

translation: Is this then a thing of that worth, that for it my soul should suffer, and become worse than it was? as either basely dejected, or disordinately affected, or confounded within itself, or terrified? What can there be, that thou shouldest so much esteem?
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.teaching: When something goes wrong, ask yourself: is this worth letting it wreck who I am? Most setbacks don't deserve that price. What matters is whether you respond with desperation, wild swings in mood, confusion about what to do, or fear—those reactions destroy your character far more than the setback itself ever could.
meaning_fields.emotions: Shame and humiliation after a failure; anxiety that spirals into panic; the sinking feeling of being overwhelmed; desperate worry that you've lost control; fear that you've become a worse person because of what happened.
meaning_fields.situations: You make a visible mistake at work and spend the next week replaying it, feeling degraded; a plan falls apart and you oscillate between angry outbursts and giving up completely; you lose money or status and feel disoriented, unsure how to think straight; someone criticizes you harshly and you're gripped by the terrifying sense that they might be right about who you are; you fail at something important and feel your self-respect crumbling.
meaning_fields.concepts: Arete (excellence of character, meaning your integrity and how you show up)—the idea that your character is your most valuable possession and nothing external is worth sacrificing it for. Pathē (disordered emotional reactions, meaning uncontrolled feelings)—the Stoic concern that we damage ourselves more through our uncontrolled responses than through external events.

translation: Nothing can happen unto thee, which is not incidental unto thee, as thou art a man. As nothing can happen either to an ox, a vine, or to a stone, which is not incidental unto them; unto every one in his own kind. If therefore nothing can happen unto anything, which is not both usual and natural; why art thou displeased? Sure the common nature of all would not bring anything upon any, that were intolerable. If therefore it be a thing external that causes thy grief, know, that it is not that properly that doth cause it, but thine own conceit and opinion concerning the thing: which thou mayest rid thyself of, when thou wilt. But if it be somewhat that is amiss in thine own disposition, that doth grieve thee, mayest thou not rectify thy moral tenets and opinions. But if it grieve thee, that thou doest not perform that which seemeth unto thee right and just, why doest not thou choose rather to perform it than to grieve? But somewhat that is stronger than thyself doth hinder thee. Let it not grieve thee then, if it be not thy fault that the thing is not performed. 'Yea but it is a thing of that nature, as that thy life is not worth the while, except it may be performed.' If it be so, upon condition that thou be kindly and lovingly disposed towards all men, thou mayest be gone. For even then, as much as at any time, art thou in a very good estate of performance, when thou doest die in charity with those, that are an obstacle unto thy performance.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: A project gets blocked by circumstances outside your control—a budget cut, a team member's illness, a client canceling—and you're tormented by what didn't happen. Your boss passes you over for promotion despite your work because the company froze hiring. You planned to start a business but a family emergency consumed the last year. You want to speak up in a meeting but your anxiety makes you freeze and you replay it for hours afterward. Someone else has power to veto your ideas and you can't stop feeling victimized by their blocking you.
meaning_fields.teaching: What happens to you is what actually happens to human beings—there's nothing abnormal or unfair about obstacles and limitations. The real question isn't whether you face resistance, but whether you're blaming yourself for things outside your control or blaming external things that don't deserve your anger. If the obstacle is truly beyond you, suffering about it adds a second injury you created yourself. The only performance that matters is your character—being kind and fair to others—and that's always available to you, even when every external plan fails.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at being blocked. Replay and rumination—obsessing over what you couldn't do. Resentment at people or circumstances in your way. Feeling like a failure when external forces stop you. Self-blame mixed with victimhood. The hollow despair that comes from thinking your whole life is wasted if one thing doesn't happen.
meaning_fields.concepts: The dichotomy of control—distinguishing between what is up to you (your choices, your character, your judgments) and what is not up to you (outcomes, other people's actions, external events). Nature and necessity—accepting that obstacles are part of the human condition, not personal injustices. The locus of suffering—recognizing that pain comes from your judgment about events, not the events themselves. text_for_embedding:
A project gets blocked by circumstances outside your control—a budget cut, a team member's illness, a client canceling—and you're tormented by what didn't happen. Your boss passes you over for promotion despite your work because the company froze hiring. You planned to start a business but a family emergency consumed the last year. You want to speak up in a meeting but your anxiety makes you freeze and you replay it for hours afterward. Someone else has power to veto your ideas and you can't stop feeling victimized by their blocking you.
What happens to you is what actually happens to human beings—there's nothing abnormal or unfair about obstacles and limitations. The real question isn't whether you face resistance, but whether you're blaming yourself for things outside your control or blaming external things that don't deserve your anger. If the obstacle is truly beyond you, suffering about it adds a second injury you created yourself. The only performance that matters is your character—being kind and fair to others—and that's always available to you, even when every external plan fails.
Frustration at being blocked. Replay and rumination—obsessing over what you couldn't do. Resentment at people or circumstances in your way. Feeling like a failure when external forces stop you. Self-blame mixed with victimhood. The hollow despair that comes from thinking your whole life is wasted if one thing doesn't happen.
The dichotomy of control—distinguishing between what is up to you (your choices, your character, your judgments) and what is not up to you (outcomes, other people's actions, external events). translation: Remember that thy mind is of that nature as that it becometh altogether unconquerable, when once recollected in herself, she seeks no other content than this, that she cannot be forced: yea though it so fall out, that it be even against reason itself, that it cloth bandy. How much less when by the help of reason she is able to judge of things with discretion? And therefore let thy chief fort and place of defence be, a mind free from passions. A stronger place, (whereunto to make his refuge, and so to become impregnable) and better fortified than this, hath no man. He that seeth not this is unlearned. He that seeth it, and betaketh not himself to this place of refuge, is unhappy.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: Someone blames you for something outside your control and you feel your reputation suffering; a setback happens (job loss, breakup, public embarrassment) that rocks your confidence; you catch yourself obsessing over what others think or say about you; circumstances pile up that make you feel helpless and reactive; you realize you've been letting external pressure dictate your mood and decisions for weeks.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your mind is your only true stronghold—the one place no one else can touch or control. When you're grounded in your own judgment and free from desperate craving for approval or comfort, external chaos loses its power over you. Building this inner stability through reason is the only defense that actually works.
meaning_fields.emotions: Feeling vulnerable to others' opinions; helplessness when things fall apart; desperation to regain control; frustration at being reactive instead of steady; anxiety about what you can't predict or prevent; relief when you realize something is actually up to you.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (your capacity to choose your own judgment, distinct from things forced on you from outside); apatheia (freedom from the tyranny of emotional reactivity, not coldness but clarity); the Stoic distinction between what is "up to us" (our will and reasoning) and what is not (reputation, health, wealth, events).

translation: Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things, as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them. It is reported unto thee, that such a one speaketh ill of thee. Well; that he speaketh ill of thee, so much is reported. But that thou art hurt thereby, is not reported: that is the addition of opinion, which thou must exclude. I see that my child is sick. That he is sick, I see, but that he is in danger of his life also, I see it not. Thus thou must use to keep thyself to the first motions and apprehensions of things, as they present themselves outwardly; and add not unto them from within thyself through mere conceit and opinion. Or rather add unto them: hut as one that understandeth the true nature of all things that happen in the world.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.teaching: The moment you hear bad news or criticism, you're getting one fact: what happened. Everything else—how bad it is, what it means about you, how it will end—you're making up in your head. Stop adding the story. Stick to what you actually know right now, and you won't suffer over invented disasters.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety spiraling into catastrophe; fear projecting worst-case outcomes; shame from rumor or criticism; dread about what might happen next; frustration at your mind running away with itself
meaning_fields.situations: Your boss says your project needs revision, and you immediately imagine getting fired; someone tells you a friend criticized you privately, and you replay it obsessively wondering if they hate you now; your kid gets a fever and you jump to worst-case scenarios about serious illness; a text from someone important goes unanswered and you assume they're angry with you; you make a mistake at work and spiral thinking about how your reputation is ruined
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (the faculty of choice between impressions and beliefs): the gap between an external event and your internal judgment about it. Phantasia (impression or appearance): the raw data arriving through your senses. The Stoic distinction between what is in your control (your judgment) and what is not (external events and rumors). Prosoche (attention and mindfulness): the practice of catching yourself adding opinion to fact.

translation: Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way? avoid them. Let this suffice. Add not presently speaking unto thyself, What serve these things for in the world? For, this, one that is acquainted with the mysteries of nature, will laugh at thee for it; as a carpenter would or a shoemaker, if meeting in either of their shops with some shavings, or small remnants of their work, thou shouldest blame them for it. And yet those men, it is not for want of a place where to throw them that they keep them in their shops for a while: but the nature of the universe hath no such out-place; but herein doth consist the wonder of her art and skill, that she having once circumscribed herself within some certain bounds and limits, whatsoever is within her that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it into herself, and of these very things can make new things; so that she needeth not to seek elsewhere out of herself either for a new supply of matter and substance, or for a place where to throw out whatsoever is irrecoverably putrid and corrupt. Thus she, as for place, so for matter and art, is herself sufficient unto herself.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: You encounter something unpleasant or broken in your day and immediately start worrying about why it had to exist or what good it serves. A plan falls through and you waste mental energy asking "what's the point of this delay?" instead of just moving on. You notice waste, inefficiency, or things that seem pointless in the world around you and get stuck questioning the universe's design. You face rejection or failure and start spiraling about why bad things happen at all. Someone else's mistakes or flaws frustrate you and you dwell on how things "shouldn't be this way."
meaning_fields.teaching: When you encounter something bitter or broken, just set it aside and move on—don't waste energy demanding to know why it exists. The universe is so efficient that it transforms everything corrupted or worn into something new; it has no need for an outside dump. Nature's skill lies precisely in this: it works only with what it has, making it sufficient unto itself. You don't need to understand the cosmic purpose of every obstacle to be able to simply avoid it.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration with the "why" of painful or pointless things; irritation at inefficiency or waste; the desire to demand cosmic justice or reason; feeling destabilized when the world doesn't make sense; anxiety about things that seem broken or wrong.
meaning_fields.concepts: Self-sufficiency (autarkeia in Greek—the idea that wholeness and power come from working only with what you have, not from external supply). The nature of the universe as rational and complete. Acceptance of limitation as the sign of wisdom, not lack. The refusal to philosophize beyond what is useful in the moment.

translation: Not to be slack and negligent; or loose, and wanton in thy actions; nor contentious, and troublesome in thy conversation; nor to rove and wander in thy fancies and imaginations. Not basely to contract thy soul; nor boisterously to sally out with it, or furiously to launch out as it were, nor ever to want employment.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.teaching: You need discipline in four directions at once: stay focused on your work instead of drifting, speak to others without picking fights, keep your mind from spinning in fantasy, and don't shrink from responsibility or swing wildly between extremes. The point is steady, moderate action—not perfection, just showing up and doing your part without drama.
meaning_fields.emotions: Restlessness, shame about wasted time, frustration with your own scattered attention, irritation at yourself for being argumentative or checked-out, the anxiety of feeling like you're not doing enough or like you're trying too hard and it shows.
meaning_fields.situations: You catch yourself scrolling for an hour and realize you've done nothing on the actual task. You replay a conversation where you got defensive or snapped at someone over nothing. You're at a meeting and your mind is somewhere else entirely, then you miss what was said. You either avoid a hard conversation out of fear, or you charge in aggressively instead of staying calm. You feel torn between being lazy and being frenetic—never quite balanced.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (your capacity for choice and directed will) is the tool here. The Stoics called the ability to stay steady and measured "sophrosyne"—often translated as temperance or self-control, but really meaning the opposite of both extremes: not rigid and not loose. The passage is about occupying the middle ground between negligence and manic intensity, which the Stoics saw as necessary for living according to nature and reason.

translation: 'They kill me, they cut my flesh; they persecute my person with curses.' What then? May not thy mind for all this continue pure, prudent, temperate, just? As a fountain of sweet and clear water, though she be cursed by some stander by, yet do her springs nevertheless still run as sweet and clear as before; yea though either dirt or dung be thrown in, yet is it no sooner thrown, than dispersed, and she cleared. She cannot be dyed or infected by it. What then must I do, that I may have within myself an overflowing fountain, and not a well? Beget thyself by continual pains and endeavours to true liberty with charity, and true simplicity and modesty.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.teaching: Your character is like a fountain—attackers throwing dirt at it don't change the water flowing from it. When people curse you, insult you, or try to damage your reputation, your inner integrity stays clean if you keep it that way. What matters is what you generate from within, not what others throw at you.
meaning_fields.emotions: Feeling attacked or defamed; being hurt by someone's words or actions; wanting to stay dignified when disrespected; rage at being wrongly treated; the despair of thinking someone else's cruelty has permanently stained you.
meaning_fields.situations: Someone spreads false rumors about you at work and you keep replaying their words; a family member says cruel things and you feel dirty or ashamed; a rival publicly criticizes your work in front of your boss; you're treated unfairly and want to retaliate but worry you'd become like them; someone you trusted betrays you and you're haunted by the violation.
meaning_fields.concepts: The Stoic doctrine of internal locus of control (what is up to us vs. what is not)—your judgments, character, and intentions belong to you alone; externals (reputation, others' opinions, physical harm) do not. Apatheia (not apathy, but freedom from being damaged by external events); virtue as the only true good; the distinction between being harmed and being insulted.

translation: He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself is. And he that knoweth not what the world was made for, cannot possibly know either what are the qualities, or what is the nature of the world. Now he that in either of these is to seek, for what he himself was made is ignorant also. What then dost thou think of that man, who proposeth unto himself, as a matter of great moment, the noise and applause of men, who both where they are, and what they are themselves, are altogether ignorant? Dost thou desire to be commended of that man, who thrice in one hour perchance, doth himself curse himself? Dost thou desire to please him, who pleaseth not himself? or dost thou think that he pleaseth himself, who doth use to repent himself almost of everything that he doth?
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: You're chasing approval from someone at work who constantly complains and undermines their own achievements. Your friend obsesses over likes on social media from people who post hate about themselves hours later. Someone criticizes your work but you realize they don't even understand what their own job is for. You catch yourself seeking validation from a family member who never seems satisfied with anything—including their own life. Your boss demands recognition for ideas they half-understand and constantly second-guess.
meaning_fields.teaching: People who don't understand their own place in the world or why they're here can't evaluate anything clearly—including you. Chasing their approval is like seeking directions from someone who's lost. Someone who despises themselves, contradicts their own choices, and doesn't know what they're actually doing can't offer you genuine praise worth having.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at wasting effort on someone's judgment. The sting of realizing that approval you craved came from someone unstable. Confusion about why someone's criticism stung when they clearly don't have their own life together. The hollow feeling when you finally get the praise you wanted but realize the person giving it is a mess.
meaning_fields.concepts: Self-knowledge (knowing your purpose and place)—without it, a person becomes unreliable even as a judge of others. The idea that external judgment is only as sound as the character of the judge. Wisdom as understanding context and meaning, not just facts. The paradox of seeking wholeness from broken sources.

translation: Not only now henceforth to have a common breath, or to hold correspondency of breath, with that air, that compasseth us about; but to have a common mind, or to hold correspondency of mind also with that rational substance, which compasseth all things. For, that also is of itself, and of its own nature (if a man can but draw it in as he should) everywhere diffused; and passeth through all things, no less than the air doth, if a man can but suck it in.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.teaching: You're not just a body breathing the same air as everyone else—you have access to the same rational intelligence that runs through everything. If you learn to draw on it properly, that universal reason is available to you anywhere, anytime, just like oxygen. It's not something you have to earn or wait for; it's already everywhere, ready to be used.
meaning_fields.emotions: Isolation, disconnection from something larger than yourself; feeling cut off from your own mind or judgment; desperation to find solid ground; a sense of smallness in the world; the relief of discovering you're not alone in your capacity to think straight.
meaning_fields.situations: You're alone at night doubting whether you can trust your own judgment on a major decision. You're in a crowded room but feel completely disconnected from everyone, like your mind works differently. You're facing a problem and realize you have access to the same problem-solving ability as the wisest people you know. You're struggling through grief and suddenly recognize you can tap into something steady and rational that doesn't depend on your mood. You're intimidated by someone smarter and then remember you have the same capacity for clear thinking available to you.
meaning_fields.concepts: Pneuma (the universal breath or rational principle animating all things); logos (the universal reason or intelligence governing nature); participation in the divine intelligence; the stoic idea that reason is not private property but a shared cosmic force; self-sufficiency through alignment with universal nature.

translation: Wickedness in general doth not hurt the world. Particular wickedness doth not hurt any other: only unto him it is hurtful, whosoever he be that offends, unto whom in great favour and mercy it is granted, that whensoever he himself shall but first desire it, he may be presently delivered of it. Unto my free-will my neighbour's free-will, whoever he be, (as his life, or his bode), is altogether indifferent. For though we are all made one for another, yet have our minds and understandings each of them their own proper and limited jurisdiction. For else another man's wickedness might be my evil which God would not have, that it might not be in another man's power to make me unhappy: which nothing now can do but mine own wickedness.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: A coworker undermines you in a meeting and you spiral thinking about how they've damaged your reputation; your partner says something cruel and you find yourself unable to move past it for days; someone cheats you in a deal and you obsess over the injustice, replaying it constantly; a family member betrays your confidence and you're consumed with anger at what they've done to you; you get passed over for a promotion because a rival sabotaged you, and you can't shake the feeling that your life is now ruined.
meaning_fields.teaching: Other people's bad choices can't actually harm you—only your own can. Someone else's wickedness is their problem to fix, not something that gets transferred to you or becomes your burden. The only thing that can genuinely make you miserable is your own poor judgment or moral failure, not what others do. This means you have complete control over whether their actions actually hurt you.
meaning_fields.emotions: Feeling victimized by someone else's actions; the helpless anger of being wronged; the urge to blame others for your unhappiness; resentment that someone else has power over your peace of mind; the weight of carrying grudges.
meaning_fields.concepts: Free will (the philosophical view that each person controls only their own choices, not others'); moral agency (the idea that you are responsible only for your own actions and character, not for controlling others); the Stoic distinction between what is "up to us" and what is not (your virtue is up to you; other people's choices are not).

translation: The sun seemeth to be shed abroad. And indeed it is diffused but not effused. For that diffusion of it is a τάσις or an extension. For therefore are the beams of it called ἀκτῖνες from the word ἐκτείνεσθαι to be stretched out and extended. Now what a sunbeam is, thou mayest know if thou observe the light of the sun, when through some narrow hole it pierceth into some room that is dark. For it is always in a direct line. And as by any solid body, that it meets with in the way that is not penetrable by air, it is divided and abrupted, and yet neither slides off, or falls down, but stayeth there nevertheless: such must the diffusion in the mind be; not an effusion, but an extension. What obstacles and impediments soever she meeteth within her way, she must not violently, and by way of an impetuous onset light upon them; neither must she fall down; but she must stand, and give light unto that which doth admit of it. For as for that which doth not, it is its own fault and loss, if it bereave itself of her light.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: A friend keeps interrupting you or dismissing your ideas in meetings, and you're tempted to push harder to make them listen. You notice your anger wants to bulldoze through their resistance. Your teenage kid won't accept advice you're trying to give them, and you're frustrated that they're "wasting" your effort. Someone is hostile or closed-minded when you're trying to help them, and you feel like your good intentions are hitting a wall. You're trying to mentor a coworker who seems resistant to feedback, and you're wondering if you should just give up or force the issue.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your goodness and good sense don't need to force their way through people's resistance. Like light passing through a room, your clarity should extend steadily in a straight line—not smashing against obstacles or collapsing when it meets them. When someone blocks you out or refuses what you offer, stand firm in what you know is right, but don't brutalize them trying to make them accept it. If they choose not to receive your light, that's on them, not a failure of your character.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration when others won't listen or accept help; anger at resistance; the temptation to escalate or push harder; disappointment that your good intentions aren't landing; the impulse to give up when blocked; resentment that your effort seems wasted.
meaning_fields.concepts: The distinction between proper force (extension, steady direction) and violent force (effusion, smashing), which comes from Stoic physics but means: the difference between holding firm in your principles and actually harming people with your righteousness. Self-sufficiency—your character's worth doesn't depend on making others change or accept you. The virtue of restraint: knowing when to stand your ground versus when you're just banging your head against a wall for ego.

Frustration when others won't listen or accept help; anger at resistance; the temptation to escalate or push harder; disappointment that your good intentions aren't landing; the impulse to give up when blocked; resentment that your effort seems wasted.
The distinction between proper force (extension, steady direction) and violent force (effusion, smashing), which comes from Stoic physics but means: the difference between holding firm in your principles and actually harming people with your righteousness. Self-sufficiency—your character's worth doesn't depend on making others change or accept you. The virtue of restraint: knowing when to stand your ground versus when you're just banging your head against a wall for ego.

translation: He that feareth death, either feareth that he shall have no sense at all, or that his senses will not be the same. Whereas, he should rather comfort himself, that either no sense at all, and so no sense of evil; or if any sense, then another life, and so no death properly.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: You're lying awake at 3 AM spiraling about your own mortality and what happens when you die. You're sitting in a waiting room before a major surgery, and your mind won't stop generating worst-case scenarios about not waking up. You've just gotten bad health news and can't stop imagining the pain and suffering that might come. You're at a funeral watching someone who was vibrant and alive just days ago now gone, and it makes your own death feel suddenly real and terrifying. You're scrolling through news of accidents or disasters and can't shake the feeling that one day it will be you.
meaning_fields.teaching: When you're afraid of death, you're actually afraid of one of two things: either you fear complete unconsciousness with no awareness at all, or you fear that you'll suffer horribly as you die. But both fears collapse under examination. If death means no consciousness, then there's nothing bad to experience—you won't feel anything. If there is some kind of afterlife or continuation, then death itself isn't the end. Either way, death itself cannot be evil, because the thing you fear most doesn't actually exist as you imagine it.
meaning_fields.emotions: Terror about ceasing to exist, the specific dread of what dying will feel like, helplessness in the face of something you cannot control, the crushing weight of contemplating your own non-existence, anxiety that spikes when you're alone or vulnerable, fear masquerading as practical worry
meaning_fields.concepts: The dichotomy of outcomes (either/or logic that eliminates the feared middle ground); what is actually within your control versus what is not; the difference between what you imagine and what is real; death as a natural limit of life rather than an evil; the unexamined assumption that death must be something to suffer through

translation: All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or bear with them.

meaning_fields.situations: Someone at work keeps making the same annoying mistakes, and you're deciding whether to point it out or just let it go. A family member has a habit you find frustrating and you're torn between speaking up and staying silent. A friend says something ignorant and you're weighing whether correcting them will help or just create tension. A roommate's careless behavior affects you daily and you're trying to figure out if it's worth the conflict to address it. You're dealing with someone's incompetence in a situation where you're both supposed to be cooperating.
meaning_fields.teaching: We're all here to live together and depend on each other. When someone wrongs you or falls short, you have exactly two choices: try to help them see better, or accept them as they are. There's no third option of resentment or contempt—you either work to improve the situation or you make peace with it.
meaning_fields.emotions: Exasperation, the urge to fix people, frustration at being dragged down by others' failings, impatience when someone doesn't get it, the strain of biting your tongue, the sting of being let down by someone's weakness
meaning_fields.concepts: Interdependence (we are designed to live together, not in isolation); prohairesis or moral choice (you always have agency in how you respond, even if you cannot control others); prosoche (mindful attention to what is in your power versus what is not)

translation: The motion of the mind is not as the motion of a dart. For the mind when it is wary and cautelous, and by way of diligent circumspection turneth herself many ways, may then as well be said to go straight on to the object, as when it useth no such circumspection.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.teaching: A careful, thoughtful approach to a problem doesn't slow you down—it actually gets you where you need to go, just as reliably as rushing straight ahead. The mind that pauses to look around and consider different angles is still moving effectively toward what matters.
meaning_fields.emotions: The anxiety that comes with feeling like you should rush; the guilt about taking time to think things through; the frustration of being told you're overthinking when you want to get things right.
meaning_fields.situations: You're about to send a difficult email and you pause to reread it from different angles before hitting send. At work, you take time to consider a problem from multiple viewpoints instead of jumping to the first solution. You're making a big decision and you keep questioning yourself, wondering if your deliberation is just procrastination. You catch yourself about to react in anger and take a moment to think through the consequences. You're solving a problem at work and someone says you're wasting time being cautious when you could just go with your gut.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prudence (practical wisdom about the right action in a specific situation). The Stoic rejection of impulsive action. The distinction between the mind's flexibility and the dart's fixed trajectory—the mind can adjust, reconsider, and still reach its goal efficiently. Premeditatio malorum (thinking through difficulties beforehand) as a tool, not a hindrance.

translation: To pierce and penetrate into the estate of every one's understanding that thou hast to do with: as also to make the estate of thine own open, and penetrable to any other.
book_theme: correcting mistakes; the self-sufficiency of a good character

meaning_fields.situations: A friend misunderstands your motives and you want them to know what you actually meant; You're defensive about criticism and realize the other person can't see where you're coming from; A work meeting where people are talking past each other and nobody understands what anyone really wants; You feel judged unfairly and wish someone could see inside your head to know you're not that person; Your partner thinks you don't care but you do care—you just can't seem to show it in a way they understand.
meaning_fields.teaching: Real understanding between people requires two things at once: genuinely trying to see how the other person actually thinks, and being willing to let them see how you actually think. You can't do just one. Most conflict comes from people protecting their inner world while refusing to enter anyone else's. If you want to be understood, you have to show up first.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at being misunderstood; loneliness from feeling unseen; defensiveness when someone gets you wrong; the vulnerability of being truly known; shame about revealing your real thoughts; relief when someone finally gets you.
meaning_fields.concepts: Mutual intelligibility—the idea that understanding is not one-directional but requires reciprocal openness. Transparency as a moral practice, not just emotional honesty but intellectual honesty about how your mind actually works. The Stoic notion that reason is universal, so if you show your reasoning clearly, a reasonable person can meet you there.

translation: He that is unjust, is also impious. For the nature of the universe, having made all reasonable creatures one for another, to the end that they should do one another good; more or less according to the several persons and occasions but in nowise hurt one another: it is manifest that he that doth transgress against this her will, is guilty of impiety towards the most ancient and venerable of all the deities. For the nature of the universe, is the nature the common parent of all, and therefore piously to be observed of all things that are, and that which now is, to whatsoever first was, and gave it its being, hath relation of blood and kindred. She is also called truth and is the first cause of all truths. He therefore that willingly and wittingly doth lie, is impious in that he doth receive, and so commit injustice: but he that against his will, in that he disagreeth from the nature of the universe, and in that striving with the nature of the world he doth in his particular, violate the general order of the world. For he doth no better than strive and war against it, who contrary to his own nature applieth himself to that which is contrary to truth. For nature had before furnished him with instincts and opportunities sufficient for the attainment of it; which he having hitherto neglected, is not now able to discern that which is false from that which is true. He also that pursues after pleasures, as that which is truly good and flies from pains, as that which is truly evil: is impious. For such a one must of necessity oftentimes accuse that common nature, as distributing many things both unto the evil, and unto the good, not according to the deserts of either: as unto the bad oftentimes pleasures, and the causes of pleasures; so unto the good, pains, and the occasions of pains. Again, he that feareth pains and crosses in this world, feareth some of those things which some time or other must needs happen in the world. And that we have already showed to be impious. And he that pursueth after pleasures, will not spare, to compass his desires, to do that which is unjust, and that is manifestly impious. Now those things which unto nature are equally indifferent (for she had not created both, both pain and pleasure, if both had not been unto her equally indifferent): they that will live according to nature, must in those things (as being of the same mind and disposition that she is) be as equally indifferent. Whosoever therefore in either matter of pleasure and pain; death and life; honour and dishonour, (which things nature in the administration of the world, indifferently doth make use of), is not as indifferent, it is apparent that he is impious. When I say that common nature doth indifferently make use of them, my meaning is, that they happen indifferently in the ordinary course of things, which by a necessary consequence, whether as principal or accessory, come to pass in the world, according to that first and ancient deliberation of Providence, by which she from some certain beginning, did resolve upon the creation of such a world, conceiving then in her womb as it were some certain rational generative seeds and faculties of things future, whether subjects, changes, successions; both such and such, and just so many.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: Injustice and dishonesty are impiety—betrayals of the universal order itself, which designed all rational beings to help one another. When you lie or hurt others, you're fighting against nature's deepest blueprint. Living justly means accepting that pain and pleasure, success and failure come indifferently to good and bad people alike, and to resist this truth through scheming for comfort or power is to wage war against reality itself.
meaning_fields.emotions: Resentment at unfairness (why do bad people prosper?), anxiety about personal loss, shame about your own dishonesty, the seductive pull of shortcuts and rationalizations, anger when your plans get blocked by circumstance
meaning_fields.situations: You're tempted to fudge the truth to save your reputation at work or in a relationship. You notice dishonest people getting ahead and feel rage that the world rewards cheating. You're gripped by fear of illness, financial loss, or humiliation and consider cutting corners to avoid it. You catch yourself resenting someone else's good fortune because they don't deserve it. You're lying to yourself about why you're pursuing wealth or status, telling yourself it's necessary when really it's about vanity.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature as the rational order underlying reality (not mysticism, but the lawful structure of how things actually work). Piety as alignment with that order, impiety as resistance to it. Indifference (adiaphora)—the Stoic distinction between things that matter for virtue (character) and things that don't (health, reputation, comfort). The rational seeds of Providence—the predetermined rational structure from which all events necessarily flow.

translation: It were indeed more happy and comfortable, for a man to depart out of this world, having lived all his life long clear from all falsehood, dissimulation, voluptuousness, and pride. But if this cannot be, yet it is some comfort for a man joyfully to depart as weary, and out of love with those; rather than to desire to live, and to continue long in those wicked courses. Hath not yet experience taught thee to fly from the plague? For a far greater plague is the corruption of the mind, than any certain change and distemper of the common air can be. This is a plague of creatures, as they are living creatures; but that of men as they are men or reasonable.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: A middle-aged executive realizes she's spent years climbing the ladder through small lies and flattery, and now faces a choice between continuing or making a genuine break; Someone in their 60s reflects on a lifetime of playing it safe, saying what others wanted to hear, and wonders if there's time to stop; A person lying awake at night knows they're trapped in cycles of people-pleasing and dishonesty, but feels too invested to change course; A dying person looks back and sees how much energy went into maintaining a false image instead of living authentically; Someone young enough to change realizes their current path—chasing status through superficial means—is poisoning how they think.
meaning_fields.teaching: Living with constant falsehood and vanity corrupts your mind in a way that's worse than any physical illness—it damages the very capacity to think clearly and be human. The good news is that even if you haven't managed to stay clean your whole life, you can still choose to stop now and leave with some dignity, tired of the whole game rather than desperately clinging to it.
meaning_fields.emotions: Regret mixed with a strange relief at finally seeing the trap; Weariness from the weight of keeping up appearances; Shame at how much time was wasted; A dawning recognition that the corruption happened gradually and invisibly; Fear of dying with this still unresolved; Stubborn pride that makes change feel like admission of failure; A hunger to be done with it all.
meaning_fields.concepts: Corruption of the soul (Greek: phthora tês psychês)—the idea that systematic dishonesty rewires how you think and what you care about. Eudaimonia as clarity—true flourishing means thinking straight, which falsehood prevents. The distinction between animal suffering (physical plague) and human suffering (mental corruption from vice). Amor fati applied negatively—what it means to depart life "weary of" something rather than still craving it.

translation: Thou must not in matter of death carry thyself scornfully, but as one that is well pleased with it, as being one of those things that nature hath appointed. For what thou dost conceive of these, of a boy to become a young man, to wax old, to grow, to ripen, to get teeth, or a beard, or grey hairs to beget, to bear, or to be delivered; or what other action soever it be, that is natural unto man according to the several seasons of his life; such a thing is it also to be dissolved. It is therefore the part of a wise man, in matter of death, not in any wise to carry himself either violently, or proudly but patiently to wait for it, as one of nature's operations: that with the same mind as now thou dost expect when that which yet is but an embryo in thy wife's belly shall come forth, thou mayst expect also when thy soul shall fall off from that outward coat or skin: wherein as a child in the belly it lieth involved and shut up. But thou desirest a more popular, and though not so direct and philosophical, yet a very powerful and penetrative recipe against the fear of death, nothing can make they more willing to part with thy life, than if thou shalt consider, both what the subjects themselves are that thou shalt part with, and what manner of disposition thou shalt no more have to do with. True it is, that, offended with them thou must not be by no means, but take care of them, and meekly bear with them However, this thou mayst remember, that whensoever it happens that thou depart, it shall not be from men that held the same opinions that thou dost. For that indeed, (if it were so) is the only thing that might make thee averse from death, and willing to continue here, if it were thy hap to live with men that had obtained the same belief that thou hast. But now, what a toil it is for thee to live with men of different opinions, thou seest: so that thou hast rather occasion to say, Hasten, I thee pray, O Death; lest I also in time forget myself.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: A parent watching their child grow up and realizing one day they'll age, decline, and die—and recognizing this is simply what happens to all living things. Someone dreading death while surrounded by colleagues, family, or friends who seem to believe different things about what matters in life—feeling isolated by their own values. A person exhausted by constant conflict in their workplace or relationships, thinking it would be easier to accept death than to keep navigating disagreements. Someone experiencing existential heaviness from being around people who dismiss or mock the things they care about. An aging person confronting that they have less time left than time already lived, and wondering if staying alive is even worth the daily friction.
meaning_fields.teaching: Death is as natural as childhood, aging, or growing a beard—it's just another stage that belongs to the order of things. You won't want to cling to life if you're surrounded by people who don't share your values; the real burden isn't death itself, but living daily among those who think differently than you do. When you accept that your departure from people of misaligned beliefs is not a tragedy but relief, death becomes easier to face.
meaning_fields.emotions: Deep weariness from being different or holding minority beliefs. Fear that accepting death means giving up on life. Loneliness in a crowd of people who don't understand what you stand for. Quiet relief at the thought of escaping constant disagreement. Resignation mixed with a strange kind of peace about mortality.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis)—the idea that death is a natural process as inevitable as aging, not an exception or violation of how things should be. Acceptance (prosoche)—alert, willing consent to what is ordained, not passive resignation. The social problem of misaligned values—the Stoic understanding that living among those with opposed beliefs is the real suffering, not death itself.

translation: He that sinneth, sinneth unto himself. He that is unjust, hurts himself, in that he makes himself worse than he was before. Not he only that committeth, but he also that omitteth something, is oftentimes unjust.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: A coworker lies to a client and you know it happened, but you say nothing and let it slide. You watch someone being treated unfairly at work or in your neighborhood and you don't speak up. You take a shortcut on a project by cutting corners, knowing it's not fully honest. You fail to correct misinformation about someone else, even though you could easily do it. You realize you stayed silent when you could have done the right thing, and now you're replaying the moment.
meaning_fields.teaching: When you act unjustly—whether by doing something wrong or by failing to act when you should—you damage yourself first, before anyone else. The harm is internal: you become a person who compromises their integrity. Inaction in the face of wrongdoing counts just as much as active wrongdoing; both make you complicit and worse than you were.
meaning_fields.emotions: Complicity, guilt about staying silent, self-disappointment at your own cowardice, the creeping feeling that you've betrayed your own standards, regret mixed with the realization that you let yourself down.
meaning_fields.concepts: Justice (dikaiosyne in Greek, meaning right action and fair dealing) is understood here as both action and omission. The Stoic view is that virtue is the only true good, and vice—including passive failure—is the only true harm. Marcus emphasizes that unjust behavior wounds the soul of the person committing it, not just the victim; wrongdoing makes you metaphysically worse, corrupting your character.

translation: If my present apprehension of the object be right, and my present action charitable, and this, towards whatsoever doth proceed from God, be my present disposition, to be well pleased with it, it sufficeth.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: Right now, you have three things within your control: seeing clearly what's actually happening, acting with genuine kindness toward others, and accepting what life brings you without bitterness. If you get these three things right in this moment, you've done everything that matters—nothing else is required.
meaning_fields.emotions: Peace despite uncertainty, letting go of the need to control outcomes, quiet acceptance, relief when you stop fighting reality, the calm that comes from knowing you did your part, freedom from resentment about circumstances
meaning_fields.situations: You make a good-faith effort to help someone and it doesn't work out the way you hoped, but you let it go. A plan falls through and instead of raging about bad luck, you move forward without complaint. You catch yourself judging a situation harshly, pause, and decide to trust that there's a reason it's unfolding this way. You help someone knowing you'll never get credit or thanks, and you're fine with that. Life deals you an unfair hand and you refuse to become bitter about it.
meaning_fields.concepts: Premeditatio malorum (negative visualization): preparing yourself to accept hardship so you're not shocked when it comes. Amor fati (love of fate): not just tolerating what happens but being genuinely willing to accept it. Prosoche (mindfulness): paying attention to what's actually true rather than what you fear or desire. The dichotomy of control: focusing effort only on what you can control—your perception, your intention, your choices—and releasing attachment to results.

You catch yourself judging a situation harshly, pause, and decide to trust that there's a reason it's unfolding this way. You help someone knowing you'll never get credit or thanks, and you're fine with that. Life deals you an unfair hand and you refuse to become bitter about it.
Right now, you have three things within your control: seeing clearly what's actually happening, acting with genuine kindness toward others, and accepting what life brings you without bitterness. If you get these three things right in this moment, you've done everything that matters—nothing else is required.
Peace despite uncertainty, letting go of the need to control outcomes, quiet acceptance, relief when you stop fighting reality, the calm that comes from knowing you did your part, freedom from resentment about circumstances
Premeditatio malorum (negative visualization): preparing yourself to accept hardship so you're not shocked when it comes. Amor fati (love of fate): not just tolerating what happens but being genuinely willing to accept it. Prosoche (mindfulness): paying attention to what's actually true rather than what you fear or desire. The dichotomy of control: focusing effort only on what you can control—your perception, your intention, your choices—and releasing attachment to results.

translation: To wipe away fancy, to use deliberation, to quench concupiscence, to keep the mind free to herself.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: You're scrolling social media and start comparing yourself to others, feeling envious. | You're about to make a major decision but realize you're being swayed by what sounds good rather than what's actually true. | You're stuck on a craving—buying things you don't need, eating when you're not hungry, or checking your phone compulsively. | You notice you're performing for other people instead of acting on your actual values. | Your mind is cluttered with worries about what others think, and you can't focus on what matters to you.
meaning_fields.teaching: Clear away the mental noise—the fantasies, the assumptions, the things you think you want. Slow down and actually think things through. Let go of the cravings that pull you away from what's real. The goal is to get your mind back under your own control, so you're free to decide based on reason, not on impulse or illusion.
meaning_fields.emotions: Overwhelm from too many desires competing for attention. The frustration of feeling out of control or reactive. The anxiety of not knowing what you actually believe. The exhaustion of performing or seeking approval. The clarity that comes when you stop chasing phantom wants.
meaning_fields.concepts: Fancy means the false stories and impressions we create—the mental noise that covers reality. Concupiscence is the appetite or craving for things, especially those we don't truly need. Deliberation is the practice of slowing down and thinking things through carefully. The passage describes the Stoic goal of autarkeia—self-sufficiency or autonomy of mind, the freedom to think and choose for yourself without being hijacked by impulse or illusion.

translation: Of all unreasonable creatures, there is but one unreasonable soul; and of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt them all. As of all earthly things there is but one earth, and but one light that we see by; and but one air that we breathe in, as many as either breathe or see. Now whatsoever partakes of some common thing, naturally affects and inclines unto that whereof it is part, being of one kind and nature with it. Whatsoever is earthly, presseth downwards to the common earth. Whatsoever is liquid, would flow together. And whatsoever is airy, would be together likewise. So that without some obstacle, and some kind of violence, they cannot well be kept asunder. Whatsoever is fiery, doth not only by reason of the elementary fire tend upwards; but here also is so ready to join, and to burn together, that whatsoever doth want sufficient moisture to make resistance, is easily set on fire. Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind. For by how much in its own nature it excels all other things, by so much more is it desirous to be joined and united unto that, which is of its own nature. As for unreasonable creatures then, they had not long been, but presently begun among them swarms, and flocks, and broods of young ones, and a kind of mutual love and affection. For though but unreasonable, yet a kind of soul these had, and therefore was that natural desire of union more strong and intense in them, as in creatures of a more excellent nature, than either in plants, or stones, or trees. But among reasonable creatures, begun commonwealths, friendships, families, public meetings, and even in their wars, conventions, and truces. Now among them that were yet of a more excellent nature, as the stars and planets, though by their nature far distant one from another, yet even among them began some mutual correspondency and unity. So proper is it to excellency in a high degree to affect unity, as that even in things so far distant, it could operate unto a mutual sympathy. But now behold, what is now come to pass. Those creatures that are reasonable, are now the only creatures that have forgotten their natural affection and inclination of one towards another. Among them alone of all other things that are of one kind, there is not to be found a general disposition to flow together. But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in their course, and apprehended. Do they what they can, nature doth prevail. And so shalt thou confess, if thou dost observe it. For sooner mayst thou find a thing earthly, where no earthly thing is, than find a man that naturally can live by himself alone.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: A person realizes they've been isolating themselves—avoiding friends, skipping family events, or refusing help from others because they think they should be self-sufficient. Someone finds themselves acting selfishly in ways that damage relationships, then feels oddly unfulfilled despite being independent. A manager undermines team collaboration by hoarding information or credit, only to watch the organization suffer and their own work feel hollow. A teenager pulls away from peers thinking they don't need anyone, then feels profoundly lonely. Someone notices they're competing with people they should be cooperating with, even though it hurts them both.
meaning_fields.teaching: We are built for connection the way water flows downward or fire rises—it's not a choice but our nature. Humans who act as if they can thrive alone are working against themselves as much as a fish trying to survive without water. When you fight your need for others, you're not becoming stronger; you're just making yourself miserable while failing anyway, because no person actually can live entirely alone.
meaning_fields.emotions: Loneliness hiding as self-reliance, the hollow satisfaction of independence, shame at needing others, a vague sense of wrongness when isolated, confusion about why being alone feels painful even when you thought you wanted it, guilt about not contributing to community.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis)—the innate drive that governs all things according to their kind. Unity and sympathy across difference. Rational nature (the logos) as humanity's highest excellence. The relationship between individual and whole. Natural tendency (hormē) as a force like gravity that cannot be permanently resisted.

translation: Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits. All things have their proper time to bear. Though by custom, the word itself is in a manner become proper unto the vine, and the like, yet is it so nevertheless, as we have said. As for reason, that beareth both common fruit for the use of others; and peculiar, which itself doth enjoy. Reason is of a diffusive nature, what itself is in itself, it begets in others, and so doth multiply.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: Every person has a unique role to play and gifts to develop—just as fruit trees bear fruit in their season, humans bear fruits through reasoning and action. Your particular talent or strength isn't just for you; it naturally creates value for others around you when you use it. When you live according to reason, you don't hoard what you have—you multiply it by sharing it, and that's how you fulfill your purpose.
meaning_fields.emotions: Feeling undervalued or purposeless; wondering if your talents matter; guilt about keeping your gifts to yourself; frustration that your work doesn't seem to reach anyone; anxiety about whether you're contributing enough; relief when you see your effort help someone else.
meaning_fields.situations: You have a skill—writing, teaching, listening, problem-solving—and you're not sure it's worth developing or sharing; your boss tells you to keep quiet and not mentor younger colleagues, but you feel called to teach; you're good at something but afraid it won't make a difference; you've been isolated during a difficult period and questioning what you have to offer; you finally help someone with your knowledge and realize how much it meant to them.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis)—each thing has its own essential function or role. Reason (logos)—the capacity to think and act according to universal principles, not selfishly. Virtue expressing itself through contribution to others, not just personal excellence. The Stoic idea that individual good and collective good are inseparable—you can't fulfill your nature in isolation.

translation: Either teach them better if it be in thy power; or if it be not, remember that for this use, to bear with them patiently, was mildness and goodness granted unto thee. The Gods themselves are good unto such; yea and in some things, (as in matter of health, of wealth, of honour,) are content often to further their endeavours: so good and gracious are they. And mightest thou not be so too? or, tell me, what doth hinder thee?
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Someone at work keeps making the same mistake and won't listen to your corrections. A family member repeats a bad habit despite you pointing it out. A friend consistently shows up late and dismisses your concerns. You're stuck explaining the same thing to a coworker who never seems to learn. Someone close to you does something frustrating over and over, and you've given up trying to change them.
meaning_fields.teaching: When you can't fix someone's problem, patience becomes your actual job—not something you do reluctantly while waiting for them to improve. Your ability to stay calm around difficult people is a strength you were given to use, not evidence that you're failing them. The gods themselves help people succeed in the things they're trying to do, and they don't withdraw their support just because people disappoint them repeatedly.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at watching someone repeat mistakes. Helplessness when your advice or criticism doesn't stick. Resentment that you have to keep your patience when someone seems determined not to change. Exhaustion from the effort of staying kind toward someone difficult. The feeling that your tolerance is being tested or taken for granted.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (your capacity to choose your response, not their choices). Apatheia (freedom from destructive anger, not emotional numbness). Oikeiosis (the natural bond of kinship with all humans that obligates you to act with goodness toward them). Cosmopolitanism (seeing yourself as part of a shared human community, not separate from flawed people). Amor fati (accepting what you cannot control about others and choosing virtue anyway).

translation: Labour not as one to whom it is appointed to be wretched, nor as one that either would be pitied, or admired; but let this be thine only care and desire; so always and in all things to prosecute or to forbear, as the law of charity, or mutual society doth require.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: Stop using your suffering or hard work to earn pity, respect, or admiration from others. Your only job is to figure out what fairness and community require in each situation, then do that—nothing more. How people judge your effort doesn't matter.
meaning_fields.emotions: The desire to be seen as suffering nobly; the need for others to recognize how hard you're working; resentment when effort goes unnoticed; guilt about not "performing" your struggles convincingly enough
meaning_fields.situations: You stay late at work and want people to see how much you sacrificed; you volunteer and feel hurt when no one thanks you; you're going through a tough time and catch yourself mentioning it repeatedly to get sympathy; you do the right thing but feel invisible because it's not dramatic; you hesitate to rest because you're worried people will think you're lazy
meaning_fields.concepts: Duty (what you're actually obligated to do) versus performance (doing things to impress an audience). The Stoic distinction between what is in your control (your choice, your effort toward what's right) and what isn't (others' opinions, recognition, praise). Oikeiōsis—natural mutual obligation to the human community you belong to.

translation: This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Getting stuck replaying an embarrassing moment and realizing you're the only one still thinking about it; being angry at someone but realizing nobody else cares anymore; waiting for an apology or justice that never comes and deciding to move on anyway; finding yourself still bitter about something that happened years ago; lying awake at night worrying about a conflict that resolved weeks ago
meaning_fields.teaching: Your trouble lives in your head, not in the world. Events happen and pass, but you keep suffering because you won't let the thought of them go. Real relief comes when you stop choosing to replay what happened and release it from your own mind—that's the only exit.
meaning_fields.emotions: Resentment that won't fade, rumination and obsessive replaying, the trap of feeling wronged, shame that keeps resurfacing, bitterness over past events, the frustration of being stuck in your own thoughts
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (choice/will)—the Stoic idea that your power lies only in your judgments and voluntary thoughts, not external events. Indifferents—what happens outside you matters far less than what you do with it mentally. Ataraxia (freedom from disturbance)—which comes not from changing the world but from mastering your internal assent to disturbing thoughts.

translation: All those things, for matter of experience are usual and ordinary; for their continuance but for a day; and for their matter, most base and filthy. As they were in the days of those whom we have buried, so are they now also, and no otherwise.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Someone getting caught up in office drama and realizing it'll blow over like it always does. A friend stressing about a health scare that turns out to be routine. Worrying obsessively about what people think at a party, then forgetting it by next week. Spending money on something trendy that everyone else is caught up in too. Lying awake over an embarrassing mistake, then realizing nobody actually remembers it.
meaning_fields.teaching: The things you're stressed about right now are the same ordinary troubles people have faced forever—they're temporary, they're not actually significant, and they'll be gone tomorrow just like they were yesterday. Stop treating your current problem like it's unique or permanent.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety about things feeling urgent and real, getting swept up in drama, the desperation that comes from believing your current stress is exceptional or that this moment defines everything, fear that something matters more than it does.
meaning_fields.concepts: The doctrine of universal recurrence and impermanence: nothing you face is novel. Perspective through time: what feels crushing today looked the same in ancient Rome and will look the same in the future. The concept of preferred indifferents—outer events have minimal real value.
