translation: The things themselves that affect us, they stand without doors, neither knowing anything themselves nor able to utter anything unto others concerning themselves. What then is it, that passeth verdict on them? The understanding.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: External events have no built-in meaning or power over you—they're just neutral facts. Your mind is what assigns them meaning and determines whether they upset you or not. You control the judgment that follows.
meaning_fields.emotions: Feeling helpless when bad things happen; rage at circumstances beyond your control; anxiety spiraling from imagining what events mean about you or your future; relief or empowerment when you realize you can choose your reaction
meaning_fields.situations: Your boss gives you harsh feedback and you spend hours convinced you're incompetent, replaying every word; someone cuts you off in traffic and your whole mood tanks for the day; you get rejected from something and immediately assume you're not good enough; you receive criticism at work and can't tell whether the feedback is actually valid or just your mind catastrophizing; you experience a setback and realize a few hours later that you had added extra meaning and doom to something that was just a practical problem
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (moral choice/faculty of assent) — the power to accept or reject impressions; the Stoic dichotomy of control — separating what happens from what it means; phantasia (presentation or impression) — the initial appearance of events to the mind before judgment occurs

translation: As virtue and wickedness consist not in passion, but in action; so neither doth the true good or evil of a reasonable charitable man consist in passion, but in operation and action.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: What matters about you is what you actually do, not what you feel or want to do. Your character is defined by your choices and actions, not by your emotions or impulses. You can feel angry, jealous, or afraid—but those feelings don't make you a good or bad person. Only what you choose to do with those feelings counts.
meaning_fields.emotions: Shame about your own impulses; guilt over angry or envious thoughts you can't control; frustration that good intentions don't seem to match your internal state; anxiety that having bad feelings makes you a bad person; hope that your mistakes don't define you if you change what you do.
meaning_fields.situations: You snap at someone in anger but immediately apologize and change how you treat them going forward. You feel tempted to lie about a mistake at work but choose to be honest instead, even though the fear doesn't disappear. You're overwhelmed with resentment toward a family member but show up and treat them with respect anyway. You struggle with selfish impulses but keep commitments to people who depend on you. You feel cowardly before doing something difficult, but you do it anyway.
meaning_fields.concepts: Virtue (excellence of character, achieved through deliberate choice); vice (failure or wrongdoing); the Stoic distinction between what is "in our control" (our choices and actions) versus what is not (our emotions and urges). The passage rejects the idea that having bad feelings makes you morally flawed—only harmful actions do.

translation: To the stone that is cast up, when it comes down it is no hurt unto it; as neither benefit, when it doth ascend.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: A promotion falls through after you invested months in preparing for it. Your business deal collapses after initial excitement. You lose a competition you trained hard for. Someone stops returning your calls after seeming like a close friend. You get rejected from something you wanted badly, then life just continues.
meaning_fields.teaching: External events—gains and losses alike—don't inherently harm or help your character or well-being. What happens to you in the world is morally neutral. Only your judgments about those events, and how you choose to respond, actually matter.
meaning_fields.emotions: Disappointment after something good falls away. The clinging hope that keeps you wound tight. Relief mixed with shame when you're forced to let go. The quiet feeling that life shouldn't affect you this much.
meaning_fields.concepts: Indifference (adiaphora)—the Stoic teaching that most things in life are "neither good nor bad" in themselves. Virtue alone is the true good. Acceptance of impermanence and the limits of your control. The distinction between what is "up to you" (your will and judgment) and what is not (external outcomes).

translation: Sift their minds and understandings, and behold what men they be, whom thou dost stand in fear of what they shall judge of thee, what they themselves judge of themselves.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: You're nervous about presenting to your boss because you're worried about being judged harshly. You obsess over what they think of your work. You realize they're insecure about their own abilities and don't actually have it figured out. You catch yourself caring intensely what someone thinks of you, then notice they don't even respect themselves. You're anxious before a performance review, imagining your manager's critical thoughts, but then realize how much they struggle with their own confidence at home.
meaning_fields.teaching: Most of the power you give to other people's judgment comes from assuming they have clear, confident thoughts about you. But if you actually look at who they are—their doubts, their contradictions, their low opinion of themselves—you realize their judgment is not the solid thing you feared. You're fearing a verdict from someone who doesn't even believe in themselves.
meaning_fields.emotions: Fear of judgment, anxiety about what others think, dread of criticism, respect mixed with doubt, deflation when you see someone's weakness, relief at realizing someone's opinion doesn't matter as much as you thought.
meaning_fields.concepts: Perception and reality (what we imagine others think versus what they actually think). Projection (we assume others are more confident judges than they are). The nature of judgment and its source (judgment has power only if we grant it power). Self-worth as independent from external verdict.

text_for_embedding:
You're nervous about presenting to your boss because you're worried about being judged harshly. You obsess over what they think of your work. You realize they're insecure about their own abilities and don't actually have it figured out. You catch yourself caring intensely what someone thinks of you, then notice they don't even respect themselves. You're anxious before a performance review, imagining your manager's critical thoughts, but then realize how much they struggle with their own confidence at home.
Most of the power you give to other people's judgment comes from assuming they have clear, confident thoughts about you. But if you actually look at who they are—their doubts, their contradictions, their low opinion of themselves—you realize their judgment is not the solid thing you feared. You're fearing a verdict from someone who doesn't even believe in themselves.
Fear of judgment, anxiety about what others think, dread of criticism, respect mixed with doubt, deflation when you see someone's weakness, relief at realizing someone's opinion doesn't matter as much as you thought.
Perception and reality (what we imagine others think versus what they actually think). Projection (we assume others are more confident judges than they are). The nature of judgment and its source (judgment has power only if we grant it power). Self-worth as independent from external verdict.

translation: All things that are in the world, are always in the estate of alteration. Thou also art in a perpetual change, yea and under corruption too, in some part: and so is the whole world.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Watching your body age and not recognize yourself in the mirror. Realizing a skill you spent years developing is becoming obsolete at work. Noticing a friendship that used to be central to your life has quietly drifted apart. Seeing your parents decline in health and capability. Revisiting a place from childhood and finding it completely transformed.
meaning_fields.teaching: Everything you see around you—including your own body, abilities, and relationships—is constantly decaying and transforming into something different. Fighting this fact or feeling betrayed by it is pointless, because change and breakdown are built into the nature of existence itself. Accepting this doesn't mean giving up; it means stopping the waste of energy pretending things should stay the same.
meaning_fields.emotions: Grief over losing what you were. Anxiety about decline and deterioration. Resentment at being caught in a process you can't control. Vertigo from realizing nothing is stable. The strange comfort of knowing you're not uniquely broken—everything decays.
meaning_fields.concepts: Flux (the constant flowing change of all material things, from Heraclitus). Corruption (natural decay and breakdown, not moral failure—the inevitable weakening of physical form). Impermanence (nothing stays the way it is). The view that resistance to natural change is itself the source of suffering.

translation: it is not thine, but another man's sin. Why should it trouble thee? Let him look to it, whose sin it is.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: When someone else does something wrong, that's their problem to fix, not yours to carry. You're only responsible for your own choices and character. Obsessing over their mistake doesn't change what happened and only wastes your own mental energy.
meaning_fields.situations: A family member makes a bad decision and you keep rehashing how they should have done it differently; Your boss treats a colleague unfairly and you find yourself angry and preoccupied with it all day; A friend breaks a promise to you and you replay the betrayal over and over; A coworker's mistake creates extra work for your team and you're still fuming hours later; Someone lies about you and you're consumed with correcting the record in your head.
meaning_fields.emotions: Resentment, preoccupation, the burden of carrying someone else's wrongdoing, frustration at not being able to control what others do, the mental exhaustion of replaying someone else's mistake, indignation.
meaning_fields.concepts: Moral agency (the idea that each person is responsible only for their own choices); the distinction between what is in your control and what is not; apatheia (not apathy, but freedom from being controlled by external events). The Stoic view that you cannot control others' actions or character, only your own response to them.

translation: Of an operation and of a purpose there is an ending, or of an action and of a purpose we say commonly, that it is at an end: from opinion also there is an absolute cessation, which is as it were the death of it. In all this there is no hurt. Apply this now to a man's age, as first, a child; then a youth, then a young man, then an old man; every change from one age to another is a kind of death And all this while here no matter of grief yet. Pass now unto that life first, that which thou livedst under thy grandfather, then under thy mother, then under thy father. And thus when through the whole course of thy life hitherto thou hast found and observed many alterations, many changes, many kinds of endings and cessations, put this question to thyself What matter of grief or sorrow dost thou find in any of these? Or what doest thou suffer through any of these? If in none of these, then neither in the ending and consummation of thy whole life, which is also but a cessation and change.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: Every ending you've already survived—leaving childhood, moving homes, changing jobs, ending relationships—was a small death. You felt the change, maybe discomfort, but no real harm came to you. Your entire life has been endings layered on endings, and you're still here. So when you're facing the final ending, the pattern is the same: it's just another cessation in a life full of them.
meaning_fields.emotions: Fear of the unknown, dread about endings, anxiety about loss and change, sadness about time passing, worry that something precious is being taken from you
meaning_fields.situations: Watching your children grow up and leave home, leaving a job or career you've built; realizing you're aging and your parents are aging; going through a breakup or major life transition; lying awake at night thinking about death; facing a deadline or finishing a long project and feeling unmoored without it
meaning_fields.concepts: Impermanence (the Buddhist-adjacent idea that nothing lasts, though Marcus frames it through change rather than suffering); the continuity of the self through radical change (you are not the same person you were at five, fifteen, or thirty-five, yet you survived it); death as a natural process rather than a violation.

translation: As occasion shall require, either to thine own understanding, or to that of the universe, or to his, whom thou hast now to do with, let thy refuge be with all speed. To thine own, that it resolve upon nothing against justice. To that of the universe, that thou mayest remember, part of whom thou art. Of his, that thou mayest consider whether in the estate of ignorance, or of knowledge. And then also must thou call to mind, that he is thy kinsman.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: When you're in conflict or uncertainty with someone, you have three places to look: first, your own judgment—to make sure you're not about to do something unfair. Second, your connection to the larger world—you're part of something bigger than just this moment. Third, the other person—whether they're acting from ignorance or knowledge, they're still your relative, your equal. This shifts you from blame to understanding.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration with someone's behavior, the urge to retaliate or punish, moral confusion about what's right, indignation at being wronged, the impulse to judge harshly
meaning_fields.situations: Your boss dismisses your concerns in a meeting and you feel the heat rising to respond harshly; a friend cancels plans last minute and you're deciding whether to send an angry text; a family member says something hurtful and you're composing a cutting reply; a coworker takes credit for your idea and you're caught between calling them out publicly or letting it go; someone cuts you off in traffic and you're about to honk and gesture aggressively
meaning_fields.concepts: Justice (dikaiosyne)—doing what is fair and right, not letting emotion override principle. The interconnectedness of all humans—we share reason and belong to one another. Ignorance versus knowledge—recognizing that people often act from a limited understanding, not malice. Kinship—the fundamental equality and relationship between all people.

translation: As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and consummation, being a member of it, of a common society; so must every action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that is truly sociable. What action soever of thine therefore that either immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is an exorbitant and disorderly action; yea it is seditious; as one among the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously divide and separate himself.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: You're weighing a career move that would pay more but requires you to leave your team mid-project. You're deciding whether to take credit for work that involved many contributors. You're in a meeting where you could advance yourself by downplaying a colleague's contribution. You're wondering if it's okay to pursue a personal goal even though it means less time helping your family or community. You're tempted to keep a financial advantage you found through a loophole, knowing others aren't aware of it.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your actions aren't yours alone—they ripple out and either strengthen or damage the group you're part of. When you act purely for yourself without regard to how it affects the people around you, you're essentially sabotaging the community you depend on. Every choice either builds trust and cohesion with others or introduces chaos and fracture.
meaning_fields.emotions: Guilt about taking more than your fair share. Resentment at having to consider others' needs when pursuing what you want. Anxiety about losing personal opportunities. Shame when realizing your actions harmed people who trusted you. Satisfaction from knowing your choices benefited others around you.
meaning_fields.concepts: Social obligation (the Greek concept of being part of a larger whole, not separate). Common good (the shared welfare that benefits everyone including yourself). Virtue through alignment (doing right because it maintains the social fabric, not just for personal gain). Sedition (breaking the implicit bonds that hold a community together).

translation: Children's anger, mere babels; wretched souls bearing up dead bodies, that they may not have their fall so soon: even as it is in that common dirge song.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Someone getting angry over a minor slight and you realize how small it actually is. Watching someone stay stuck in resentment over old hurts, still carrying the weight long after. Noticing your own irritation building over something trivial and catching yourself. Someone complaining endlessly about a problem without actually trying to fix it. Feeling the urge to hold onto anger because letting it go feels like admitting defeat.
meaning_fields.teaching: Anger over small things is childish—it wastes your energy propping up something already dead. When you cling to resentment or carry old grievances, you're just delaying the natural ending of something that should have fallen away already. Let go of what's already gone.
meaning_fields.emotions: frustration at petty things, the exhaustion of holding onto old anger, the futility of grudges, recognition that you're making something worse by refusing to let it die, the relief of finally letting something go
meaning_fields.concepts: Indifference to externals (the Stoic idea that externals like reputation and minor slights are not real goods and don't deserve your emotional energy); the natural order of impermanence (things arise and fall away—fighting this law wastes you); dignity through reason (childish reaction versus rational perspective)

translation: Go to the quality of the cause from which the effect doth proceed. Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is material. Then consider the utmost bounds of time that that cause, thus and thus qualified, can subsist and abide.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Someone is caught in an endless worry loop about a difficult situation—a failed relationship, a health scare, a career setback—and keeps imagining worst-case futures. A person inherits a family pattern of anxiety or resentment and feels trapped by it. Someone obsesses over another person's motives and can't stop constructing narratives about their character. A person faces a chronic problem—chronic pain, an ongoing conflict, a persistent limitation—and catastrophizes about how long it will last. Someone is haunted by what someone else said or did and projects their behavior as permanent and defining.
meaning_fields.teaching: When you're caught in worry or blame, strip away the emotional story and look at the bare fact underneath: what is actually causing this? Then ask: how long can this actual cause really sustain itself? Most things that feel eternal have a natural expiration date. This one practice—seeing what's actually happening, not your story about it, then seeing its real limits—dissolves much of the power worry and resentment hold over you.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety about the future, obsessive rumination, resentment toward someone, feeling trapped by a situation, catastrophizing, helplessness in the face of something that feels permanent or relentless
meaning_fields.concepts: Primal cause (the actual root, not the narrative); material versus immaterial (the difference between what's actually happening and the story you've added); time as a limit (even negative things are temporary, though we feel them as absolute)

translation: Infinite are the troubles and miseries, that thou hast already been put to, by reason of this only, because that for all happiness it did not suffice thee, or, that thou didst not account it sufficient happiness, that thy understanding did operate according to its natural constitution.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: You've made yourself miserable by demanding that external things deliver happiness, when your mind functioning well is already enough. All your suffering traces back to this one mistake: thinking you need more than a working mind to be okay.
meaning_fields.emotions: dissatisfaction despite having good things, the gnawing feeling that what you have isn't enough, frustration with yourself for always wanting more, exhaustion from chasing happiness through circumstances
meaning_fields.situations: You get a promotion but immediately fixate on what you didn't achieve instead; you have a stable job and home but can't shake the sense that something's missing; you accomplish a goal you worked toward for years and feel empty; you keep upgrading your life (better apartment, better relationship, more money) expecting to finally feel content, but the satisfaction never lasts; you're healthy and successful but spend your time worrying about things that might go wrong
meaning_fields.concepts: Natural constitution (your mind operating according to its design); sufficiency (the idea that some things are genuinely enough and don't need addition); the root cause fallacy (tracing all unhappiness back to one error rather than blaming circumstances)

translation: When any shall either impeach thee with false accusations, or hatefully reproach thee, or shall use any such carriage towards thee, get thee presently to their minds and understandings, and look in them, and behold what manner of men they be. Thou shalt see, that there is no such occasion why it should trouble thee, what such as they are think of thee. Yet must thou love them still, for by nature they are thy friends. And the Gods themselves, in those things that they seek from them as matters of great moment, are well content, all manner of ways, as by dreams and oracles, to help them as well as others.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Someone spreads rumors about you at work and you keep checking to see who believes it. A family member says something cutting during an argument and you replay their words for hours. A rival takes public credit for your effort and you fantasize about correcting everyone. You get a scathing review from a boss and obsess over whether they see you as incompetent. A friend sides with someone against you and you wonder if they ever respected you at all.
meaning_fields.teaching: When someone attacks your reputation or treats you badly, stop focusing on what they think of you and instead look at who they actually are. Understanding their nature—their struggles, limitations, blindness—dissolves the sting of their judgment. Your worth doesn't depend on their opinion of you, and even people acting from ignorance remain capable of good and deserve your care.
meaning_fields.emotions: Indignation at being misrepresented or wronged. Shame and self-doubt when criticized. Wounded feelings from betrayal or dismissal. Anger at unfair treatment. Desperate need to correct the record or prove yourself right.
meaning_fields.concepts: Logos—the rational principle that connects all human beings. Proairesis—the power of choice and perspective that lies within you alone. Nature and physis—the shared humanity and limits built into every person, including those who harm you. Cosmopolitanism—recognizing others as fellow members of humanity despite their flaws.

translation: Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of the world; being still the same. And either of everything in particular before it come to pass, the mind of the universe doth consider with itself and deliberate: and if so, then submit for shame unto the determination of such an excellent understanding: or once for all it did resolve upon all things in general; and since that whatsoever happens, happens by a necessary consequence, and all things indivisibly in a manner and inseparably hold one of another. In sum, either there is a God, and then all is well; or if all things go by chance and fortune, yet mayest thou use thine own providence in those things that concern thee properly; and then art thou well.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: You're facing an unexpected setback—a job loss, a relationship ending, a health scare—and you're tormented by the "why me?" question. You're stuck in blame-spiraling, replaying decisions that might have prevented it. You're watching friends seem to breeze through life while you get dealt hard cards. You're trying to figure out whether you have any real control or if you're just a pawn. You're exhausted from trying to change something that already happened.
meaning_fields.teaching: Either the universe has a rational intelligence guiding it toward something good, or everything is chaotic and random—and in either case, you're not the victim. If it's rational, trust it. If it's random, stop wasting energy on blame and focus on what's actually in your hands right now. Either way, you're okay.
meaning_fields.emotions: Rage at unfairness, powerlessness, bewilderment at why bad things happen, feeling singled out by fate, exhaustion from wrestling with the past, bitter resentment that others have it easier, grasping for control, fear that nothing you do matters.
meaning_fields.concepts: Determinism (the idea that everything follows necessarily from prior causes); providence (the rational ordering of the universe); fate vs. free will; the dichotomy of control (what is and isn't genuinely in your power); logos (the intelligence or reason operating throughout nature).

translation: Within a while the earth shall cover us all, and then she herself shall have her change. And then the course will be, from one period of eternity unto another, and so a perpetual eternity. Now can any man that shall consider with himself in his mind the several rollings or successions of so many changes and alterations, and the swiftness of all these rulings; can he otherwise but contemn in his heart and despise all worldly things? The cause of the universe is as it were a strong torrent, it carrieth all away.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: Everything you own, every relationship, every achievement—all of it gets swept away by time and replaced by something else. When you zoom out and see how fast everything changes and how small you are in the face of endless cycles, clinging to your stuff and your status starts to look ridiculous. The universe is a force that carries everything along; you cannot hold on.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety about loss and impermanence, the sting of status-seeking, feeling overwhelmed by how much you care about things that don't last, the relief of accepting you can't control it anyway
meaning_fields.situations: You've just bought something expensive and you're already worried about it breaking or becoming obsolete. You worked for years to get a promotion and suddenly realize it won't matter in fifty years. You're grieving someone and can't stop thinking about how fast their memory will fade. You're envious of a colleague's success and lying awake at night about it. You're stressed about your legacy and what people will remember about you.
meaning_fields.concepts: Memento mori (the remembrance that death comes for everyone); the impermanence of all conditioned things; contempt for externals (indifference to things outside your control like wealth and reputation); the cosmic perspective (seeing your life against the scale of eternity)

translation: And these your professed politicians, the only true practical philosophers of the world, (as they think of themselves) so full of affected gravity, or such professed lovers of virtue and honesty, what wretches be they in very deed; how vile and contemptible in themselves? O man! what ado doest thou keep? Do what thy nature doth now require. Resolve upon it, if thou mayest: and take no thought, whether anybody shall know it or no. Yea, but sayest thou, I must not expect a Plato's commonwealth. If they profit though never so little, I must be content; and think much even of that little progress. Doth then any of them forsake their former false opinions that I should think they profit? For without a change of opinions, alas! what is all that ostentation, but mere wretchedness of slavish minds, that groan privately, and yet would make a show of obedience to reason, and truth? Go too now and tell me of Alexander and Philippus, and Demetrius Phalereus. Whether they understood what the common nature requireth, and could rule themselves or no, they know best themselves. But if they kept a life, and swaggered; I (God be thanked) am not bound to imitate them. The effect of true philosophy is, unaffected simplicity and modesty. Persuade me not to ostentation and vainglory.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: A manager takes credit in meetings for your team's work while privately knowing it was your effort. You see colleagues get promoted by talking loudly about their accomplishments while you focus on actual results. Someone lectures you about ethics and integrity but cuts corners when no one is watching. You watch successful people around you succeed through image-building and self-promotion while you try to do good work quietly. A friend asks why you don't brag more about your achievements since everyone else does.
meaning_fields.teaching: Stop waiting for perfect conditions or perfect colleagues before you act rightly. Do what's actually required of you now, regardless of whether anyone notices or praises you. Real integrity means being the same person in private and in public—not performing virtue while compromising it behind closed doors. Don't measure your worth by whether others change or whether you get credit; measure it by whether you're actually doing what's right.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at the gap between what people claim to believe and how they actually behave. Resentment at watching hypocrites succeed. Exhaustion from trying to do right while others game the system. Doubt about whether integrity matters if it goes unrecognized. Disgust at your own temptation to compromise and perform.
meaning_fields.concepts: Hypocrisy (claiming virtue while acting against it); Nature and duty (what your role actually requires); Appearance versus reality (the gap between public image and private behavior); Integrity (being internally consistent); False progress (appearing to improve while keeping corrupted values underneath).

translation: From some high place as it were to look down, and to behold here flocks, and there sacrifices, without number; and all kind of navigation; some in a rough and stormy sea, and some in a calm: the general differences, or different estates of things, some, that are now first upon being; the several and mutual relations of those things that are together; and some other things that are at their last. Their lives also, who were long ago, and theirs who shall be hereafter, and the present estate and life of those many nations of barbarians that are now in the world, thou must likewise consider in thy mind. And how many there be, who never so much as heard of thy name, how many that will soon forget it; how many who but even now did commend thee, within a very little while perchance will speak ill of thee. So that neither fame, nor honour, nor anything else that this world doth afford, is worth the while. The sum then of all; whatsoever doth happen unto thee, whereof God is the cause, to accept it contentedly: whatsoever thou doest, whereof thou thyself art the cause, to do it justly: which will be, if both in thy resolution and in thy action thou have no further end, than to do good unto others, as being that, which by thy natural constitution, as a man, thou art bound unto.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: When you zoom out and see how vast the world is—billions of people, countless generations before and after you, most who have never heard of you—your own reputation and status shrink to nothing. So stop chasing fame or worrying about what others think. Instead, accept what happens to you without complaint, and focus your actions on genuinely helping people, which is what you're made for as a human being.
meaning_fields.emotions: The sting of being forgotten, anxiety about your legacy, frustration when people's praise turns to criticism, a sense of your own smallness or insignificance, relief at letting go of caring what people think, quiet purpose when you focus on actually helping rather than impressing
meaning_fields.situations: You get passed over for a promotion and realize the senior people you admired won't even notice; someone who used to praise your work suddenly criticizes it publicly and you spiral; you spend months on a project hoping it will make your name in your field, then it gets buried or someone else gets credit; you lie awake worrying about whether people at work respect you; you finally stop checking social media metrics and notices how much mental energy that frees up; you help a stranger or mentor someone with no chance of recognition and feel more satisfied than any public win
meaning_fields.concepts: Prosoche (attention to what is in your control versus what isn't)—your reputation and fame are not in your control, so they shouldn't be your target. The dichotomy of control is central here: you control your actions and intentions, not outcomes or others' opinions. The concept of living according to nature (kata physin)—your nature as a human is to be just and to benefit others, not to pursue status. Amor fati (acceptance of what befalls you) applies to the neutral events of life.

translation: Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and then thou shalt have room enough.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: You're stressed about an email from your boss that you've read five times, each time finding new reasons to worry. Your teenager won't clean their room and you're mentally adding it to your list of failures. You're annoyed at yourself for gaining a few pounds and keep thinking about it throughout the day. You're anxious about a conversation you had last week and can't stop replaying it. A minor scheduling conflict at work feels like it's derailing your whole week.
meaning_fields.teaching: Most of what's suffocating you right now isn't actually a problem—it's a story you're telling yourself about it. The weight, the email, the mess, the awkward conversation—these feel enormous only because you've wrapped them in fear and judgment. Strip away the interpretation, the catastrophizing, the shame, and suddenly you have space to breathe and actually move.
meaning_fields.emotions: Suffocation, mental claustrophobia, overwhelm, anxiety about things that might not matter, frustration that your own mind is making life harder, the feeling of being trapped by your own thoughts
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (the power of choice over your judgments, not just external events); the Stoic dichotomy of control (you control your opinion, not the thing itself); phantasia (the initial impression or appearance that creates the sensation of trouble); ataraxia (the mental spaciousness that comes when you stop manufacturing problems through false belief)

translation: To comprehend the whole world together in thy mind, and the whole course of this present age to represent it unto thyself, and to fix thy thoughts upon the sudden change of every particular object. How short the time is from the generation of anything, unto the dissolution of the same; but how immense and infinite both that which was before the generation, and that which after the generation of it shall be. All things that thou seest, will soon be perished, and they that see their corruptions, will soon vanish away themselves. He that dieth a hundred years old, and he that dieth young, shall come all to one.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: You're stressed about a career setback and can't stop replaying it, treating it like it matters forever. You're anxious about getting older and running out of time. You're grieving someone's death and the loss feels infinite. You're caught up in daily drama—workplace conflict, family tension—and can't zoom out. You're afraid of dying, or afraid you haven't accomplished enough before you die.
meaning_fields.teaching: Everything you see right now—every problem, achievement, relationship, even your own life—is temporary. The span of time you exist is tiny compared to the vastness before you were born and after you'll be gone. Whether someone dies at 30 or 100, the outcome is the same. Zooming out to this reality should shrink whatever is consuming your thoughts right now.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety about time running out, obsessive replay of small conflicts or failures, dread about mortality, the feeling that your problems are permanent and enormous, fear of irrelevance or of dying with nothing to show for it.
meaning_fields.concepts: Memento mori—the practice of remembering you will die, used not to depress but to clarify what actually matters. The infinite versus the finite; the cosmic perspective, or what moderns call "zooming out." Impermanence (anicca), the Buddhist and Stoic insight that all things arise and pass away. Perspective as a tool for emotional relief.

translation: What are their minds and understandings; and what the things that they apply themselves unto: what do they love, and what do they hate for? Fancy to thyself the estate of their souls openly to be seen. When they think they hurt them shrewdly, whom they speak ill of; and when they think they do them a very good turn, whom they commend and extol: O how full are they then of conceit, and opinion!
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: Most people are driven by vanity and shallow concern for how others perceive them. When they criticize someone, they think they're causing real harm; when they praise someone, they think they're conferring real benefit. In both cases, they're deluded about their own importance and the actual impact of their words.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration at people's pettiness; exasperation with how much energy people waste on reputation and gossip; feeling disconnected from the vanity that drives others around you; a kind of sad amusement at human self-importance.
meaning_fields.situations: Watching a coworker spend an entire meeting bad-mouthing someone who isn't present, acting like they're delivering devastating criticism; listening to people obsess over whether someone important complimented them or snubbed them; noticing how much your own worth fluctuates in your mind based on a single comment from a boss or friend; realizing how many arguments start because people believe their insults have cut deep; watching people seek out and repeat praise they've received, needing to remind themselves they're valued.
meaning_fields.concepts: Conceit and false opinion (doksa in Greek philosophy)—the gap between what we think matters and what actually does. The illusion that our words and judgments have power they don't possess; the confusion between having an opinion about someone and actually affecting their character or worth.

translation: Loss and corruption, is in very deed nothing else but change and alteration; and that is it, which the nature of the universe doth most delight in, by which, and according to which, whatsoever is done, is well done. For that was the estate of worldly things from the beginning, and so shall it ever be. Or wouldest thou rather say, that all things in the world have gone ill from the beginning for so many ages, and shall ever go ill? And then among so many deities, could no divine power be found all this while, that could rectify the things of the world? Or is the world, to incessant woes and miseries, for ever condemned?
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: You've just lost your job and can't stop thinking about how unfair it is; you're watching your body age and feeling like something is being taken from you; your relationship ended and you keep replaying what went wrong; you invested time in a project that fell apart despite your best effort; you're facing a diagnosis and everything you planned feels like it's disappearing.
meaning_fields.teaching: Everything you experience as loss or damage is just the natural process of things changing form—it's not a failure or a punishment. The universe operates through constant transformation, and this process itself is how things work as they should. When you resist this fact, you're demanding the world be something it has never been.
meaning_fields.emotions: Grief about losing something you counted on; anger that things didn't stay the way you wanted; helplessness watching circumstances change despite your efforts; resentment that life feels unfair; dread about inevitable decay and endings.
meaning_fields.concepts: Impermanence (the Stoic doctrine that all things are in flux and nothing material lasts); the view that apparent harm is simply the operation of nature's design; the distinction between things that change (which is their nature) and our judgment that change is bad (which is optional).

translation: How base and putrid, every common matter is! Water, dust, and from the mixture of these bones, and all that loathsome stuff that our bodies do consist of: so subject to be infected, and corrupted. And again those other things that are so much prized and admired, as marble stones, what are they, but as it were the kernels of the earth? gold and silver, what are they, but as the more gross faeces of the earth? Thy most royal apparel, for matter, it is but as it were the hair of a silly sheep, and for colour, the very blood of a shell-fish; of this nature are all other things. Thy life itself, is some such thing too; a mere exhalation of blood: and it also, apt to be changed into some other common thing.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: You're stressed about your appearance or your possessions and feel like they define you. Someone you know is obsessed with luxury goods or status symbols and you want to cut through that. You're afraid of aging, decay, or mortality and it's paralyzing you. You catch yourself chasing money or designer clothes and feel hollow. You're grieving someone and struggling with the fact that their body will decompose.
meaning_fields.teaching: Everything your body is made of—water, minerals, dust—is the same stuff that makes up garbage. Your fancy clothes are just processed animal hair and shellfish blood. Your life itself is just air leaving blood. This isn't depressing; it means these things have no real value in themselves, so you're wasting energy protecting and obsessing over them. Once you see what they actually are, you stop being controlled by them.
meaning_fields.emotions: Disgust at decay and mortality, shame about caring so much about appearance or status, anxiety about aging, fear of death, hollowness from pursuing luxury, grief about the body's fragility
meaning_fields.concepts: Memento mori (remembering you will die): using the visual truth of decomposition to strip away illusions about what matters. Cosmopolitanism (seeing through local values): recognizing that what culture calls "precious" is materially base. Apatheia (freedom from destructive passions): when you see marble as "earth's kernels" and gold as "earth's faeces," vanity loses its grip. The body as impermanent: understanding the body not as something to be proud of, but as temporary arrangement of elements.

translation: Will this querulousness, this murmuring, this complaining and dissembling never be at an end? What then is it, that troubleth thee? Doth any new thing happen unto thee? What doest thou so wonder at? At the cause, or the matter? Behold either by itself, is either of that weight and moment indeed? And besides these, there is not anything. But thy duty towards the Gods also, it is time thou shouldst acquit thyself of it with more goodness and simplicity.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Someone keeps replaying a frustrating conversation at work, running through what they should have said differently. A friend vents for the third time about the same problem nobody can fix. Someone finds themselves complaining to family about minor setbacks, even after things have mostly worked out. A person realizes they've been irritable all week, snapping at people over small things when they're really upset about something bigger they can't control.
meaning_fields.teaching: Complaining and rehashing don't change what happened—they just keep you stuck in it. When you catch yourself murmuring about something, stop and ask: is this actually new, or am I just refusing to accept it? Even if the situation is real, you're making it worse by dwelling on it. Do what you can, accept what you can't, and let the rest go.
meaning_fields.emotions: Irritation, frustration, indignation at unfairness, the helpless feeling of being stuck, resentment at having to accept something you didn't choose, impatience with how long a bad thing has lasted.
meaning_fields.concepts: Acceptance (not passive resignation, but clear-eyed recognition of reality); duty or proper action (doing what's in your control with straightforwardness, not complaint); the Stoic distinction between what is in your control and what is not; virtue as the only true good (not comfort or getting your way).

translation: It is all one to see these things for a hundred of years together or but for three years.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Lying awake at 3am worrying you haven't accomplished enough in your 40 years and won't have time for everything that matters. Watching your kids grow up and feeling the days blur together, realizing you're already halfway through their childhood. Scrolling through years of photos and realizing you've been so focused on the future that you barely noticed the present. Facing a health scare that forces you to think about mortality and wonder if you've wasted time on things that don't matter. Comparing your progress to others and feeling behind, as if you need twice as long to catch up.
meaning_fields.teaching: The actual duration of your life—whether you live 30 years or 100—doesn't change what you face or what matters. What you see and experience in three years is the same essential human reality you'd see in a century. The length of time you have isn't what determines whether your life is wasted or well-lived; the clarity of your attention to what's in front of you is.
meaning_fields.emotions: Dread about running out of time, urgency that you're falling behind, anxiety about death and impermanence, frustration that your lifespan feels unfairly short compared to others, desperation to fit everything in before it's too late
meaning_fields.concepts: Memento mori (remembering that you will die) and the Stoic view that external length of life is not a real good—only virtue and clear judgment are. The transience of all things (impermanence), and the Stoic paradox that a life well-lived can be complete even if it's cut short.

translation: If he have sinned, his is the harm, not mine. But perchance he hath not.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Someone cuts you off in traffic and you're furious; a friend doesn't return your text and you assume they're mad at you; your boss makes a critical comment and you ruminate about what you did wrong; a family member says something hurtful and you replay it for hours wondering if you deserve it; someone spreads a rumor about you and you're consumed by anger at the injustice.
meaning_fields.teaching: When someone wrongs you, the damage they suffer is theirs to carry, not yours. But more importantly—you don't even know for certain that they actually wronged you. Stop assuming the worst interpretation. You're torturing yourself with a story you've invented.
meaning_fields.emotions: Resentment, anger at being wronged, the urge to punish someone mentally, the pain of feeling victimized, the sting of believing someone did something deliberately cruel to you.
meaning_fields.concepts: Just desserts (the Stoic belief that wrongdoing naturally harms the wrongdoer's character); the limits of your control (prohairesis—only your judgments and intentions are truly yours); the danger of presumption (we almost always get other people's motives wrong).

translation: Either all things by the providence of reason happen unto every particular, as a part of one general body; and then it is against reason that a part should complain of anything that happens for the good of the whole; or if, according to Epicurus, atoms be the cause of all things and that life be nothing else but an accidentary confusion of things, and death nothing else, but a mere dispersion and so of all other things: what doest thou trouble thyself for?
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: When something goes wrong, you face a choice: either accept that everything serves a larger order you're part of, or believe the universe is random atoms colliding with no purpose. Either way, complaining doesn't fix anything. Pick one view and stop torturing yourself with resentment.
meaning_fields.emotions: Resentment at unfair situations; anxiety about whether life has meaning; the grinding frustration of replaying what went wrong; helplessness when you can't control outcomes; fear that suffering is pointless
meaning_fields.situations: You get passed over for a promotion and spend weeks angry about it being "unfair"; a health scare happens and you can't stop asking "why me?"; a relationship ends and you obsess over what you did wrong; someone treats you badly and you keep imagining confrontations; a project fails despite your effort and you feel victimized by circumstance
meaning_fields.concepts: Providence (the idea that events serve a rational cosmic order); determinism versus randomness; the nature of the good (bonum); the Stoic view that complaining violates reason; Epicureanism (mentioned as a contrast—the view that atoms and chance, not order, govern reality); the part and the whole (a fundamental Stoic image: you are a cell in a body)

translation: Sayest thou unto that rational part, Thou art dead; corruption hath taken hold on thee? Doth it then also void excrements? Doth it like either oxen, or sheep, graze or feed; that it also should be mortal, as well as the body?
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: Your rational mind—your capacity to think, judge, and reason—doesn't decay like your body does. When your body fails and breaks down, your ability to understand truth and act with integrity remains intact. Degradation of the flesh doesn't touch the core of who you are as a thinking being.
meaning_fields.emotions: Fear that aging or illness has broken your mind; worry that physical weakness means you've lost your ability to think clearly; dread that decline robs you of what makes you yourself; shame about bodily deterioration
meaning_fields.situations: Recovering from a serious illness and wondering if you're still capable of making good decisions; watching your parents age and losing physical ability while remaining sharp mentally; facing your own mortality and fearing dementia more than death itself; going through chemotherapy or chronic pain and feeling disconnected from your body but noticing your judgment is still sound; sitting in a hospital bed, immobilized, but your mind is working perfectly fine
meaning_fields.concepts: The distinction between the rational faculty (logos) and the body (soma); the immortal versus the perishable; the Stoic belief that your essential self is the capacity for reasoned judgment, not flesh; the idea that virtue and character operate independently of physical condition

translation: Either the Gods can do nothing for us at all, or they can still and allay all the distractions and distempers of thy mind. If they can do nothing, why doest thou pray? If they can, why wouldst not thou rather pray, that they will grant unto thee, that thou mayst neither fear, nor lust after any of those worldly things which cause these distractions and distempers of it? Why not rather, that thou mayst not at either their absence or presence, be grieved and discontented: than either that thou mayst obtain them, or that thou mayst avoid them? For certainly it must needs be, that if the Gods can help us in anything, they may in this kind also. But thou wilt say perchance, 'In those things the Gods have given me my liberty: and it is in mine own power to do what I will.' But if thou mayst use this liberty, rather to set thy mind at true liberty, than wilfully with baseness and servility of mind to affect those things, which either to compass or to avoid is not in thy power, wert not thou better? And as for the Gods, who hath told thee, that they may not help us up even in those things that they have put in our own power? whether it be so or no, thou shalt soon perceive, if thou wilt but try thyself and pray. One prayeth that he may compass his desire, to lie with such or such a one, pray thou that thou mayst not lust to lie with her. Another how he may be rid of such a one; pray thou that thou mayst so patiently bear with him, as that thou have no such need to be rid of him. Another, that he may not lose his child. Pray thou that thou mayst not fear to lose him. To this end and purpose, let all thy prayer be, and see what will be the event.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Your boss denies you a promotion you were counting on, and you catch yourself obsessing over it for weeks. You see someone attractive and feel the pull of desire, then guilt, then try to suppress it. A friend disappoints you repeatedly and you keep fantasizing about cutting them out entirely. Your child is sick and you lie awake terrified something will happen to them. You want something badly—a relationship, a job, a purchase—and your whole peace of mind hinges on getting it.
meaning_fields.teaching: Stop praying for different outcomes in the world. Pray instead to not want the wrong things, and to not suffer when you don't get them. The real freedom isn't getting what you desire—it's not being enslaved to the desire itself. You have power over your own mind and what you choose to care about; use that power instead of wasting it chasing things outside your control.
meaning_fields.emotions: Craving and frustration when you can't have something. Dread about losing what matters to you. The grinding anxiety of wanting external circumstances to be different. Shame about your own desires. The helplessness of chasing things you can't control and feeling controlled by them.
meaning_fields.concepts: Voluntary servitude (choosing to be enslaved by desires and fears). Liberty of mind versus liberty of circumstance (freedom of thought and will versus control over external events). Lust as a disorder of judgment. The distinction between what is "up to us" (our choices, values, and mental states) and what is not (outcomes, other people's actions, possession of things).

translation: 'In my sickness' (saith Epicurus of himself:) 'my discourses were not concerning the nature of my disease, neither was that, to them that came to visit me, the subject of my talk; but in the consideration and contemplation of that, which was of especial weight and moment, was all my time bestowed and spent, and among others in this very thing, how my mind, by a natural and unavoidable sympathy partaking in some sort with the present indisposition of my body, might nevertheless keep herself free from trouble, and in present possession of her own proper happiness. Neither did I leave the ordering of my body to the physicians altogether to do with me what they would, as though I expected any great matter from them, or as though I thought it a matter of such great consequence, by their means to recover my health: for my present estate, methought, liked me very well, and gave me good content.' Whether therefore in sickness (if thou chance to sicken) or in what other kind of extremity soever, endeavour thou also to be in thy mind so affected, as he doth report of himself: not to depart from thy philosophy for anything that can befall thee, nor to give ear to the discourses of silly people, and mere naturalists.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.teaching: When you're sick or facing hardship, your mind can stay calm and content even while your body suffers—if you refuse to obsess over the problem and instead focus on what matters. You don't need to surrender control to experts or expect rescue from outside; the real work is keeping your thinking steady.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety during illness or crisis; feeling helpless or dependent; the urge to catastrophize; worry that your suffering means something is deeply wrong; frustration at not being able to control outcomes; resentment of being told what to do by authorities.
meaning_fields.situations: You have a diagnosis and keep googling worst-case scenarios instead of living your actual day; you're injured or chronically ill and everyone around you treats you as fragile or broken; you're in financial trouble and keep rehashing it with anyone who listens; you're waiting for test results and can't stop spiraling; a therapist or doctor tells you what's wrong with you and you feel like your whole life is now defined by that label.
meaning_fields.concepts: The dichotomy of control—what is and isn't up to you. The body-mind relationship: your body's state (pathos) naturally affects your mind, but your mind retains the power to remain untroubled (ataraxia) by not feeding the suffering with obsessive thought. Logos—the rational principle that keeps you oriented toward what actually matters rather than what merely feels urgent.

translation: It is common to all trades and professions to mind and intend that only, which now they are about, and the instrument whereby they work.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: A parent trying to cook dinner but checking their phone every few seconds. A surgeon during an operation thinking about their personal problems. A student in an exam worrying about their grade instead of focusing on the question in front of them. An employee in a meeting mentally rehearsing a difficult conversation they need to have later. A craftsperson trying to do repairs while their mind keeps drifting to something that upset them earlier.
meaning_fields.teaching: Whatever you're doing right now deserves your full attention—your mind and your tools. The moment you're in requires everything you have. Mastery in any field, from medicine to cooking to repair work, comes from this single-minded focus. When your attention splits, the quality of what you're doing splits with it.
meaning_fields.emotions: Distraction and frustration when your mind won't stay in the present. Guilt about not being fully there for what matters. The pull of competing worries that steal focus. Restlessness when you can't settle into what's in front of you.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prosoche (attention or mindfulness applied to your present task). The idea that virtue and excellence emerge through complete engagement with the work at hand, not through wandering attention. This reflects the Stoic belief that you cannot control outcomes, only the quality of your focus and effort in this moment.

translation: When at any time thou art offended with any one's impudency, put presently this question to thyself: 'What? Is it then possible, that there should not be any impudent men in the world! Certainly it is not possible.' Desire not then that which is impossible. For this one, (thou must think) whosoever he be, is one of those impudent ones, that the world cannot be without. So of the subtile and crafty, so of the perfidious, so of every one that offendeth, must thou ever be ready to reason with thyself. For whilst in general thou dost thus reason with thyself, that the kind of them must needs be in the world, thou wilt be the better able to use meekness towards every particular. This also thou shalt find of very good use, upon every such occasion, presently to consider with thyself, what proper virtue nature hath furnished man with, against such a vice, or to encounter with a disposition vicious in this kind. As for example, against the unthankful, it hath given goodness and meekness, as an antidote, and so against another vicious in another kind some other peculiar faculty. And generally, is it not in thy power to instruct him better, that is in an error? For whosoever sinneth, doth in that decline from his purposed end, and is certainly deceived, And again, what art thou the worse for his sin? For thou shalt not find that any one of these, against whom thou art incensed, hath in very deed done anything whereby thy mind (the only true subject of thy hurt and evil) can be made worse than it was. And what a matter of either grief or wonder is this, if he that is unlearned, do the deeds of one that is unlearned? Should not thou rather blame thyself, who, when upon very good grounds of reason, thou mightst have thought it very probable, that such a thing would by such a one be committed, didst not only not foresee it, but moreover dost wonder at it, that such a thing should be. But then especially, when thou dost find fault with either an unthankful, or a false man, must thou reflect upon thyself. For without all question, thou thyself art much in fault, if either of one that were of such a disposition, thou didst expect that he should be true unto thee: or when unto any thou didst a good turn, thou didst not there bound thy thoughts, as one that had obtained his end; nor didst not think that from the action itself thou hadst received a full reward of the good that thou hadst done. For what wouldst thou have more? Unto him that is a man, thou hast done a good turn: doth not that suffice thee? What thy nature required, that hast thou done. Must thou be rewarded for it? As if either the eye for that it seeth, or the feet that they go, should require satisfaction. For as these being by nature appointed for such an use, can challenge no more, than that they may work according to their natural constitution: so man being born to do good unto others whensoever he doth a real good unto any by helping them out of error; or though but in middle things, as in matter of wealth, life, preferment, and the like, doth help to further their desires he doth that for which he was made, and therefore can require no more.
book_theme: justice, truthfulness, and dying without complaint

meaning_fields.situations: Someone lies to you or betrays your trust and you can't stop replaying it in your head. A coworker is ungrateful for work you did for them and acts coldly toward you. You do someone a favor expecting they'll remember it or return it, and they don't. You encounter dishonest or manipulative people and feel outraged that they exist. You help someone improve their life—loan them money, give them advice, connect them to an opportunity—and they don't acknowledge it or seem to care.
meaning_fields.teaching: People who lie, betray, or act ungratefully aren't aberrations—they're inevitable parts of how the world works. Your anger at them doesn't hurt them; it only damages your own mind. When someone wrongs you, your only real injury is internal, and that's entirely under your control. The real mistake is expecting people to act differently than their nature or conditioning has made them act—that's like blaming your eyes for seeing or your feet for walking. Do good because it's what humans are made for, not because you expect payment or gratitude in return.
meaning_fields.emotions: Indignation at betrayal or dishonesty, hurt from ingratitude, resentment when favors go unacknowledged, wounded pride after being cheated, frustration with people who seem hardwired to deceive or manipulate.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature and natural function (humans are designed to help others just as eyes are designed to see). The distinction between what's in your control and what isn't (other people's character and choices are not your business). Virtue as antidote (you have the capacity for kindness and patience built into your nature as a counter to others' vices). The true nature of harm (only your mind can be harmed; external events and others' actions cannot damage your character unless you let them).

translation: O my soul, the time I trust will be, when thou shalt be good, simple, single, more open and visible, than that body by which it is enclosed. Thou wilt one day be sensible of their happiness, whose end is love, and their affections dead to all worldly things. Thou shalt one day be full, and in want of no external thing: not seeking pleasure from anything, either living or insensible, that this world can afford; neither wanting time for the continuation of thy pleasure, nor place and opportunity, nor the favour either of the weather or of men. When thou shalt have content in thy present estate, and all things present shall add to thy content: when thou shalt persuade thyself, that thou hast all things; all for thy good, and all by the providence of the Gods: and of things future also shalt be as confident, that all will do well, as tending to the maintenance and preservation in some sort, of his perfect welfare and happiness, who is perfection of life, of goodness, and beauty; who begets all things, and containeth all things in himself, and in himself doth recollect all things from all places that are dissolved, that of them he may beget others again like unto them. Such one day shall be thy disposition, that thou shalt be able, both in regard of the Gods, and in regard of men, so to fit and order thy conversation, as neither to complain of them at any time, for anything that they do; nor to do anything thyself, for which thou mayest justly be condemned.
book_theme: simplicity, wholeness, and seeing things as they actually are

meaning_fields.situations: You're scrolling through social media seeing other people's curated highlights and feel like your life is missing something. A friend gets a promotion you wanted and you find yourself wanting things to prove your worth. You're sitting at home on a rainy Saturday with no plans and feel restless, like you should be doing something more. You catch yourself constantly checking your phone for messages or validation from others. You realize you've been chasing experiences or possessions thinking they'll finally make you feel complete.
meaning_fields.teaching: You can reach a state where you stop constantly reaching for what's missing and start recognizing what you already have is enough. This happens when you stop blaming circumstances or other people for your satisfaction, and stop doing things you'd regret. True freedom comes from wanting what you actually have, trusting that life is working toward your genuine wellbeing, and conducting yourself so cleanly that you have no reason to complain or feel ashamed.
meaning_fields.emotions: Restlessness and the gnawing sense that something is missing. Envy when seeing others have things you want. Resentment toward people or circumstances you blame for your dissatisfaction. The anxiety of needing external approval or validation. The quiet shame of knowing you've acted in ways you regret. Relief and stillness when you stop fighting reality.
meaning_fields.concepts: Apatheia (freedom from destructive desires). Ataraxia (tranquility through acceptance). Premeditatio malorum (seeing clearly what you can and cannot control). Amor fati (loving what actually is rather than what you wish for). Oikeiosis (recognizing your place in a rational whole). Prosoche (attention to your own choices and character).

translation: As one who is altogether governed by nature, let it be thy care to observe what it is that thy nature in general doth require. That done, if thou find not that thy nature, as thou art a living sensible creature, will be the worse for it, thou mayest proceed. Next then thou must examine, what thy nature as thou art a living sensible creature, doth require. And that, whatsoever it be, thou mayest admit of and do it, if thy nature as thou art a reasonable living creature, will not be the worse for it. Now whatsoever is reasonable, is also sociable, Keep thyself to these rules, and trouble not thyself about idle things.
book_theme: simplicity, wholeness, and seeing things as they actually are

meaning_fields.teaching: Work through your decisions in layers: first, what does my basic survival need? Then, what does my body need as a living creature? Finally, what does my mind and reason say about this? If something passes all three checks—if it doesn't harm you physically, mentally, or your ability to live with others—then it's worth doing. Everything else is just noise.
meaning_fields.emotions: The frustration of being pulled in too many directions; the paralysis of overthinking small choices; anxiety that you're missing something important; the relief of having a clear filter for what actually matters
meaning_fields.situations: You're scrolling social media for an hour and wonder if it's hurting you—checking it against: does it harm my sleep? Does it make me anxious? Does it damage how I relate to people? Deciding whether to take a job that pays well but requires being dishonest with clients. Wondering whether to go to every social event you're invited to, or skip some to rest. Standing in the grocery store, torn between two purchases and not knowing which one is "right." Feeling guilty about basic needs like rest or exercise because you think you should be doing something more productive.
meaning_fields.concepts: Nature (physis)—the underlying order of reality that includes your body, mind, and social bonds. Reason (logos)—the human capacity to think and live deliberately. Indifference (adiaphora)—things that don't ultimately matter to virtue or your flourishing. The three layers of your nature: the universal (being part of existence), the animal (needing food and rest), and the rational (needing to think clearly and connect with others).

translation: Whatsoever doth happen unto thee, thou art naturally by thy natural constitution either able, or not able to bear. If thou beest able, be not offended, but bear it according to thy natural constitution, or as nature hath enabled thee. If thou beest not able, be not offended. For it will soon make an end of thee, and itself, (whatsoever it be) at the same time end with thee. But remember, that whatsoever by the strength of opinion, grounded upon a certain apprehension of both true profit and duty, thou canst conceive tolerable; that thou art able to bear that by thy natural constitution.
book_theme: simplicity, wholeness, and seeing things as they actually are

meaning_fields.teaching: You have a real capacity built into you—test what you can actually handle by looking at what your mind genuinely believes is right and worthwhile to endure. If you can bear something through reason, you already have the strength for it; if you truly cannot, it will pass quickly anyway. Stop pretending difficulty is your problem when lack of conviction is.
meaning_fields.emotions: Shame about struggling, doubt about your own toughness, frustration when you tell yourself you should handle something but don't, relief when you stop fighting what's actually too much, quiet confidence when you choose to endure something you truly believe in.
meaning_fields.situations: You're facing a painful medical procedure and keep telling yourself you're weak for being afraid, when really you haven't decided if it's worth the suffering. Your job is demanding and draining—you resent yourself for complaining, but you haven't actually convinced yourself the work matters enough to justify the cost. A relationship requires hard conversations; you avoid them, then hate yourself for avoiding, without ever settling whether the relationship is worth the discomfort. You're training for something difficult and quit halfway, then wonder if you're just lazy—but you never actually believed in the goal. A family obligation is exhausting you; instead of accepting you can't do it, you torture yourself trying, resentful and depleted.
meaning_fields.concepts: Natural capacity (what you're actually built to do, not what you imagine you should do). Opinion grounded in reason (when you genuinely believe something serves your real duty and good, not when you shame yourself into endurance). The difference between physical limit and mental conviction—stoic philosophy teaches that suffering you accept through rational judgment becomes bearable, while suffering you resist or half-believe in will destroy you.

text_for_embedding:
You're facing a painful medical procedure and keep telling yourself you're weak for being afraid, when really you haven't decided if it's worth the suffering. Your job is demanding and draining—you resent yourself for complaining, but you haven't actually convinced yourself the work matters enough to justify the cost. A relationship requires hard conversations; you avoid them, then hate yourself for avoiding, without ever settling whether the relationship is worth the discomfort. You're training for something difficult and quit halfway, then wonder if you're just lazy—but you never actually believed in the goal. A family obligation is exhausting you; instead of accepting you can't do it, you torture yourself trying, resentful and depleted.
You have a real capacity built into you—test what you can actually handle by looking at what your mind genuinely believes is right and worthwhile to endure. If you can bear something through reason, you already have the strength for it; if you truly cannot, it will pass quickly anyway. Stop pretending difficulty is your problem when lack of conviction is.
Shame about struggling, doubt about your own toughness, frustration when you tell yourself you should handle something but don't, relief when you stop fighting what's actually too much, quiet confidence when you choose to endure something you truly believe in.
Natural capacity (what you're actually built to do, not what you imagine you should do). Opinion grounded in reason (when you genuinely believe something serves your real duty and good, not when you shame yourself into endurance). The difference between physical limit and mental conviction—stoic philosophy teaches that suffering you accept through rational judgment becomes bearable, while suffering you resist or half-believe in will destroy you.

translation: Him that offends, to teach with love and meek ness, and to show him his error. But if thou canst not, then to blame thyself; or rather not thyself neither, if thy will and endeavours have not been wanting.
book_theme: simplicity, wholeness, and seeing things as they actually are

meaning_fields.situations: You try to give constructive feedback to someone who hurt you—a friend who broke a promise, a family member who said something harsh, a coworker who made a mistake—and they get defensive or dismiss you. You're left wondering if you should have said something differently, or whether it's even your job to help them see what they did. You replay the conversation thinking maybe you weren't kind enough, or maybe you explained it wrong. Someone acts wrongly toward you repeatedly, and you debate internally whether to keep trying to reach them or just accept that some people won't change.
meaning_fields.teaching: When someone wrongs you, your responsibility is to try—with genuine kindness and gentleness—to show them their mistake. But your responsibility ends there. If they won't listen or change, you're not to blame if you tried with a sincere heart and real effort. Don't torture yourself over outcomes you cannot control.
meaning_fields.emotions: Frustration when someone won't listen or take feedback; doubt about whether you handled a difficult conversation right; the weight of trying to fix someone else; guilt when your attempts fail; helplessness in the face of someone's stubbornness; the relief of realizing you actually did your part.
meaning_fields.concepts: Prohairesis (what is within your power)—your intent, effort, and kindness are yours; the other person's response is not. The boundary between your responsibility and theirs. Oikeiosis (appropriate action)—you are called to correct with love, not force. Amor fati (acceptance of what lies outside your control)—their obstinacy, their refusal to change.
