translation: What doest thou desire? To live long. What? To enjoy the operations of a sensitive soul; or of the appetitive faculty? or wouldst thou grow, and then decrease again? Wouldst thou long be able to talk, to think and reason with thyself? Which of all these seems unto thee a worthy object of thy desire? Now if of all these thou doest find that they be but little worth in themselves, proceed on unto the last, which is, in all things to follow God and reason. But for a man to grieve that by death he shall be deprived of any of these things, is both against God and reason.
book_theme: the final accounting — living the remainder well, letting go

meaning_fields.situations: You're scared of getting older and losing your mental sharpness, worried you won't be able to think clearly someday. You catch yourself wanting to live as long as possible, but then realize you're not sure why—what's the point if your body just decays and your mind eventually goes. You're facing a health scare or watching a parent age, and it hits you that the things you thought made life worth living (staying sharp, being useful, having energy) all fade anyway.
meaning_fields.teaching: Stop asking "how long can I live?" and start asking "what am I trying to do with this life?" When you examine what you actually value—physical sensation, appetite, strength, thinking—you'll see none of them last or satisfy. The only thing worth wanting is to align yourself with reason and what's actually good. Fearing death for taking these away is foolish; it's like grieving that a temporary rental ends.
meaning_fields.emotions: Fear of aging and decline, dread of losing mental ability, anxiety about mortality, the hollow feeling when you realize chasing longevity has no real purpose, resignation mixed with relief when you accept what you can't control
meaning_fields.concepts: The difference between living long and living well (a central Stoic distinction); the nature of what's genuinely valuable versus what merely appears desirable; the logos or rational principle that orders the universe and should order your will; the cosmological view that seeing yourself as temporary and part of nature is acceptance, not defeat

translation: What a small portion of vast and infinite eternity it is, that is allowed unto every one of us, and how soon it vanisheth into the general age of the world: of the common substance, and of the common soul also what a small portion is allotted unto us: and in what a little clod of the whole earth (as it were) it is that thou doest crawl. After thou shalt rightly have considered these things with thyself; fancy not anything else in the world any more to be of any weight and moment but this, to do that only which thine own nature doth require; and to conform thyself to that which the common nature doth afford.
book_theme: the final accounting — living the remainder well, letting go

meaning_fields.situations: You're spending weeks perfecting something at work that no one will remember in a year. You're upset about a social slight and can't let it go. You're grinding toward a promotion that suddenly feels hollow. You're worried about your reputation or legacy after you're gone. You're caught up in proving yourself in front of people who won't matter to you in five years.
meaning_fields.teaching: Your life is a tiny flash in an enormous stretch of time, and you occupy an infinitesimal speck of the world. Once you truly feel the weight of that reality, stop chasing things that don't matter. Focus only on what your nature actually requires and what the world genuinely offers—nothing else deserves your attention.
meaning_fields.emotions: Insignificance, relief from pressure, smallness, a kind of peaceful unimportance, being cut loose from needing to matter, the vertigo of seeing how little time you have, freedom from comparison
meaning_fields.concepts: Perspective (seeing yourself against the scale of time and space), acceptance of human limitation (recognizing you are not the center), living according to nature (aligning your actions with what is genuinely required rather than what your ego wants), the cosmic view (stepping back to see your life from the vantage point of eternity)

translation: What is the present estate of my understanding? For herein lieth all indeed. As for all other things, they are without the compass of mine own will: and if without the compass of my will, then are they as dead things unto me, and as it were mere smoke.
book_theme: the final accounting — living the remainder well, letting go

meaning_fields.situations: You're stuck worrying about a job interview result you can't control and it's eating up your mental energy. Your adult child makes life choices you disagree with, and you keep cycling through anger and disappointment. You're diagnosed with a health condition and spending hours researching worst-case scenarios. Your business partner makes a decision that might hurt the company, and you can't do anything to stop it. Someone publicly criticized your work and you can't shake the replay of it in your head.
meaning_fields.teaching: The only thing actually in your control is what you think and decide right now. Everything else—other people's choices, outcomes, circumstances—is fundamentally outside your power, so treating it as though you can control it is futile and exhausting. Stop pouring your mental energy into things that are already dead to you because they were never yours to begin with.
meaning_fields.emotions: Anxiety about things you can't change, frustration at your own powerlessness, obsessive replaying of events, the mental exhaustion of trying to prevent the unpreventable, relief when you finally accept what's not your responsibility.
meaning_fields.concepts: Will and control (prohairesis)—the Stoic distinction between what is "up to us" (your judgments, intentions, and responses) and what is not (outcomes, other people's actions, external events). Indifference to externals (adiaphora)—not that external things don't matter morally, but that your peace of mind should never depend on controlling them. The concept of things being "as smoke" suggests the illusory solidity we grant to things we cannot actually grip or change.

translation: To stir up a man to the contempt of death this among other things, is of good power and efficacy, that even they who esteemed pleasure to be happiness, and pain misery, did nevertheless many of them contemn death as much as any. And can death be terrible to him, to whom that only seems good, which in the ordinary course of nature is seasonable? to him, to whom, whether his actions be many or few, so they be all good, is all one; and who whether he behold the things of the world being always the same either for many years, or for few years only, is altogether indifferent? O man! as a citizen thou hast lived, and conversed in this great city the world. Whether just for so many years, or no, what is it unto thee? Thou hast lived (thou mayest be sure) as long as the laws and orders of the city required; which may be the common comfort of all. Why then should it be grievous unto thee, if (not a tyrant, nor an unjust judge, but) the same nature that brought thee in, doth now send thee out of the world? As if the praetor should fairly dismiss him from the stage, whom he had taken in to act a while. Oh, but the play is not yet at an end, there are but three acts yet acted of it? Thou hast well said: for in matter of life, three acts is the whole play. Now to set a certain time to every man's acting, belongs unto him only, who as first he was of thy composition, so is now the cause of thy dissolution. As for thyself; thou hast to do with neither. Go thy ways then well pleased and contented: for so is He that dismisseth thee.
book_theme: the final accounting — living the remainder well, letting go

meaning_fields.situations: A person in their 60s or 70s, still healthy but aware of mortality, wondering if they've done enough with their life or if they should keep pushing for more accomplishments. Someone facing a terminal diagnosis who feels robbed because they had plans for the next decade. A middle-aged person realizing they'll never achieve all their earlier ambitions and feeling the weight of unfinished business. A retiree struggling to find meaning after stopping work, feeling like life should still have more acts to play. Someone at any age asking "how much longer do I really have, and does it matter if I got cut short?"
meaning_fields.teaching: You've already lived a full life by showing up and doing good work, however many years that turned out to be. The number of years or accomplishments doesn't measure whether you've done enough—what matters is whether your actions were good. Death isn't terrible because it's the same natural process that brought you into existence; fighting its timing only adds suffering to what's simply the stage being cleared for the next actor.
meaning_fields.emotions: Dread about running out of time, regret over incomplete plans, the pressure to justify your existence by measuring what you've done, fear that an early death means your life was wasted, frustration that you can't control how long you get to play your part, a stubborn resistance to accepting limits
meaning_fields.concepts: The natural order (accepting what belongs to nature versus what belongs to you): Marcus distinguishes between what you control—the quality of your actions—and what you don't—the length of your life or when you exit. Cosmic citizenship (living as part of a larger whole): you're a member of the world-city with obligations that are finite, not infinite. The actor and the stage (your role is temporary by design): life is a play with natural length, not a debt you owe that requires proving yourself through endless accumulation.
